2026-11-10: Scott's approved core bug fixes (camera validate-before-publish, outward-rounded bounds, restore budget) took core from 21,828 B to 22,031 B and core + stage from 24,432 B to 24,630 B; 2026-11-10: bundling the shared helpers measures core at 21,828 B and core + stage at 24,432 B; 2026-11-09: core uploads the unit light direction so no shader normalizes that uniform-only value, core 21,553 B to 21,584 B and core + stage 23,924 B to 23,950 B; 2026-11-07: `CADCameraControls` moved to the stage, core 21,586 B to 20,672 B and core + stage 23,013 B to 23,016 B; stable instance rows with changed-row uploads then added 382 B and `Engine.writePoses` 231 B, so core + stage was 23,626 B; CSP diagnostics then added 171 B, taking it to 23,837 B); the 2026-10-30 core cleanup, which removed the view target depth copy pass, `mesh.euler` and four small duplicates, took core from 21,176 B to 20,790 B and core + stage from 22,580 B to 22,189 B; storing a caller's 4x view target depth then added 23 B to each, a package's frame in one render pass 293 B to core + stage, and `Engine.renderTarget` 44 B), and every
other capability is an optional package. That size is a decision, and so are the boundaries below. Each one exists
for one of two reasons: it keeps core small and frozen, or it follows the limits WebGPU guarantees on every adapter
(Margo's device requests none above them, so an app that runs on a laptop also runs on a phone). This page lists every
hard limit, where it starts, what you see when you reach it, and the package or tool that takes you past it.

How to read "Starts at":

- **Enforced**: an exact constant in the source (linked), usually with the test that asserts it.
- **Measured**: a committed result file (linked). Unless a row says otherwise: ASUS Zenbook S 14, Intel Core Ultra 7
  258V with an Intel Arc 140V integrated GPU, Windows 11, Edge 155, AC power.
- **Not measured**: the boundary exists, but nobody has run the case. No number is given.

Every number here has a row in [whitepaper/claims.md](whitepaper/claims.md) (LIM-001 to LIM-682). Past losses and their
fixes are in [whitepaper/perf-history.md](whitepaper/perf-history.md).

## Scale

| Limit | Starts at | Why | What you see | Escape hatch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Entities (core meshes, assembly nodes included) | Enforced: 8,388,608 slots (2^23; [kernel.ts](../packages/core/src/kernel.ts), [core-dirty-transforms.test.js](../tests/core-dirty-transforms.test.js)). The store starts at `capacity` (default 1,024) and doubles on demand. Measured ([results-scale-node.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/parts/results-scale-node.json), Node 24, quiet-gated): 352.1 B of kernel memory per slot at 1,048,576 slots (351 B by layout); a static kernel tick costs 3.3 ms at 100,006 entities, 20.2 ms at 499,992 and 41.5 ms at 1,000,012. Above 1,048,576 slots: not measured. | One float32 structure-of-arrays Wasm kernel computes every transform, bound and visibility. It is the reason core is small and fast, and its per-entity cost is linear: about 41 ns per entity per frame even when nothing moves. | Growth is automatic. Past the cap `createMesh` throws `RangeError: Capacity`; `Engine.create` with a larger `capacity` throws `RangeError: Capacity: 1..8388608`. A growth that cannot allocate throws and leaves the store as it was. Before the cap, frame time grows with entity count. | `@margoengine/culling`. `CulledInstances` keeps parts out of the entity store entirely: 0.41-0.55 ms CPU per frame at 89,883 parts, flat in part count ([results-culling.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/parts/results-culling.json)); parts lose picking, hierarchy and section caps. `CulledMeshes` GPU-culls parts that must stay core meshes; it removes GPU work, not the kernel tick. |
| Nodes and parts per file in packages | Enforced, default 100,000 ([limits.js](../packages/shared/limits.js), [count-limits.test.js](../tests/count-limits.test.js)): glTF nodes ([gltf](../packages/gltf/src/index.ts), [gltf/pbr asset.ts](../packages/gltf/src/asset.ts)), `.margo` nodes ([blender](../packages/blender/src/index.ts)). | Input validation that bounds memory for untrusted files: every node or part becomes a core mesh. | `RangeError: Too many glTF nodes (100001 > 100000; raise the maxNodes option)`; likewise `Too many .margo nodes` (`maxNodes`). | The option the error names, up to core's 8,388,608 entities: `maxNodes` on the glTF, gltf/pbr and `.margo` loaders; a value outside 1 to 8,388,608 throws `maxNodes must be an integer from 1 to 8388608`. Load time and memory past 100,000: not measured. |
| Buffers per geometry | Enforced: a geometry's vertex, index and instance buffers (96 B per instance) must each fit the device's `maxBufferSize`. Since 2026-11-10 core asks `requestDevice` for the adapter's own `maxBufferSize` and `maxStorageBufferBindingSize` (and `maxTextureArrayLayers`), at creation and on every device restore, so a desktop GPU that offers more than WebGPU's 256 MiB / 128 MiB defaults gets it ([renderer.ts](../packages/core/src/renderer.ts), [core-timestamp-feature.test.js](../tests/core-timestamp-feature.test.js), [scale.browser.mjs](../packages/core/tests/scale.browser.mjs)). Work per frame unchanged: the request runs once per device. Core's own draws and picks bind a geometry's instance rows as a vertex buffer (`setVertexBuffer`), never as a storage binding, so only `maxBufferSize` bounds them. The buffer grows to (meshes + 1) x 2 rows, so one geometry takes up to 2,097,150 meshes on a default 256 MiB device (the next size, 4,194,302 rows, is 402 MB); on the RTX A6000's 2 GiB the entity cap of 8,388,608 comes first. Proved with 1,200,000 instances of one geometry (a 201 MB buffer, past one 128 MiB binding) drawing the same pixels as two geometries of 600,000, natively and on the WebGL2 layer, before and after this change ([scale.browser.mjs](../packages/core/tests/scale.browser.mjs)). A package that binds core's instance buffer as storage must bind only the rows it uses (`CulledMeshes` does since 2026-11-10). | WebGPU's defaults are the floor every adapter meets; asking for what the adapter offers costs nothing per frame and lets the same scene use a large GPU's memory. A scene sized past the defaults then needs that adapter: check `engine.gpu.limits`. | `RangeError: GPU buffer limit` when the geometry is first drawn. | Split the geometry, or draw the copies with `CulledInstances`. |
| Instance rows after culling flips (2026-11-07) | By method: a mesh that culling or `visible` shows takes its batch's next row and one hidden gives its row to the batch's last, so row order inside a batch, and with it draw order among one geometry's instances, follows the order of flips. Proved exact as a set, row for row and in the uploaded GPU rows on 200 random frames of flips and moves ([core-instance-cache.test.js](../tests/core-instance-cache.test.js)) | A one-bit change costs one row (2 map lookups, 24 floats, 96 uploaded bytes), not a full collection and a full upload | Two core meshes of one geometry at exactly the same depth may swap which one shows after a flip. Several cameras on one scene flip most rows and cost what a full collection costs. The WebGL2 renderer still uploads every row each frame | Give coincident surfaces a small offset or separate geometries |
| Backbuffer size per side (2026-11-10) | Enforced ([engine.ts](../packages/core/src/engine.ts), [backbuffer-cap.test.js](../packages/core/tests/backbuffer-cap.test.js), [scale.browser.mjs](../packages/core/tests/scale.browser.mjs)): the canvas's CSS size times the pixel ratio (at most 2, at most 4 / MSAA samples, and the quality tier's cap), then at most the device's `maxTextureDimension2D` per side, both sides scaled by one factor so the aspect holds. 8192 on a default WebGPU device and on the WebGL2 layer of an RTX A6000 (core asks for no more); 4096 for a fallback renderer with no WebGPU device. Before 2026-11-10 a fixed 4096 for every device. Measured on the RTX A6000: 5120 x 1440 kept natively and on the WebGL2 layer (4096 x 1152 before); 10240 x 16 becomes 8192 x 13. Work per frame for canvases under 4096 px a side: unchanged. | The canvas, MSAA and depth targets cannot be larger than the device's largest 2D texture; the pixel-ratio and MSAA caps keep a desktop canvas at its CSS pixels with 4x MSAA, so a normal window's frame cost does not change. | A canvas past the limit draws at the limit and is stretched by the browser; `canvas.width` and `canvas.height` show the size used. A 5120 x 1440 canvas now costs its 7.4 M pixels with 4x MSAA (1.56 times the old 4096 x 1152): frame time at that size is not measured (speed phase). | `exactSize` to choose the backing size yourself; `@margoengine/quality` `ResolutionScaler` to trade resolution for frame time. |
| Vertices per core `Geometry` (2026-11-10) | Enforced: 3 to 11,184,810 vertices, or none ([geometry.ts](../packages/core/src/geometry.ts), [vertex-cap.test.js](../packages/core/tests/vertex-cap.test.js)); 1,000,000 before. 11,184,810 is the most 24-byte vertices (position + normal, interleaved) one buffer of WebGPU's default 256 MiB `maxBufferSize` holds (268,435,440 B). The uint32 index buffer must fit `maxBufferSize` too: 67,108,864 indices (22,369,621 triangles) on a default device, more where the adapter offers more (see Buffers per geometry). Proved on an RTX A6000 natively and on the WebGL2 layer: a 1,212,201-vertex, 2,420,000-triangle plane draws every pixel with no validation error ([scale.browser.mjs](../packages/core/tests/scale.browser.mjs)). Frame time at the cap: not measured (speed phase). | One vertex buffer per geometry, sized to the limit every WebGPU device meets, so a geometry that loads draws on every device. Work per frame does not change with the cap; a bigger mesh costs its own vertices. | `RangeError: Invalid geometry` past 11,184,810 vertices; `RangeError: GPU buffer limit` when the index buffer passes the device's `maxBufferSize`. Packages with their own lower caps keep them (`@margoengine/loaders` `CORE_MAX_VERTICES`, `@margoengine/geometry/gpu`, gltf/pbr's 1,000,000 per primitive, the light glTF loader). | Split the mesh into several geometries. |
| Failed allocations in core (2026-11-07) | By method: `Engine.retain` makes the instance array and the GPU buffers before it changes anything, and `Renderer.add` frees old buffers only after the new ones exist. Covers what throws: the `GPU buffer limit` check, a failed CPU array, `@margoengine/webgl2-compat/preview`'s GL errors. Proved on a fake device with the real `Engine` and `GPURenderer` ([deep-core-allocation-failure.test.js](../tests/deep-core-allocation-failure.test.js)), and on a real destroyed device in `npm run test:lifecycle:browser` (LIM-330). A failed `rebootDevice` leaves the engine and the canvas on the device they had: the canvas moves last, proved on a real healthy device in the same suite | While a batch grows it holds both sets of buffers, about 1.5 times the new size at the peak. WebGPU reports a real out-of-memory from `createBuffer` asynchronously, not as a throw | A real out-of-memory from an allocation made outside an error scope is reported once (`failed`, help `gpu-lost`, "GPU out of memory") and core rebuilds the device as after a loss (2026-11-11, KB6434a): frames draw nothing until the restore finishes, then every batch and plugin is back | Size geometry to the device's `maxBufferSize`; retry a failed `setGeometry` after freeing memory |
| Failed allocations in packages (`CulledMeshes`, 2026-11-11, KB6434c) | By method: `CulledMeshes` makes its frame buffer, slot buffers and occlusion set inside `out-of-memory` and validation error scopes (`packages/shared/error-scope.js`) and uses each only once the device confirms it; on a device without error scopes (a CPU recorder) at once. A failure is reported once through `engine.onError` (`failed`, help `gpu-lost`) and holds until the next device restore, which tries again. Proved on a fake device ([culling alloc-failure.test.js](../packages/culling/test/alloc-failure.test.js)) and in a real browser, natively and on the WebGL2 layer, by `scripts/restore-fault-sweep.mjs` (every allocation of a restore failed in turn: reported once, no frame throws, the next frame draws the scene). | WebGPU reports a failed allocation only later; using the object before then is a validation error that core treats as a fault of every frame. | Confirmation takes a round trip to the GPU process: the first frames after an attach or a restore draw unculled (core draws every instance; frame buffer first, then each slot, so two frames), which looks the same. A slot's occluder lists are made inside its own check, and a new slot's instances all start as occluder candidates, so a geometry occludes from its first culled frame and a new one never holds the others' occlusion off (AMD GPU hunt R7 row 35, [culling occlusion-first-frame.test.js](../packages/culling/test/occlusion-first-frame.test.js)). Steady frames do the same work as before. Packages that make their resources outside error scopes rely on core's device rebuild (row above): `Shadows` and `VirtualShadows` do so on purpose, so the first frame after an attach, a restore or a new map size is shadowed (KB6434b, KB6434d, KB-C34g; [shadows alloc-failure.test.js](../packages/shadows/test/alloc-failure.test.js)). | None needed. |
| Automatic device restores in core (2026-11-10) | Enforced ([engine.ts](../packages/core/src/engine.ts), [restore-budget.test.js](../packages/core/tests/restore-budget.test.js)): core restores a lost device at most 3 times in a row; 120 drawn frames after a restore give the 3 back | A driver that resets again and again would otherwise hold the page in a restore loop, asking for a new device on every loss | A fourth loss within that run reports `MargoError` `failed` `GPU lost 4 times; reload the page` through `onError` once; core then asks for no new device and frames draw nothing | Reload the page, or call `engine.rebootDevice()` yourself once the cause is gone |
| Caller GPU objects across a device restore (2026-11-15, KB-RESTORE-BORROWED1) | By rule ([conventions.md](conventions.md#borrowed-gpu-objects), [borrowed.js](../packages/shared/borrowed.js), [borrowed.test.js](../tests/borrowed.test.js), [borrowed-gpu.test.js](../tests/borrowed-gpu.test.js)): a `GPUTexture`, view, sampler or buffer the caller made stays on the device that made it; Margo never destroys it or moves it. The packages listed `ruled` in `scripts/borrowed-registry.json` follow the rule; rows still `pending` keep their old behaviour (see docs/known-bugs.md) | WebGPU objects belong to one device and a lost device takes them with it; no API asks an object for its device | After a restore a plain object is dropped and reported once through `engine.onError` (`state`, help `borrowed-lost`); the frame keeps drawing without it (the part that needs it is skipped, a modulating map uses its default) | Pass `(device) => object`, called once per device, or hand in a new object through the option's setter |
| BatchedMesh item sort and shared geometry (`@margoengine/materials/batched`, 2026-11-27) | Enforced: stored geometries within `maxGeometryVertices` (3 to 1,000,000, default `maxVertices`); the sort keys up to the next power of two of the item slots used (at most 1,048,576). Checked by `packages/materials/test/batched-sort-browser.mjs` (sorted index order from both sides, blend equal to three sorted meshes, live sort modes, shared geometry) on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer. | A sort costs (log2 n)(log2 n + 1)/2 + log2 n + 3 compute dispatches and a copy of the used indices, only on a frame where the camera, an item or the order changed; a sorting batch holds three more index-sized buffers. | Each item of a shared geometry still draws its own posed vertex range (80 bytes per vertex per item): the stored copy, packing and its upload are shared, the drawn vertices are not. The order follows the frame graph's camera, so a second view in the same frame sees it. | `createInstancedMesh` for thousands of copies of one geometry; one batch per view where each view needs its own transparent order. |
| GPU curve flow (`@margoengine/materials/curve-flow`, 2026-11-27) | Enforced: a `CurveFlow` of 1 to 8,191 segments (2 to 8,192 frames, one texel column of an rgba32float texture each, WebGPU's guaranteed `maxTextureDimension2D`); `RangeError` past it. The GPU bend matches `CurveFlow.deform` pixel for pixel on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer (`packages/materials/test/curve-flow-browser.mjs`). | 64 bytes of texture per frame (16 KB at the default 256 segments), one plugin uniform block, eight texel loads per vertex in every pass that draws the mesh. | The vertex tangent is not bent (normal maps on a bent mesh shade as unbent); mesh `bounds`, CPU raycasts and exporters see the unbent mesh. | Use `CurveFlow.deform` on the CPU for normal-mapped or exported meshes; give a culled mesh bounds that cover the curve. |
| GPU instanced curve flow (`@margoengine/materials/instanced-curve-flow`, 2026-11-27) | Enforced: 1 to 2,048 curves (four rows of one rgba32float texture each, inside WebGPU's guaranteed `maxTextureDimension2D`), 2 to 8,192 frames a curve and 1 to 1,000,000 instance rows; `RangeError` past them. Every instance matches `CurveFlow.deform` on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer (`packages/materials/test/curve-flow-browser.mjs`). | 64 bytes of texture per frame of the longest curve for every curve (33 MB for 2,048 curves of 256 segments), 12 bytes per instance on the GPU, eleven texel loads and one row load per vertex in every pass that draws the mesh. | As for `curveFlow`: vertex tangents are not bent and bounds, CPU raycasts and exporters see the unbent mesh. Past the instance capacity a row reads curve 0 at distance 0. | Keep curves at similar segment counts; give a culled mesh bounds that cover every curve. |
| Models and sources per `Picking` (`@margoengine/selection`, 2026-11-26, KB-PICK-BUDGET1) | Enforced: at most 4,096 sources registered by hand with `add` (`RangeError` at `add`), each of at most 65,536 primitives (`RangeError` at `add` and at attach). By method: the gltf/pbr and materials models of a scene are found each frame and count against no budget; 5,000 models render and pick their first and last on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer ([many-models.browser.mjs](../packages/selection/test/many-models.browser.mjs)). Pick IDs (core slots, then model primitives, pick proxies and instance rows) travel as float32 in the pick shader's uniform, exact up to 16,777,216 in all. | One uniform and bind group per drawn model primitive; the micro pass draws every model primitive near the pixel. | Past 16,777,216 IDs a pick can name a neighbouring primitive. | Merge static models (gltf/pbr baked batches) for very large scenes. |
| `Picking.pickMany` points per call | Staging memory: 768 bytes a point, freed when the call ends ([picking.ts](../packages/selection/src/picking.ts)). No enforced count. | One 3 x 3 tile a point at WebGPU's 256-byte row pitch. All points read the scene at the call's turn, where separate `engine.pick` calls each read it at their own. | Memory use during a call grows with the number of points, 768 bytes each, until the call ends. | Split a very large list into several calls. |
| Action manager pick callback (`ActionManager` `pick` in `@margoengine/selection/actions`, 2026-11-25) | By method: `pick(x, y)` is called synchronously inside `pointerDown`, `pointerUp` and `pointerMove` and must return the node (or null) at once; a returned promise is not awaited. | Pick, double pick, long pick and over/out are worked out in the same pointer event, in order, so no event waits on another. | A GPU pick (`Picking.pick`, `engine.pick`) is asynchronous and cannot be passed in directly. | Resolve the GPU pick to a node first (for example cache the last `await picking.pick(x, y)` result from a `pointermove` handler, or use a CPU raycast) and pass a callback that returns that node. |
| One-file playable ads (`margo-convert playable`, 2026-11-25) | Enforced: a network size budget, default `unity` (4,999,999 bytes raw); presets `applovin`, `liftoff`, `moloco` 5,000,000, `chartboost` 3,000,000, `meta` 2,000,000 raw and `iab` 300,000 gzipped, or any `{bytes, measure}`; over it the build fails (MargoError `failed`, `error.report`) unless `allowOverBudget`. By method: files go in as base64 (a third larger, kept in memory twice once decoded); modules go in as text through an import map of blob URLs; only `new URL(<string literal>, import.meta.url)`, literal `import()` and `fetch` of a bundled path are redirected; a module that imports a package by name, CSS `@import`, a page with its own import map and any network URL in the page or a module specifier are refused. | Ad networks take one HTML file and allow no requests at run time; text modules keep JavaScript at its own size instead of base64. | A 5 MB file holds about 3.7 MB of binary assets. Workers that import modules, `XMLHttpRequest`, and `img.src` set from a computed (non-literal) `new URL` do not reach the bundled files. Shadows and post-processing add passes, so they add wrappers. Measured and left as they are: the frame-resources view set clears about 120 B per frame in the post scene (a fix changes the protocol between copies of the resources, judged risky for a frozen core), the SSAO scene walk makes an iterator and an options literal, the fixture setters box about 216 B in the shadowed scene, and each returned WebGPU object costs 16 B. Core's changed-row upload walks its dirty-row words 16 bits at a time, so no tier boxes a full 32-bit word (it cost 3,744 B a frame for 10,000 moving rows until 2026-11-11, KB0378); `tests/frame-alloc.test.js` fails it over 0 B a call at the baseline tier and at Maglev. Edge 157 reads the instanced and shadowed scenes 12 to 20 B over their floors on the RTX A6000 (open in docs/known-bugs.md). Number boxing in V8's middle tier (Maglev) is gated too: `tests/frame-alloc.test.js` fails a core frame over 780 B, shadows over 620 B and the cascade fit over 128 B there on V8 14 (Node 26) and newer. V8 13 (Node 24, the minimum Node) passes the core limit (628 B) but its Maglev calls Math.sqrt with a boxed argument and result, 32 B a call, so it has its own row for the other two: shadows over 1,120 B (measured 1,081 B, 704 B of it 22 square roots) and the cascade fit over 256 B (measured 242 B, 224 B of it 7 square roots); a square root in JavaScript arithmetic with the same bits would cost every engine more time. Node 22 has no Maglev by default, so the middle-tier probes skip there. A late frame once deoptimized core's frame loop (its delta clamp first ran a compare on a frame past `maxDelta`, with no type feedback), and the loop then ran its next thousands of frames in a tier that boxes numbers: 24 to 84 B more per frame in every scene, seen only when `check:merge` loaded the machine. Fixed in core, and gated twice: the browser check's late warm-up frame, and `tests/frame-alloc.test.js`, which fails when a late frame leaves the loop unoptimized. The Node probes compile on the main thread (`--no-concurrent-recompilation`), so a package build running beside them cannot make them measure a lower tier. `npm run test:frame-alloc:nodes` runs the test on every Node it finds; the probes leave out windows in which V8 collected garbage. In these runs 0 to 3 of 600 recorded frames held a collection. On the WebGL2 compatibility layer (`MARGO_COMPAT=1`, the check installs the layer in its pages) the check measures the same scenes against the same floors, and the layer is within them since 2026-11-18 (KB-COMPAT-FRAMEALLOC1, ten parts): median frames on the layer, Edge 156 on the RTX A6000, basic 252 B, instanced 228 B, shadowed 800 B, post 1,464 B (1,324 B since KB-GPUMAIN1, 2026-11-28), dynamic 264 B (15,652 B, 12,684 B, 154,856 B, 155,712 B and 497,716 B when it was first measured, 2026-11-16). The layer's objects WebGPU returns per call are a browser wrapper's size or near it (a pass encoder and a default texture view 16 B, an encoder and a command buffer 20 B); its present makes one 16 B ImageBitmap a frame, the zero-copy way to show a WebGL2 frame on a page canvas. | Keep your own `onFrame` callbacks allocation-free (the check's scenes keep their clock in a `Float64Array`). `node scripts/frame-alloc-browser.mjs --profile --source` names the functions that allocate per frame. |

| Voxel-net lag compensation (`@margoengine/voxel-net/rewind`, 2026-11-09) | Enforced: `maxRewind` above 0 and at most 4,000 ticks (default 0.5 s); a view tick older is checked `maxRewind` back, a future one now; `maxDistance` default 64 blocks. Measured over real sockets on one machine only, a walker at 2.5 blocks per second. | A client draws others about `interpolationDelay` behind, so without rewinding its aim is behind the target. | A client can claim any view tick up to `maxRewind` back. Blocks are not rewound: one placed since the view tick stops the shot. Shapes blend in a line between ticks, as the client draws them. | Lower `maxRewind` to give a cheat less; pass `hitbox` for heads or capsules; call `shoot` yourself for shots of your own. |
| Voxel-net database store (`@margoengine/voxel-net/sql-store`, 2026-11-09) | Enforced: `table` letters, digits and `_`, at most 63 characters, optionally after one `schema.` (default `margo_chunks`); chunk coordinates -2^26 to 2^26-1. Tested on `node:sqlite` only; the Postgres SQL runs through SQLite, never against a Postgres server. | A folder with a file per chunk grows past what file systems list and back up well for large worlds. | On SQLite each query runs on the server's thread, so a slow disk stalls ticks. The store cannot list its chunks. | Use a Postgres `Pool` to keep queries off the thread; turn on SQLite WAL (`PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL`); one `table` per world. |
| Voxel-net built-in TLS (`@margoengine/voxel-net/server` option `tls`, 2026-11-09) | Enforced: `tls` needs PEM `key` and `cert` that build a secure context, checked when the server is made and on `setTls`; a TLS handshake must finish within `helloTimeout` (default 3,000 ms). Tested over loopback with a self-signed certificate only. | Small hosts want `wss://` without running a reverse proxy. | `maxPending` and `maxPerAddress` count from the WebSocket upgrade on, so bare TLS handshakes are not capped by them. One certificate per server (no SNI choice between names); no HTTP/2. | A firewall or reverse proxy in front for floods, many names or HTTP/2; `setTls` for renewals; `tls: { ca }` on Node clients for a certificate of your own. |

## CAD import and the B-rep kernel (2026-11-13)

`@margoengine/cad` reads STL and OBJ on the page and STEP, IGES, ACIS SAT, Parasolid XT and JT through
`@margoengine/brep` in a worker. Each cap fails with a `RangeError` that names it and the way past it (regression tests
in `packages/cad/test/cad-limits.test.js`).

| Limit | Starts at | Why | What you see | Escape hatch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CAD file size | Enforced: 64 MiB per file ([cad-parser.ts](../packages/cad/src/cad-parser.ts)) | Bounds the worker's memory for untrusted files | `RangeError: CAD exceeds 64 MiB (...); tessellate it offline with @margoengine/brep, export it as GLB with @margoengine/exporters and load it with @margoengine/gltf/pbr` (STL and OBJ: `export it as GLB`) | A GLB through `@margoengine/gltf/pbr`, which has no CAD cap |
| Vertices per geometry, distinct triangle indices | Enforced: 1,000,000 vertices, 3,000,000 indices | One geometry's buffers stay within what every backend draws in one call | The same `RangeError` form, naming the cap | As above |
| Meshes per file | Enforced: `maxParts`, default 100,000 ([limits.js](../packages/shared/limits.js)) | Every mesh becomes a core entity | `Too many CAD parts (...; raise the maxParts option)` | `maxParts`, up to core's 8,388,608 entities |
| Worker time | Enforced: `timeoutMs`, default 120,000 ms | A file the kernel cannot finish does not hold a worker for ever | `RangeError: CAD import did not finish within 120000 ms (raise the timeoutMs option)`; the worker is terminated | `timeoutMs` |
| Placed bodies per assembly | Enforced: `maxInstances`, default 1,000,000 ([structure.ts](../packages/brep/src/step/structure.ts)) | Bounds memory for an assembly that places one body many times | A `RangeError` that names `maxInstances` | `maxInstances` on `parseSTEP` |
| Vertices per tessellated face | Enforced: `maxFaceVertices`, default 50,000 (at least 64; [tessellate.ts](../packages/brep/src/mesh/tessellate.ts)) | Refinement of one face stops before it runs away | The face stops refining at the cap | `maxFaceVertices` on `tessellateSTEP` |
| Tessellation bytes across CPUs (2026-11-15) | By method: analytic surfaces (cylinders, cones, spheres, tori, revolutions) are evaluated with `Math.sin`, `Math.cos`, `Math.atan2` and `Math.acos`, which ECMA-262 leaves implementation-approximated | The JavaScript engine supplies them; a portable sine and cosine in the kernel would slow every surface evaluation | The same STEP file can mesh to vertex positions and normals that differ in the last bit between an x64 and an arm64 machine (14 of 24 test meshes did on an arm64 Mac), and such a bit can tip a refinement decision | Hash meshes only on one machine, or compare them within float32 rounding; `packages/brep/tests/step-tessellate.test.js` pins its digests with `tests/support/exact-math.js` in place of the engine's trigonometry |
| Reader warnings | Enforced: at most 100 in `model.warnings` | A broken file does not flood the caller | Later warnings are dropped | None |
| B-rep modelling: sweep and loft (`model.sweep`, `model.loft`) | Enforced: a sweep takes a closed planar profile across the start tangent of a tangent-continuous path of lines and arcs, with analytic faces only (no helix or spline path); a loft is ruled between closed planar sections with the same number of segments (no loft to a point, no spline sections) | The solid stays exact: its volume and area are the closed forms the tests hold it to, and it passes `checkBody` | A `RangeError` that names the cause: a corner, an arc tighter than the profile reach, path pieces within twice the reach, a twist between sections | Split the path at its corners and `boolean` the pieces, or revolve or extrude the profile |
| B-rep body check (`model.checkBody`): touch margin | Enforced: an edge touches a face it does not bound when it comes within ten times its own tolerance (at least 1 um) along its length, or ten times a vertex's tolerance inside that reach of the vertex; a crossing inside a vertex's reach is the edge meeting its neighbours and is not reported. A loop's sense counts each curve's end where it lies apart from the next curve's start by more than a millionth of the face's size | Tolerant topology: a vertex's tolerance is a ball round its point and an edge's a tube round its curve (Jackson 1995, docs/clean-room.md BR12); the factor of ten is the margin the check keeps over the distances it samples | An edge nearer a face than that margin but not within the stated tolerances can be taken as lying in it; a face narrower than a millionth of its size whose curve ends are apart by less than that can be read with the wrong sense | Give edges and vertices the tolerances the geometry has (an import measures them) |
| B-rep modelling: offset, shell and draft (`model.offsetFaces`, `model.shell`, `model.draft`) | Enforced: faces on planes, cylinders, cones, spheres and tori; a line or circle edge stays one where its faces still meet in one, and any other edge (or one whose faces move apart into another curve, as a plane moved off a torus's axis) is the faces' new intersection traced between its new ends; an offset that changes the topology (a face moved past a neighbour, walls thicker than the part) is refused, and so are B-spline faces | A re-solved body is checked on both faces of every new edge; a topology change needs a different construction | A `RangeError` that says why; nothing is returned half done | Build the thicker or thinner shape with `extrude`, `revolve` and `boolean` |
| B-rep sewing (`model.sew`) | Enforced: a closed edge matches another only when their vertices join; the nearest-open-edge search grows with the square of the open edges | Bounds the search a loose-face set can cost | The `SewReport` lists open edges with their gap distances; a very large loose set is slow | Sew the faces in groups, or raise the tolerance to the gap the report shows |
| Mesh-only JT parts, `.brep` files | Not read: a JT part with only triangle LODs is listed in `warnings`; the native format of the earlier importer's kernel is not a supported input | No exact B-rep to mesh, a format outside the published standards the kernel is written from | The model warns; a `.brep` URL makes `loadCAD` throw a `TypeError` that lists the formats it reads | Export the part as STEP |
| Load time and memory | Not measured on the engine's machines yet | | | |

## Rendering

| Limit | Starts at | Why | What you see | Escape hatch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| An `-srgb` view target (core, 2026-11-26) (LIM-673) | Enforced by WebGPU: a view's `target.color` in an `-srgb` format names its non-srgb twin in `viewFormats` (`rgba8unorm` for `rgba8unorm-srgb`, `bgra8unorm` for `bgra8unorm-srgb`). Core draws it through a view in the twin format, so the colour is encoded once. Measured (Intel Arc 140V, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer, `packages/core/tests/view-srgb.browser.mjs`): a `rgba8unorm-srgb` target stores byte for byte what a `rgba8unorm` target stores, #808080 as 128 and core's clear colour as 5,6,9, with 4x MSAA and with 1 sample. Before 2026-11-26 it stored the colour encoded twice (188 for #808080, docs/known-bugs.md, KB-VIEW-SRGB1). | Every pass of a frame writes display colour, and an `-srgb` attachment would encode it again; WebGPU allows a view in the twin format only of a texture that names it. | Without `viewFormats`, native WebGPU reports a validation error for the view and the view draws nothing; the WebGL2 layer draws it either way. Sampling the target returns linear light. Blending and the 4x resolve work on display values, as on the canvas. | Create the texture with `viewFormats`, or use a `rgba8unorm` or `bgra8unorm` target and decode in the shader that samples it. |
| A scene's `background` under a post effect (core, 2026-11-26) (LIM-670) | By design: the canvas shows the colour's sRGB bytes as given; in a linear HDR capture (tone mapping, bloom, a `PostStack` with an HDR effect) the colour is decoded to linear light (IEC 61966-2-1) and tone-mapped with the scene, as `ColorBackground` is. Measured (Intel Arc 140V, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer, `packages/post/test/scene-background-browser.mjs`): #808080 shows as 128 with no effect and as 116 under Tonemap and PostStack (117 under Bloom); #07090f as 0,2,9; #2a6cba as 11,101,183. Before 2026-11-26 the capture took the bytes and encoded them twice (181 for #808080, docs/known-bugs.md, KB-CLEAR-CAPTURE1). | An effect's tone map, exposure, bloom and grading act on the whole captured frame, so no clear value shows as its own bytes under every chain. | A background a little darker under an effect than on the bare canvas; dark colours fall towards black under the default curve. | Pick the colour under the chain you ship. Core's own clear colour (no `background`, 5,6,9 on the canvas) takes the same path since 2026-11-26: 0,1,4 under Tonemap and PostStack and 0,2,5 under Bloom, as a `#050609` background (7,20,38 before, docs/known-bugs.md, KB-CLEAR-DEFAULT1). |
| Black hole ray budget (`@margoengine/shader/black-hole`) | Enforced by design: each ray gets at most `steps` (default 260) fourth-order Runge-Kutta steps through Kerr spacetime. The null condition stays under 1e-5 on escaping rays (packages/shader/test/black-hole.test.js) and drifts more on retrograde captured rays inside 4 M. | A fixed budget keeps the full-screen pass bounded. | Rays that graze the photon orbit and neither escape nor fall in within the budget end dark, a hair inside the photon ring. | Raise `hole.steps` for stills. |
| Negated scaled components in a division on the Radeon 680M (D3D12) | Measured 2026-11-14 with packages/shader/test/negated-division-check.mjs (driver 32.0.21030.2001, Edge 157): `(-(v * 2.0).z) / (v * 2.0).x` and the same inside atan2 lose their sign; the RTX A6000 and every WebGL2 path are exact. | Below Margo: the driver's D3D12 shader compiler (docs/known-bugs.md). | Margo's own shaders avoid the pattern; a user shader that divides a negated component of a constant-scaled vector gets the wrong sign on that GPU. | Negate outside the call (`-atan2(v.z, v.x)`), negate before scaling, or divide by a length. |
| A derivative used only inside a per-pixel branch, WebGL2 layer on ANGLE Direct3D 11 (RTX A6000) | Fixed 2026-11-15 in the layer: every derivative and implicit-derivative sample of a fragment feeds the outputs through a select that never takes it, so the Direct3D 11 compile can no longer move it into the branch (docs/known-bugs.md). | One add per derivative or implicit sample on the layer; webgl2-compat/glsl +294 B gzip. | None for output: the layer returns WebGPU's differences (features.html derivativeBranch). | None needed; the black hole still keeps its derivatives in uniform control flow, which is right on every backend. |
| Texture units and large uniform blocks in one stage, WebGL2 layer on ANGLE Direct3D 11 (RTX A6000) | Fixed 2026-11-25 in the layer (KB-BOUNCE-COMPATUNITS1): ANGLE gives a uniform block of 50 or more rows a shader resource after the textures, and past 16 the GPU process crashed at the first draw ([d3d11-srv-crash-repro.mjs](../packages/webgl2-compat/test/d3d11-srv-crash-repro.mjs)). A stage whose texture units and uniform blocks pass its texture unit limit declares its blocks inside a struct of the same layout, kept as a constant buffer. | Stages within the limit are unchanged; a stage past it reads its blocks as constant buffers on Direct3D 11 (on Vulkan and GL they already are). | None: the scene of [compat-units-gpu-check.js](../scripts/compat-units-gpu-check.js) draws on ANGLE Direct3D 11, Vulkan and native WebGPU. | Texture units themselves still stop at the GL limit (16 here). Since 2026-11-26 the layer counts them per stage before linking (`device.textureUnits(descriptor)`) and refuses a pipeline past a limit with code `unsupported` (errors#texture-units, naming the stage and each binding); gltf materials past it pack their five base maps first, four units fewer. The WGSL corpus records khronos-gallery's material unpacked (as built on WebGPU, 16 sampled textures plus a storage data texture: 19 layer units); its checks count that recording as refused, and the packed material draws on the layer (KB-COMPAT-CORPUSRED1). |

The writer checks the extension's rules but neither unites nor clips the geometry, takes no composite or textured beam property, and appends the lattice's points after the mesh's vertices without joining equal ones. A merged assembly takes no lattice. Slice stacks are written from `objectInfo`'s `slices` (2026-11-27; `packages/exporters/tests/threemf-slice.test.js`, read back through `parse3MFLattice`, which with this entry `parse3MF` now passes by: it stopped at a layer's vertices before). A layered part is one part under `/2D/` at most, and a segment takes colours only. No print of these files was checked, and no consumer other than Margo's readers has read them. The writer checks node names, input types and graph order but not a graph's values; image sheets are checked for one size, colour type and bit depth only; a private extension function is not written; a lattice a function names takes no clipping or representation mesh; a volume needs a node's own object. Where the specifications disagree with their schemas, the schema is followed (`disp2dcoord`, `height`, `matvecmultiplication`, `functioncall`), the matrix builders' output is named `result` as their examples name it, and a `volumeid` is written qualified and read with or without its prefix. `parse3MF` gives a displacement mesh's base triangles, marked `displaced`, and refuses a level set object. Boolean shapes are written from `objectInfo`'s `boolean` (2026-11-27; `packages/exporters/tests/threemf-boolean.test.js`, read back through `parse3MFBoolean`): union, difference and intersection chained over a node's mesh, with each operand's triangles baked into the node's frame (a mesh named at several places is a copy for each node) and no build or boolean transform of their own. `parse3MFBoolean` evaluates the shapes with `@margoengine/mesh-edit`'s exact boolean (2026-11-27; `packages/loaders/tests/threemf-boolean.test.js`): inputs must be closed outward solids (triangles with no area are removed first), at most 400,000 vertices and faces a shape; a face keeps its source's colour (core colours only, no textures or material identity); `parse3MFBoolean` itself evaluates no base of another extension and refuses a package that builds a level set. `parse3MFEvaluated` (2026-11-27; `packages/loaders/tests/threemf-{evaluate,beams}.test.js`) evaluates displacement, level sets, beam lattices and booleans of one package in one call. Its limits: the exact boolean of a finely meshed curved surface is slow (a level set sphere of about 26,000 triangles cut by a box took 52 s on the development PC, 1.8 s at `levelSetResolution` 24; the BSP tree of a convex surface grows as the square of its faces), and a lattice that is clipped or used as a boolean base counts against the 400,000 limit (a beam of 16 sides is a few hundred triangles). A lattice's shells are not united unless clipped or cut, so they overlap. The beam distance is not the distance to the union's surface inside overlapping beams. A level set domain and a mesh distance read a lattice object's triangles without its lattice. Volume colour is sampled at the vertices, at most 512 samples along a shape's longest side, and a coloured surface is written with three vertices a triangle, so a fine spacing meets the vertex limit; in a union the volume colour of an overlap is the last object's only where its faces have no colour of their own; a composite is painted only where the volume has no color, as the base materials' display colors mixed in linear light (no halftone or printer material model; 2026-11-27), and volume properties are not painted: an object's `sample` reads color, composite and properties at points the caller gives (2026-11-27, `packages/loaders/tests/threemf-volume-sample.test.js`), on the CPU, and with `parse3MFEvaluated` a boolean shape's operands have it too; volume data on a displacement mesh is refused, as the volumetric extension allows it on mesh and level set shapes only. A boolean result is rounded to Float32 by the boolean (`precision: 'float32'`), which joins corners and removes triangles thinner than 2^-20 of their coordinates (about 1e-5 at 10 units): real detail under that is lost. Triangles that rounding makes cross are then joined or split (2026-11-27; the exact boolean row below), except in the cases `selfIntersections` counts, which the 3MF readers do not report. The results were rendered by the engine and looked at (spheres, displaced, lattice, level set and coloured booleans); nothing was sliced or printed. `parse3MF` refuses a boolean shape. | Video output (`@margoengine/headless/video`, `/ffmpeg`, 2026-11-05) | `encodeVideo` builds the whole file in memory and needs WebCodecs: browsers and workers have it, Node does not. The default bitrate is `width * height * fps / 10` and at least 100,000 bits a second (2026-11-25); at 16 x 16, AV1 in Edge 158 then reads a solid colour within 5 of 255 at any bitrate tried up to 2 Mbit/s. WebM times are whole milliseconds, as its default timestamp scale gives. Alpha is dropped unless `alpha` keeps it (2026-11-15): WebM with VP9 or VP8 only, since MP4 and the AV1 WebM mapping have no binding for it (code `'unsupported'`; `streamVideo` keeps it with `format: 'webm'` and refuses it for its default MP4 the same way). `encodeVideo` then runs a second encoder of the same codec and settings over each frame's alpha as luma (flat chroma), roughly doubling the encode work and adding the alpha stream's bytes, and writes each frame as a BlockGroup with BlockAdditions (BlockAddID 1) and a ReferenceBlock on frames that are not key, AlphaMode 1 and MaxBlockAdditionID 1 on the track (RFC 9559 5.1.3.5, 5.1.4.1.16, 5.1.4.1.28.4; Matroska codec mappings V_VP8 and V_VP9). A frame is a key frame, and gets a cluster and cue, only when both encoders made it one, so a seek never lands on alpha that needs an earlier frame. Colour under full transparency is the frames' own (black from `readPixels`), and 4:2:0 chroma at an edge mixes it in. `encodeWithFFmpeg` keeps alpha as VP9 `yuva420p` for `.webm` with the default arguments. `streamVideo` `format: 'webm'` (2026-11-15) writes a live WebM (RFC 9559 6.2): the Segment's size is unknown and the header states no duration and has no SeekHead, since it goes out before the end is known, so the joined file reports no duration (ffprobe N/A, a Chromium `<video>` Infinity until it has read to the end) and a reader finds the Cues at the end only by walking the file; `encodeVideo`, or a remux (`ffmpeg -i in.webm -c copy out.webm`), gives a file with both. Clusters are whole when written, so each states its size. Frames are 8-bit RGBA, so no HDR video. `encodeVideo` converts each frame on the CPU to limited-range BT.709 4:2:0 (one pass over the pixels, 1.5 bytes a pixel held per frame) and states BT.709 primaries and matrix, sRGB transfer and limited range in the file, since encoders that convert RGBA themselves misreport their range (WebKit and Chromium on macOS, 2026-11-14). Chroma is made on the even luma columns between rows (ITU-T H.273 chroma_sample_loc_type 0, the H.264 and H.265 default; a 1/4, 1/2, 1/4 weighting across columns) and stated so in VP9 `vpcC` and CodecPrivate (chroma 0) and Matroska ChromaSiting (left, half), 2026-11-15; an AV1 file states what its encoder wrote in the sequence header. `encodeWithFFmpeg` states the same sRGB transfer (H.273 code 13) and left chroma as `encodeVideo` (2026-11-15; it said BT.709 transfer before), since both take sRGB-encoded renders. H.264 and H.265 4:2:0 state picture sizes in steps of two (ITU-T H.264 7.4.2.1.1 CropUnitX and CropUnitY; H.265 7.4.3.2.1), so both video paths give an odd frame one repeated last column or row for those codecs and report the even size (2026-11-15; before, the encoder refused it); VP8, VP9 and AV1 keep odd sizes. Frames may carry their own times (`timestamp`, 2026-11-15): MP4 then states each frame's length in `stts` at the fps x 1000 time unit, and WebM states none by default, so block times are whole milliseconds and the last frame's length lives only in the segment duration. Sound is Opus in WebM and AAC or else Opus in MP4, one or two channels, and comes as plain samples held in memory. The containers follow their codec bindings (2026-11-15): AV1 units are stored without temporal delimiter and padding OBUs and an AV1 MP4 lists the `av01` brand (AV1 Codec ISO Media File Format Binding 2.1 and 2.4; Matroska AV1 mapping); Opus in MP4 counts time at 48 kHz, states 48000 in its sample entry, cuts the OpusHead pre-skip with an edit list and carries `roll` groups for 80 ms of pre-roll (Encapsulation of Opus in ISO Base Media File Format 0.6.8, 4.3 and 4.4); WebM Opus states the OpusHead input rate and WebM VP9 the codec feature CodecPrivate (Matroska codec mappings A_OPUS and V_VP9); each MP4 track header holds its own length (ISO/IEC 14496-12 8.3.2). The AV1 record (`av1C`, and the WebM CodecPrivate) is read from the sequence header the encoder wrote, which follows it as its config OBU, since WebCodecs gives no AV1 description and the codec string can name another level than the encoder chose (AV1 ISOBMFF binding 2.3.3; AV1 specification 5.5). | A file built whole has every size known up front, so nothing is patched afterwards and the MP4 index can sit first for playback before the download ends. WebCodecs is the only encoder a page has; shipping one would be a large download. | A very long capture must fit in memory, as compressed bytes only. In Node, `encodeWithFFmpeg` streams to a file instead, and needs ffmpeg installed. The H.264 and VP9 arguments and the rawvideo input ran on real ffmpeg 9.0.2 (`npm run test:real-ffmpeg --workspace @margoengine/headless`): 12 frames each, BT.709 tags read back, colours within 2 of 255 levels. a flame's noise seed follows its place among its engine's flames, not the process's; post `Stylize`, its wave clock, to 54,000 steps (KB-FILM-SCANGAP1, 2026-11-18); `CameraBrain` and its camera stages are not a clock yet (KB-FILM-BRAIN1). An update with a delta of 0 (a `Reflector`, `Refractor` or `CubeCamera` capture inside the frame) moves no counter, so a mirror in view does not change the jitter phase, grain or seeds (KB-FILM-TAAPHASE1). Measured bounds of the history (RTX A6000, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer, 2026-11-16): particles after a seek and a 150 frame warm-up keep the live count within 5 % of a continuous run on a 2,000 particle effect (0.4 and 2.0 % at 600 and 1,800 steps, packages/vfx/test/seek-check.mjs); TAA at historyWeight 0.9 after 53 warm-up frames differs from a continuous run by at most 1 level of 255 on an LDR frame (0.016 measured, packages/taa/test/seek-check.mjs; without the seek the jitter phase differs and the gap was 41 levels); auto exposure snaps on the first metered frame and keeps e^(-1.5 P) of the gap after P seconds, measured equal to that bound (packages/tonemap/tests/seek-browser.mjs); `AstroSky` without a `date` starts at the wall clock's now; `unseekable` names the others, which restart. History on the GPU (live particles, FFT foam, ripples, trample) and view history (TAA, auto exposure, autofocus) come from the scene's warm-up frames, within the bounds of the GAP-FILM-TIME plan, not exactly; a seek back in one process needs every clock to reset: `resetClocks` (GAP-FILM-RESET, 2026-11-25) puts the clocks with `resetTime` back to 0 and lists the others, pinned in tests/film-reset-pending.json (63 on 2026-11-25), which keep their time. Measured on the GPU (RTX A6000, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer, 2026-11-25): `TAA`, `Tonemap` (grain and auto exposure) and `VolumetricFog` (wind and temporal history) after a 450 step seek, 240 live frames and `resetClocks` draw a frame bit-equal to a fresh clock's, and the same run without the reset differs (tests/support/reset-frame-browser.mjs, run by packages/taa/test/reset-browser.mjs, packages/tonemap/tests/reset-browser.mjs and packages/environment/tests/fog-reset-browser.mjs). Cost: CPU only, 54,000 steps for 15 minutes at 60 fps. | Render the scene's warm-up frames after the seek for history effects; keep a liquid shot inside one scene. |
| Film time class A, exact (GAP-FILM-TIME, 2026-11-16) | CPU clocks a seek replays: every field and the uniforms the next draw uploads equal a continuous run bit for bit at 1, 600 and 54,000 steps (each package's `seek.test.js`), and the HDR frame float for float at 1 and 600 steps where a `seek-check` exists (sky, weather, scatter, water), on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer. | Equal by construction: the same `advanceTime(1 / fps)` sums in the same order. | Only clocks with `advanceTime`; listeners that change state are not replayed; `unseekable` names the rest. | Give a new clock `advanceTime`; the gate's class check fails without it. |
| Film time class B, world history on the GPU (GAP-FILM-TIME, 2026-11-16) | Live particles: births per step equal, and after a seek and 150 warm-up frames (longer than the longest lifetime) on a 2,000 particle effect the same particles as a continuous run, every live slot's 64 bytes equal in other slots (GAP-FILM-VFXSEED: a birth is seeded by its step and birth number, not its slot). Exact only while every birth finds a free slot in both runs; a capped step (no free slot) drops other births, and the live count then stays within 5 %. Computed from the decay constants, not measured: FFT foam keeps e^(-P / tau) of older foam after a P second warm-up (tau 4 s by default), and Gerstner foam decays as e^(-3 t), under 1 level of 255 after 2 s; terrain's wet-sand record keeps e^(-P / wetDryTime) of older moisture (wetDryTime 900 s by default), so sand the warm-up's swash does not reach holds up to that much less moisture than a continuous run. | GPU state is large, differs per backend and scenes render in any order, so the warm-up rebuilds it instead of carrying it. | Not exact: particles when births wait for free slots, and the draw order of equal particles in other slots (blend order of unsorted particles); foam (GAP-FILM-FOAM); liquid and whitewater are chaotic, no bound. | Warm up for the longest lifetime plus trail length; keep a liquid shot, and a beach whose sand is seen drying, inside one scene. |
| Film time class C, view history (GAP-FILM-TIME, 2026-11-16) | TAA at historyWeight w keeps w^n of a gap after n frames: 53 frames at 0.9 leave under 1 level of 255 (0.016 measured, packages/taa/test/seek-check.mjs; 41 levels without the seek). A 2 s warm-up covers TAA, exposure and Gerstner foam. | A cut resets view history on purpose, as a camera cut does in film tools. | The first warm-up frames differ from a continuous run within these bounds. | Render the scene's warm-up frames on its own camera before frame 0. |

Luminance-only files are not converted. Min+gzip before to now: exr-tiled 8,106 to 8,823 B, load 10,860 to 11,576 B, loaders 11,130 to 11,843 B, environment root 31,492 to 32,197 B, exr-codecs worker 2,557 to 3,314 B. | Write a listed ID or `chromaticities` into such a file; `image.colorInteropID` and `image.primariesConverted` report what was read. |

| Download reader memory (`readResponse` in [loading.js](../packages/shared/loading.js), used by every loader that fetches, 2026-11-19) | Measured ([shared-read-bytes.test.js](../tests/shared-read-bytes.test.js), counts, not timings): a response with a plain `Content-Length` within the budget is read straight into one buffer of that size and handed back as is, so a 100 MiB file makes 104,857,600 B in the reader and never holds more than the file and one chunk; a body with no length, or a coded one (`Content-Encoding` other than `identity`), keeps each chunk once as it arrived and copies it once into the result, 104,857,600 B made for 100 MiB. Before 2026-11-19 (KB-LOADBYTES1) every chunk was copied as it arrived and again into the result: 209,715,200 B made and twice the file held at the end. | A declared length lets the reader skip the join; without one the result has to be joined from the chunks. | A body with no length still holds its chunks and the result together for the moment of the join (2x, briefly). A server that declares more than it sends costs a buffer of the declared size (within `maxBytes`) until the read ends, then one copy of what arrived; a chunk that views part of a larger or shared buffer is copied when held. | Serve files with `Content-Length`; set the loader's byte budget to what the app expects. |
| glTF download budget | Enforced: gltf/pbr reads at most `maxDownloadBytes` (default 512 MiB, 536,870,912 B: `assetLimit`, 64 MiB before 2026-11-11) of JSON, buffers and images per load, and decoded accessors, packed geometry and decoded images may each use 4x that (2 GiB by default); one image decodes to at most 8192 x 8192 pixels (67,108,864, the side every WebGPU device supports; 4096 x 4096 before 2026-11-17, which refused a film's 8192 x 4096 maps) and a side over the device's `maxTextureDimension2D` is refused at upload ([image-limit.ts](../packages/gltf/src/image-limit.ts), [async-images.test.js](../packages/gltf/test/async-images.test.js)); a Draco primitive takes up to 16,777,216 vertices and 50,331,648 indices (1,000,000 each before), and `@margoengine/decoders` outputs at most 384 MiB (402,653,184 B) per Draco decode (256 MiB before 2026-11-11), the most whose measured peak Wasm memory fits 90% of the prebuilt decoder's 2 GiB ([draco-output-limit.test.js](../packages/decoders/tests/draco-output-limit.test.js)): a 9,999,392-triangle grid with normals and UVs (a 5.8 MB stream, 280,126,112 B decoded) peaks at 1,035,534,336 B of Wasm memory in the prebuilt decoder and 812,449,792 B in the clean-room one, 3.7x and 2.9x its output; positions only, the worst measured mix, takes 4.5x (`node packages/decoders/scripts/draco-scale.mjs [side] [--positions]`). Draco connectivity can be a few KB for millions of regular triangles, so input size cannot bound decode memory: a 4 KB cut of that grid claims 666 MB (clean-room) or 795 MB (prebuilt) before it fails with `MargoError failed`, within the ceiling; the stage's `addGLTF` reads up to 512 MiB and sends a file over 64 MiB to gltf/pbr; `@margoengine/gltf` reads at most 64 MiB ([asset.ts](../packages/gltf/src/asset.ts), [loading.js](../packages/shared/loading.js); [accessors.test.js](../packages/gltf/test/accessors.test.js), [gltf-draco-limits.test.js](../tests/gltf-draco-limits.test.js), [gltf-routing.test.js](../packages/stage/tests/gltf-routing.test.js)). Khronos ABeautifulGame (a 43 MB GLB whose 33 2048x2048 textures decode to 528 MiB) fits the default image budget. | Bounds memory for any URL an app is handed, at a size where a 10M-triangle scan (about 300 MB raw, or about 800 MB decoded from a 40 MB Draco file) loads with no options; the decoded budget does not shrink with compression. | gltf/pbr names the option for the download and packed-geometry budgets, e.g. `RangeError: glTF exceeds download budget (536870912 bytes; raise the maxDownloadBytes option)`; decoded accessors and images over 4x throw `RangeError: Decoded glTF exceeds byte budget` or `RangeError: glTF images exceed decoded size limit`; the light loader refuses with `MargoError` code `unsupported`, `glTF download is over the light loader's 64 MiB; use @margoengine/gltf/pbr` (or `glTF buffers are ...`), so `loadAuto` moves on to gltf/pbr (KB-GLTFA B5, 2026-11-19). | gltf/pbr's `maxDownloadBytes` option, which also lowers the budget for apps that load untrusted URLs on small devices; for the light loader, use gltf/pbr. |
| Malformed and hostile files | Enforced at each parser's trust boundary (glTF, gltf/pbr with its parse worker and progressive stream, `.margo`, Draco, KTX2, meshopt, HDR, EXR, UltraHDR, FBX), checked by seeded fuzzers (`npm run fuzz`, [targets-formats.js](../scripts/fuzz/targets-formats.js); regressions in [fuzz-formats-regressions.test.js](../tests/fuzz-formats-regressions.test.js)): every input ends in a result or the package's own error. Limits added with them: a gltf/pbr document nested deeper than 256 levels ([asset.ts](../packages/gltf/src/asset.ts)); an EXR chunk that decodes to more than 256 MiB, or chunks too small to hold the image ([exr.ts](../packages/environment/src/exr.ts)); a Draco or KTX2 decode running longer than 10 s plus 4 s per MiB of input ([pool.ts](../packages/decoders/src/pool.ts)). How long large valid Draco and KTX2 files take to decode: not measured. | Files from a URL are untrusted: a malformed one must fail with an error the app can show, not crash, hang, read outside its bytes or claim memory its size cannot justify. | `TypeError: Invalid glTF JSON: nested deeper than 256 levels`, `RangeError: Unsupported EXR: a chunk decodes to more than 256 MiB`, `RangeError: Invalid EXR: chunks are too small for the image size`, `MargoError: Draco decode timed out after <limit> ms (corrupt data?); the decoder worker was restarted`. | The decoders' `timeout` option (`Infinity` turns the limit off). No real glTF comes near 256 levels; EXR: fewer channels per file. |
| Vertices per primitive | Enforced: gltf/pbr takes up to 16,777,216 vertices per primitive (2^24), loaded as parts of at most `maxPartVertices` (default 262,144, 1,024 to 1,048,576) each, skinned and morphed ones included (each part reads `JOINTS_n`, `WEIGHTS_n` and morph deltas through `part.vertexMap`, and deforms bit for bit as the mesh split by hand and as the whole primitive: [split-skin.test.js](../packages/animation/tests/split-skin.test.js), [test-skinned-parts-browser.mjs](../packages/gltf/scripts/test-skinned-parts-browser.mjs), natively and on the WebGL2 layer, RTX A6000 2026-11-17); `loadGLTFProgressive` streams them part by part, each part drawn as it arrives ([progressive.test.js](../packages/gltf/test/progressive.test.js)); the light `@margoengine/gltf` loader takes up to 1,000,000 vertices in total ([parts.test.js](../packages/gltf/test/parts.test.js), [accessors.test.js](../packages/gltf/test/accessors.test.js)). Packed geometry is still bounded by the decoded budget (4x `maxDownloadBytes`; 80 B a vertex, 4 B an index). Measured (Node 26, busy machine, diagnostic): a 1,001,000-vertex grid loads as 4 parts with 0.37% of its vertices copied onto the cuts, packed in about 240 ms. At 10M triangles ([test-parts-browser.mjs](../packages/gltf/scripts/test-parts-browser.mjs), native and WebGL2 layer; RTX A6000 and Radeon 680M 2026-11-11, Apple M6 2026-11-14): a 2,237 x 2,237-vertex field (5,004,169 vertices, 9,999,392 triangles, one primitive, a 240,093,656 B GLB) loads with no options through `loadGLTF` and `loadGLTFProgressive`, and with `maxPartVertices` 65,536 and 1,048,576, and in a far, a low and a close view draws exactly what the field pre-split at export into the same parts in the same order draws (the test splits it itself as parts.ts documents: same multisample samples, draws and triangles, and the parts hold the reference primitives' vertices and indices bit for bit; the reference with a part dropped, two parts' index lists swapped or a part drawn twice fails), and covers exactly the samples the field pre-split into 20 row bands covers. Until 2026-11-14 the split was compared exactly with the row bands, which passed on the A6000 and the 680M but never on the Apple M6, whose samples depend on the order of the draws at this triangle count ([known-bugs](known-bugs.md), "Apple M-series: multisample values of a multi-million-triangle frame depend on draw order"); the row bands, drawn in another order, are now compared by coverage only, which no draw order changes; Node's `prepareGLTF` peaks at 782,875,020 B of ArrayBuffers, 3.26 bytes per input byte. Work counts with `CulledModels`, close view (far view: every part): `maxPartVertices` 65,536: 78 parts, 12 drawn, 1,550,309 triangles; 262,144 (default): 20 parts, 9 drawn, 4,683,190 triangles; 1,048,576: 5 parts, 4 drawn, 8,363,067 triangles. Without `CulledModels` the draw loop tests each part's bounding sphere against the camera frustum on the CPU (one test per primitive per draw, 2026-11-11, [parts.test.js](../packages/gltf/test/parts.test.js)), so a part out of view issues no draw; instanced, rigged, deformed, own-shader and displaced primitives are drawn untested. Parts follow Hoppe 1999, Sander et al. 2007, Yoon et al. 2005, Isenburg and Lindstrom 2005, Cignoni et al. 2005, Kerbl et al. 2018 and Karis et al. 2021 (cited in [parts.ts](../packages/gltf/src/parts.ts)). | Over 2^24: `MargoError` code `unsupported` naming 16777216; a part over a device's binding: `RangeError` naming its bytes and `maxPartVertices`; the light loader: `RangeError: glTF exceeds one million vertices`. | Split a primitive over 2^24 vertices at export; lower `maxPartVertices` for a device with a small storage binding. |

## XR AR edges on the WebGL2 layer

By method (2026-11-27, stand-in headset only, no AR device): at 4 samples a capturing effect copies its depth back to the
eye one sample at a time, which the WebGL2 layer answers with the resolved depth (GLSL ES 3.00 has no multisample
samplers), so under an effect an AR edge pixel's coverage there is 0 or 1, where WebGPU keeps quarters; the colour's
brightest channel still gives a partly covered pixel partial alpha where coverage is 0. With no effect the two match.
Content drawn after the main pass that writes no depth (a line with depthWrite false, a glow) takes its own alpha as
coverage on both (KB-XR-ARNODEPTH1, fixed), and so do transparent glTF and materials meshes that write no depth: gltf/pbr
draws them at frame-graph order 1, after xr's AR alpha pass, and core's main pass holds no blended draw. Under
FXAA a depthless line's one-pixel rim is partly covered, colour and alpha alike, as the filter blends it.

Entry 3,864 B gzip. | Closed forms are the exact solution a joint model tracks and a readout shows. | The physics-joint models in `tests/machinery-mechanisms-physics.test.js` (a hinge motor, sliders, a pin in a slot, a gear joint) follow the poses to 2e-4 m and 2e-3 rad at 60 Hz. | For loads, friction, backlash or governor dynamics, build the mechanism from `@margoengine/physics` joints and step it. |
| Mechanism rigs on physics (`@margoengine/machinery/rigs`, 2026-11-27) (LIM-680) | Enforced by method: fourteen rigs (Scotch yoke, Geneva, Oldham, epicyclic, harmonic drive, ball-and-disk integrator, Archimedes screw, stroboscope, toggle press, gimbal, differential, Watt governor, rose engine, Reuleaux drive) on `@margoengine/physics` joints, with no gravity, friction or load but the governor's gravity and hinge drag; the input is a position-driven body stepped at most 2 degrees per 60 Hz step. Interiors (2026-11-27): every storey of a furnished multi-storey building gets a stair: a dog-leg, or one straight flight between two floors, in a room that holds it with its approach and a way past, clear of doorway approaches and 1.2 m off outer doors, else in a stair hall of up to five columns, else a spiral, else a fixed ladder through hatches (the ladder may stand close to a door). Of 400 random plans of the five multi-storey styles, 5 to 17 m a side, 399 get a dog-leg and 1 one straight flight; a walk test reaches every storey and room of 1,500 random buildings, 3 to 60 m a side, and every storey of 500 random L, T, U, cross and tower plans. | Rectangular footprints and closed-form roofs from the straight skeleton of a rectangle: every roof face is exact, and the rules stay small data a slider panel can drive. | One rectangular mass per call (`procedural/building-plans` joins several into L, T, U and cross plans with dormers and towers); only a sill bay at up to 0.47 m keeps Japan's three floor-area conditions (Setagaya 4-92-1a), the IRC floor cantilever table R502.3.3(1) is not checked, no bay is made on a door, shop window or balcony, a top storey one comes down under the eaves (under every side of a shed roof), and none carries its own pitched hip roof, window seat joinery or a bay across two facade bays; a second escape stair (2026-11-27, `escapeStair`, on by default) is added where Japan's Order arts. 120 and 121 or IBC Table 1006.3.4(2) (the business row of the 2021 table, read at up.codes/s/single-exits and in Washington's WAC 51-50-1006; the residential table 1006.3.4(1) was read there too: one exit up to the third storey with at most 4 dwelling units and 125 ft of travel, sprinklered buildings with escape openings only, which the rules do not model, so western commercial blocks are judged as business areas whatever their rooms) give a storey no single stair, never a third however long the walk (`escapes` reports it), none where neither a room nor a second stair hall holds a framed or winder stair apart from the first (no asked storey of 4,500 random 8 to 58 m by 6 to 26 m buildings, 4 in 100 of those of 3 to 70 m by 3 to 8 m; a roof stair (`roofStair`, 2026-11-27) goes to flat roofs only, from one framed or winder stair (never the escape stair, a spiral or a ladder), its house a plain box with a closed door that no code of rooms or guards inside is checked against beyond the flights' own, IBC 1011.12's ladder or hatch for an unoccupied roof, roof drains, equipment and Japan's department store roof refuge (art. 126 para. 2) are not built, and IBC 1011.12 and 1015.3 were read from secondary quotations; | Flow fields (`@margoengine/behavior/flowfield`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: size and stamp sizes are whole numbers of 1 or more, `cell` above 0, costs whole numbers from 1 to 255, goals three finite numbers, `steer` count, speed and delta 0 or more. | The field is one flat grid built in one call, so cost follows the whole map. | By method: one flat grid, with no sectors, portals or tile cache, so memory and build time grow with the whole map; one field per goal and movement type; every change rebuilds the whole field in one synchronous call; no clearance, so a gap of one cell passes a unit of any size; the ground is flat, and height is ignored; line of sight flags are built for a single goal only and can miss a few cells at the edge of a shadow; first order fast marching reads over the true distance on the diagonal, by 21% one cell from the goal, under 11% past 5 cells and under 3% past 40; units do not avoid each other. Cost is per cell, so `integration` is in cells, not world units. | Task network planner (`@margoengine/behavior/htn`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: task names are unique, a compound task has a method, every subtask exists, symbols are booleans, strings or finite numbers and none is called `__proto__`, `maxSteps` is 1 or more. Not measured on a real game domain. | The planner is total order only, with no costs and no task parameters. | A recursion that never ends returns `null` at `maxSteps` (10,000), the same as no plan. | Use a task per place or a symbol for something like `NavigateTo(x)`. |
| Physical point-mass steering (`@margoengine/behavior/steering`) | `locomotion` accepts a positive finite mass, nonnegative quadratic drag and turn limits, and a finite fluid velocity. The method splits propulsive acceleration and exact drag over each tick. Limits apply to motion relative to the fluid. | Newton's force law, quadratic coasting and the local curvature limit are covered by the steering tests. | Each member is a point mass. The method leaves body attitude, shape, lift, contact and thrust production to other solvers. | Set `dragFactor` to half the density times drag coefficient times area. The measured steering entry grew from 3,871 to 4,736 B gzip and the root from 8,891 to 9,791 B. A separate physical entry would duplicate the steering integration path or add another public import to configure one option. |
| Context steering (`@margoengine/behavior/context`, 2026-11-07) | Enforced: `resolution` is a whole number of 4 or more, `blur` a whole number of 0 or more, `memory` 0 or more and below 1, `slack` 0 or more, `chase` `range` above 0 and `spread` 0 or more, `avoid` `clearance` above 0 and `radius` 0 or more. | A behaviour sees only what it is given and steers locally. | By method: headings lie on the ground plane; the racing lane mode of the chapter is left out; a behaviour sees only what it is given, with no navmesh or walls, so it steers locally and can sit in a dead end; a gap narrower than a slot can be missed at a low `resolution`; `strength` caps at 1; `memory` is a plain blend, so two pulls that swap places every update with equal averages still swap, by a smaller margin.
