## Copies of a model

| Limit | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Textures of `cloneModel` copies | Shared: one GPU texture per device, image and format, freed with its last holder (`p-morph`: 7 textures for 100 copies, not 700). A second model loaded from the same file holds its own images, so it uploads its own textures. |
| Geometry of `cloneModel` copies (2026-11-06) | Shared: vertex and index buffers per device, asset and array, and in the deformation arena one copy of the bind-pose vertices, morph deltas and skin influences per page. Each animated copy still adds 80 B per vertex of deformed output, 64 B per bone and its morph weights, because those are what differ between copies. A second model loaded from the same file packs and uploads its own. |
| GPU morph weights (`@margoengine/animation/morph-gpu`, 2026-11-06) | Not measured for speed yet: the 16 B a frame and one dispatch per page are counted, the frame time is not. `Animation.upload` still loops over each copy to check its weights and bones, so CPU work is smaller per copy, not zero. Time is float32 in the shader: steps of about 0.24 ms after an hour of play. Copies must share one asset. Driven weights ignore `setMorph`, and `primitive.weights` on the CPU does not follow them. Why: The tracks are shared, and reading weights back would stall the frame. What you see: A long-running crowd loses fine timing slowly. CPU code that reads `primitive.weights` sees old values. Escape hatch: Set `player.time` back by whole loops of the clip (exact for copies at `speed` 1; a copy at another speed samples `time * speed`, so it jumps unless the step is whole loops at its speed too). Use `Animation` for a character whose weights you read or set by hand. |
| Animation LOD (`@margoengine/animation/lod`, 2026-11-06) | CPU only, and not measured for speed yet: how many copies update is counted, the frame time is not. Every copy still goes through the GPU deform dispatch each frame, and each still draws. Visibility is a sphere at the model root against the view, with no occlusion. `depth` counts node levels from the scene roots, so its meaning depends on the rig. A tier with a depth does not play `KHR_animation_pointer` channels. Deeper bones hold, so a far character can show a slightly wrong pose until it comes closer. Why: A skipped pose must still draw, and the deformed output is what draws. What you see: A crowd limited by the GPU gains little. A copy far larger than its `radius` can stop updating while part of it shows. Escape hatch: Set `radius` to cover the character. Use `VATCrowd` when the GPU is the limit. |
| Clip editing (`@margoengine/animation/clip-utils`, 2026-11-06) | By method: an eased or cubic segment that a cut passes through becomes straight keys at `fps` (default 60), so it follows the curve only to that step; segments kept whole stay exact. Works on `KeyframeClip`s, not glTF clips. `makeAdditive` leaves property tracks out, and `applyAdditiveClip` poses a `Skeleton` only, without morph weights. Why: An eased curve is defined over its whole segment, so one key cannot carry part of it. What you see: Very fine motion inside a cut curve can flatten between samples. Escape hatch: Pass a higher `fps`. For a glTF clip use an `@margoengine/animator` additive layer. |
| Engine ticks per `cloneModel` copy (2026-11-06) | None when the copy can take its source's static batches, skinned models included, so a crowd no longer costs a tick of every mesh per copy. One when the source moved since baking, has a parent, or had its geometry rewritten: the copy bakes for itself. A copy's world matrices publish with the next tick; a direct `node.matrix` read before it sees the old value. The time saved is not measured yet. |
| Work per `cloneModel` copy (2026-11-10, accepted difference) | A copy builds what it needs to draw at once: a core node per glTF node plus its root (75 for RobotExpressive), a uniform slot and bind groups per primitive; `destroy` disposes them. three's `SkeletonUtils.clone` makes JavaScript objects only and builds GPU state at its first render, so `p-skeleton-clone` times less work on three's side. The node copy itself makes one array a copy and the constructor groups primitives in one pass. The like-for-like row "clone + first draw" is pending the quiet rerun. |
| Work at load of an animated glTF (2026-11-10, accepted difference) | `parseGLTFAsync` packs vertices, bakes static batches and uploads GPU buffers, and `Animation.attach` places the deformation resources, so the model draws on its first frame with no further setup. three's loader defers buffer uploads to its first render, so `p-gltf-animated` times less work on three's side. The like-for-like row "parse + first frame" is pending the quiet rerun. |
| Dual quaternion skinning (`@margoengine/animation/dqs`, 2026-11-06) | Per `Animation`, fixed when it is created. `Skin` on raw data, `bakeVAT` and bone-texture crowds stay linear. Stretch blends linearly about the mesh origin, so between bones of different scale the result differs from a linear blend. Each bone costs a polar decomposition on the CPU every frame. Frame time is not measured yet. |
| Skinning about centres of rotation (`@margoengine/animation/cor`, 2026-11-28; `addPerson`'s default) | The centres are a CPU precompute per skinned mesh at load: about 0.3 s for a 75,525 vertex coat and 2.4 s for a 154,923 vertex Character Creator body (Node, workstation), on the main thread; each vertex carries four more numbers. The centre follows the bind pose, so a mesh whose weights change at run time keeps its old centres. Weights decide the result: cloth weighed evenly across both thighs still swings out whole (KB-SKIN-SKIRT1). Frame time is not measured yet. |
| Bone-texture crowds (`@margoengine/animation/instanced-skin`, 2026-11-06) | One material, opaque, no CPU culling, like `VATCrowd`. Morph targets are frozen at bake time, and bones blend linearly. Two clips a member: more needs another bake. Texture rows cap at 8,192 of 2,048 texels, about 5.5 million bone frames. Each vertex reads up to 96 texels when two clips blend across eight influences (24 for one clip and four). Frame time against `VATCrowd` and `Animation` is not measured yet. |
| Geometry caches (`@margoengine/animation/geometry-cache`, `/point-cache`, 2026-11-06) | PC2 and MDD are read, proved on files Blender's published add-ons wrote; the triangles come from the caller, as neither format holds them. Alembic is not read: the format has no published specification, and Margo is built from specs and papers. Mesh sequences (FG-11, 2026-11-24): `encodeMeshSequence`/`streamMeshSequence` and `margo-convert sequence` (per-frame OBJ, PLY or STL) write any per-frame mesh bake, the topology free to change each frame, so baked fluids from Blender come in through a per-frame mesh export instead of Alembic; every topology change is a new chunk, so a fluid that changes every frame stores its triangles every frame (no compression across frames). 3 to 1,000,000 vertices a chunk, one mesh, one material. The CPU interpolates and writes the whole mesh to the GPU every changed frame, so upload bandwidth is the ceiling: 80 bytes a vertex. Vertices are uncompressed. A seek back on a URL rereads from the start of the file, and a loop rereads it every lap unless it is one chunk: no range requests and no index of chunks. A stream source keeps every chunk it read. No mix across a change of mesh: the last frame holds. Motion vectors, frame time and upload cost are not measured yet. |
| Animator crossfades and graph exit times (`@margoengine/animator`, `/graph`, 2026-11-14) | By method: the state a crossfade leaves keeps playing at the current state's clip rate until its weight reaches 0; a transition taken during a crossfade fades from the blended pose it cut in on, held still, because no one state is left to play. By design: `exitTime` is the normalized time from which a transition may be taken, so on a looping state `exitTime: 0.5` with a condition fires as soon as the condition holds anywhere past the first half cycle, not only at the half mark of each later loop as in the controller of some desktop engines. Escape hatch: a base Animator transition whose `when` predicate reads `animator.normalizedTime % 1`. |
| Inertialization (`@margoengine/animator/inertialize`, 2026-11-06) | By method: an offset fades along one line per bone, so speed sideways to the offset is dropped at the switch; the new pose shows from the second frame after the switch. Not a published speed: diagnostic, shared machine, 58 bones, 14.5 to 17.1 us a frame during a fade against 16.5 to 21.5 for a crossfade, and about the same once idle. |
| Sync groups (`@margoengine/animator/sync`, 2026-11-06) | By design: clips are looping cycles, every clip of a marker group has the same markers in the same order, and a state is in one group. A crossfade keeps the old state in phase at the new state's rate. Not measured for speed. |
| Warping (`@margoengine/animator/warping`, 2026-11-06) | By method: travel past `maxTurn` (default 90 degrees) needs a clip for that direction, and a clip cannot play backward, so feet slide on the part of a turn past the limit. Stride scales about the hips on flat ground; it does not follow slopes, for which `addFootPlacement` runs after it. The clip rate changes one frame after the speed does. A pelvis drop past `maxPelvisDrop` leaves the foot short. On real CMU walks a planted foot slides 24 to 50 mm at 0.7 to 3 m/s against 21 mm in the take itself: the take's own slide scales with the stride and the hips' surge is not scaled away. The surge stays on its recorded axis when the hips turn, so a walk 90 degrees off the facing slides 51 mm. A take that curves is warped along the requested straight line, 62 mm on subject 2 at 1.6 m/s. Clip speed and a distance warp's travel are measured along the world ground through the travel joint's ancestors' current rotations and scales (a centimetre rig under a 0.01 scale or a scaled model reads in world units). Not measured for speed. |
| Full-body IK (`@margoengine/animator/fbik`, 2026-11-06) | By method: the torso is solved from the animated pose every frame in up to 12 steps, with no memory of the last frame, so a set of targets that needs more steps stops short and says so in `result`. Limbs are three-joint chains; hands, feet and head are the only targets, and a spine joint turns at most `maxBend` from the animated pose. Balance is static (centre of mass over the support hull, about world +Y, from fixed segment shares and centres (Winter's table: arm 0.530 from the shoulder, leg 0.447 from the hip, on the straight line from the limb's root to its end, so a bent elbow or knee is weighed as if straight) taken over the segments the rig lists, so a rig with no head or arms weighs only its trunk and legs): it knows nothing of momentum or of the model's real masses. A pinned foot on a limb with no target holds its animated place, so a walking clip keeps its steps. Speed not yet measured. |
| IK on a fitted body (`@margoengine/animator/ik`, `@margoengine/rigging/ik`, 2026-11-28) | Enforced: with a body named by `setAnatomy` (or `body` on a chain) and `limits` not false, no solver bends an elbow or knee past straight or past its stop, and no joint it turns passes the structural tier (10,000 seeded reaches per limb). By method: `solveLimbIK` needs a hinge whose reference bone is the limb's upper bone, else the limb is solved as before; the swivel is searched in 5 degree steps, so a legal swivel window narrower than that can be missed and the shoulder or hip is then stopped at its range; a FABRIK chain and its ranges take at most 8 turns, and a CCD chain holds a joint that reaches further one way than the other as its nearest cone during the solve and at its exact reach after it, so such a chain can end short of a target that a joint search would reach. Full-body IK keeps its priorities as weights (feet 30, balance 4, hands and head 1), not as strict levels, and eases a trunk or neck only when both ends of that region are spine joints of the rig. The Animator stores rotations as 32-bit floats, so a joint held at its stop reads within 0.001 degrees of it. The Animator's built-in `footIK` option does not read the body yet (KB-ANIM-FOOTIK-ANATOMY1). Speed not yet measured. |
| Pose checks (`@margoengine/rigging/validate`, 2026-11-28) | By method: limb and trunk volumes are capsules of the ANSUR II mean girths, shrunk to 0.7, so the check catches an arm through the chest or a leg through a leg, never a finger through cloth or a mesh through itself; same-side arm and thigh are not paired, as a hanging arm rests on the thigh. Ground checks read joints and any skin points passed in, not the whole mesh. A foot is planted after 3 frames within 0.02 of stature of its lowest height and slides above 0.1 of stature per second, so a clip whose feet never reach their lowest height is not checked for sliding, and a clip played in place needs `velocity`. A pop is a turn faster than 9,000 degrees per second (Fleisig 2017 mean plus 3 SD), a step four times both neighbours above 1,000 degrees per second, or a one-frame blip. Proportion bands: heights the ANSUR II share plus or minus 0.05 of stature, lengths 0.8 to 1.2 of the share; asymmetry above 5 percent is a warning. An elbow or knee past straight is a warning from 0.5 degrees even inside its clinical range. Speed not yet measured. |
| Coupled motion (`@margoengine/rigging/coupling`, 2026-11-28) | By method: a rule fills in only a follower the pose holds at its rest or its anatomical neutral, so a clip that moves the collarbone, a twist bone or a finger tip itself keeps its own motion, coupled or not. The girdle curve is the Ludewig 2009 mean at 0, 30 and 120 degrees of elevation, held past 120, with no spread between people. Run by `addCoupling` it sees the pose after the clips and the solvers added before it, so an IK solver added later moves the arm without the collarbone. Twist bones are found as unmapped bones along an arm or leg segment. No wrist and finger tenodesis (KB-RIG-TENODESIS1). Speed not yet measured. |
| Motion matching (`@margoengine/animator/motion-matching`, 2026-11-06) | By method: the character does what its clips show, so a request with no matching clip plays the nearest row; the weights are defaults made for loops with no start or stop clips, so a real set may want its own. The root is the hips' smoothed ground path about +Y, with a yaw-only character; ground slope is left to foot placement. Scale tracks on the hips' ancestors are read at build but not in the running pose step. Proved on stand-in clips, on Fox.glb's real clips with hand-labelled speeds, and on eight CMU takes (769 rows). A row whose path runs past the end of its take cannot be landed on, so a take has to outlast `trajectory` by a good margin: a 1.1 s run jumps 19 times in 4 s, a 3.5 s walk 4. Foot slide at a jog and a run is not measured. Speed not yet measured on a large table. |
| Runtime mirroring (`@margoengine/animator/mirror`, 2026-11-06) | By method: partners need the same place in the tree on both sides, or `addMirror` refuses them. A rig whose rest pose is not symmetric keeps its own proportions, so the mirrored pose lands that far from an exact reflection. Scale tracks trade between partners as they are. Switching `enabled` is a hard cut. Speed not yet measured. |
| Spline IK (`@margoengine/animator/spline-ik`, 2026-11-06) | By method: bones are chords, so a bend tighter than a bone is cut across, and a chain longer than the curve carries on straight past its end. The curve's frames are rebuilt every frame, and a curve of points is rebuilt too, so a very long chain costs more than one on a fixed `Spline`. `space` needs a uniform scale. Speed not yet measured. |
| Spring bones (`@margoengine/rigging/springs`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: 256 joints a chain, a joint in one chain only, 8 steps a frame (longer frames slow the swing), jiggle up to 15 Hz. By method: a tail can pass through a collider it crosses within one step, as in the specification; after the push the length hold can leave up to 1 mm of overlap; colliders hold their pose for the frame during a long frame's steps; spheres and capsules only, no planes or inside shapes; a chain has no twist, each bone turns by the shortest arc; strips do not pull on their neighbours, so a skirt of chains can part. 144 Hz differs from 60 Hz by up to 2% of the chain's length. Speed not yet measured. |
| VRM avatars (`@margoengine/rigging/vrm`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: VRM 1.0 only; VRM 0.x files are refused with a coded error. By method: MToon draws as its glTF fallback, and a colour bind only MToon has is listed in `unsupported` and not shown; `VRMC_node_constraint` is kept on write and does not run; `firstPerson` runs through `@margoengine/rigging/vrm-first-person` (next row); colour binds are checked by value, not in a picture. Not proven: no outside VRM tool has read a file `writeVRM` made (stand-in: read back by Margo only). Not measured: speed. |
| VRM first person (`@margoengine/rigging/vrm-first-person`, `xr.layers`, 2026-11-15) | Enforced: VRM 1.0 only (convert VRM 0.x with `convertVRM0Bytes`); `loadVRM` downloads at most 64 MiB; layers 0 to 31 and the two must differ; an `auto` mesh left in a loaded model is refused with a coded `state` error naming `loadVRM`. By method: the `auto` split is the specification's (any head weight above `threshold`, default 0, makes a triangle head), so stray head weights put collar triangles in the head part; an unskinned `auto` node is third person only under the head bone, else `both` (the specification is silent); a split primitive's old bytes stay in the BIN chunk; a view, mirror or probe with no mask draws every layer, `firstPersonOnly` meshes included; shadows are not filtered by a view's layers, so the whole avatar casts in every view; a set mask replaces the caller's own layer on that node until `dispose()`. Proven: CPU split exactness on the Twist sample, Seed-san and built files; on the GPU, native and WebGL2, the masked first-person view equals the render with the head hidden pixel for pixel, the mirror shows the head, and both XR routes filter both eyes ([evidence](rigging-vrm-first-person.md)). Not measured: speed. |
| Uneven bone scales in IK (`@margoengine/rigging/ik`, `@margoengine/animator`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: flat and mirrored bones are refused. By method: any positive scale is taken, and an uneven scale stretches the bones under it as they turn, so a chain lands as close as that stretch allows (within 0.14% of its length at 0.9995, 1, 0.9986). A `CCDSolver` keeps one scale per joint, so `addCCDChain` uses the mean of the three, and `setParentMatrix` still takes uniform scales only. |
| Hands (`@margoengine/rigging/hands`, `@margoengine/humans`, 2026-11-17) | Enforced: grip diameter 5 to 120 mm, flexion -30 to 130 degrees, spread -40 to 40, key weight 0 to 1, threshold 0 to 90. By method: poses are joint angles, not contact: `grip(d)` closes on a bar the size you give from each finger's measured lengths, but nothing finds the bar in the scene, so a hand that misses the rail closes on air (contact grip is not built yet). A rig with no fingertip bones has its last phalanx guessed at 3/4 of the middle one. The relaxed pose leaves the thumb to the clip, since bind poses splay it. Clips that key their own fingers are left alone, so a clip baked with a poor grip keeps it. Proven: a 30 mm grip puts every fingertip within 2 mm of the bar and none more than 1 mm in, on Mixamo, VRM and MPFB names; seeks equal playing. Not measured: speed. |
| Repeated bone names (`@margoengine/rigging`, 2026-11-15) | Enforced: `checkRig`, `rigJoints` and every entry that takes `RigJoint`s refuse two joints with one name, with a TypeError that names it. glTF 2.0 (3.4) does not require node names to be unique, but rig joints, IK chains, retarget maps and the VRM tools find bones by name, so a repeat would bind the wrong bone. Rename repeated nodes before rigging (for example add the node index). |
| Voxel weights (`@margoengine/rigging/voxel-weights`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: resolution 8 to 512, closing 0 to 8. By method: parts closer than about one voxel join, so a finer grid is what keeps fingers apart, and memory grows with the cube of `resolution` (about 20 bytes a voxel). An open mesh is filled only from a bone inside it, through voxels with surface on four of six directions. A part no bone reaches takes straight-line distances, counted in `unreached`. Authored weights are the yardstick by strongest bone, not by value: the mean row gap to the authored weights is 0.30 to 0.54, as bone heat's is 0.32 to 0.43. Not measured: speed in a quiet run (Seed-san's hair mesh took about 3 s at resolution 64 and 33 s at 128 while other lanes ran). |
| Automatic rig (`@margoengine/rigging/autorig`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: resolution 32 to 384, closing 0 to 8. By method: one humanoid standing in a T or A pose, arms clear of the body, two separate feet at the lowest point of the mesh, so a figure on a plinth, with its feet joined, or in another pose fails with code `failed` or gets a wrong skeleton. Fingers are not placed; the hand is one bone. Joints go by body proportion along the solid's paths, so a joint sits 2 to 4 percent of the height from where people put it (LIM-282), and more on a body far from adult proportions. A skirt or coat that joins the legs on a figure of over 4.5 heads puts the hips by proportion, not by what the mesh shows. Facing comes from the feet; on feet with no clear front +z is assumed and `facingFound` is false. A figure turned more than two degrees against the grid is voxelized again square on, which costs a second pass; a turned figure's joints still move by up to 0.03 of the height, a voxel or two. Bone rotations are all zero: the pose carries offsets only. Stand-in: the refused box and the README's figure of boxes are written by hand. Run only by hand and not committed, as their licences do not allow it: two more unrigged figures, which gave plausible skeletons with nothing to mark them against. Not run: a rigged mesh drawn on a GPU or opened in another tool. Not measured: speed in a quiet run (0.5 to 3 s a figure without weights while other lanes ran). |
| Corrective shapes (`@margoengine/rigging/correctives`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: 1 to 64 samples a pose space. By method: `pose` and the joint's rotation are read as rotation vectors from `rest`, so a shape reads up to half a turn from rest and the reading jumps sign past it; a clip's track on a driven target is overwritten. Not proven: no real file with correctives was found, so the proof is a real rig and clip with a stand-in morph target. Not measured: speed. |
| Weight transfer (`@margoengine/rigging/transfer`, 2026-11-06) | By method: the two meshes must be in one pose and space. Either facing passes the angle test, so a layer with its surface parallel to the wrong limb's and inside `maxDistance` takes that limb. The fill is a weighted average, so it blends and never sharpens. A target with nothing of the source around it gets the nearest weights, which can be far from an author's: 41% to 69% agreement on parts of the Twist sample with no surface around them. Not measured: speed in a quiet run. |
| Face tracking (`@margoengine/rigging/face`, 2026-11-06) | By method: morph targets and VRM expressions only, so a jaw or eye moved by a bone is not driven; the VRM presets are a fixed reading of the 52, and no value stands for `relaxed`. A clip's track on a driven target is overwritten. Not proven: no real model named with these shapes was found and no live tracker has been run; the name matching is proven on stand-in targets, the avatar path on a real VRM avatar with frames the test wrote. Not measured: speed. |
| Powered ragdolls (`@margoengine/ragdoll/powered`, 2026-11-06) | By method: joint motors keep a pose and cannot lift a character, so standing needs the `root` spring, which is an outside force. Motors add mass and inertia to small bodies (up to an eighth of the heaviest neighbour, a tenth of the heaviest limb), so a powered ragdoll is a little heavier than a limp one. A joint's torque cap and gains come from the limb's real centre of mass and inertia in the pose motors were added in, so a limb whose mass sits close to its joint gets a soft motor: with the hips pinned, Seed-san's head sags 0.080 rad and stays there, where a rod per body read 0.030, and Knight's holds at 0.000 where a rod per body fell 0.82 rad. A higher `frequency` stiffens it. The default cone clips most clips. Measured on the Rig_Medium walk at 6 Hz: mean 0.1 rad behind the clip, the worst bones (hands, feet) 0.5 rad at peak. Not proven: Rapier 0.21 is the only version run; no timing yet. |
| Partial ragdolls (`Ragdoll.activate(limb)`, 2026-11-06) | By method: a limb is a bone and everything under it, so a hand without its fingers takes a list of parts of `ragdoll.bones` instead. A limb hangs from bodies that reach each frame's pose at that frame's physics step, so it is drawn up to one step behind a fast parent. A bone of the limb under a limp parent that is handed back alone follows its parent's drawn pose a frame late. |
| Getting up (`@margoengine/ragdoll/getup`, 2026-11-06) | By method: two clips, chosen at the root bone only, so a body on its side takes whichever is nearer. `root` is a top-level node. The character turns about the up axis only and the blend covers the rest; a limb far from the clip's pose crosses the body during the blend, with no collision. Not proven on an authored get-up clip: none is in the repository, so the proof plays the rig's Death_A and Death_B backward (stand-in clips, real rig, real physics). |
| Body shapes from the skin (`@margoengine/ragdoll/hulls`, 2026-11-06) | By method: one skin is read, the first that holds the root bone, since skins have separate bind spaces. A bone the skin has no bind pose for keeps its capsule. Vertices shared evenly by bones count for none at the default `minWeight`, so a hull can stop short of a joint. A hull is convex: a bone that carries a concave part overshoots into the hollow. The box lies along the bone, the smallest over 18 turns 5 degrees apart. Measured on Knight.glb, ray silhouette overlap with the mesh over a front and a side view: capsules 0.13, boxes 0.65, hulls 0.93; on Fox.glb, capsules 0.43, hulls 0.78. Thicker shapes reach the floor sooner: with limits the body cannot meet lying down, such as the default quarter-turn cone on a T-posed arm, a limit and a contact fight and the limb keeps moving (hand at about 0.8 m/s after 16 s on Knight.glb, limits held to under 1 rad over). Skipping the limit correction on touching limbs settled it, but let a spine fold 2.3 rad past its limit, so it is not done; give a fitted body limits it can reach (`swing` 2.5 settles under 0.05 m/s). |
| Saved profiles (`@margoengine/ragdoll/profile`, 2026-11-06) | By method: bones bind by node name, so a renamed rig needs its profile edited. Limits are measured from the pose the ragdoll is built in, so a profile fits only that pose; the humanoid preset reads a T or A pose and its hinges and ranges are wrong for any other. One cone per joint is narrower than a real shoulder or hip in some directions and wider in others. Mass shares are one published adult male table, de Leva 1996. A hinge is a knee or an elbow only: spines, shoulders and ankles are cones. Proved on Knight.glb, with Mixamo names only as stand-in names on the same rig. |
| Character-ragdoll bridge (`@margoengine/ragdoll/character`, 2026-11-27) | By method: the capsule takes one collision group of the 16 (default 14, or the highest the ragdoll leaves free), so a ragdoll that fills all 16 is refused. A knockdown hands the fall the velocities the hit boxes had at the last step, so a character that stopped walking a step before is hit standing still. Recovery puts the capsule on the first fixed surface under the hips (a raycast of 100 m), and with no get-up clip blends the bones back where they lie. The bridge keeps no state in a physics snapshot: a restore needs the bridge in the state it had then. |
| Shared physics debug view (`@margoengine/physics/debug-view`, 2026-11-27) | Enforced: a positive `width`, a live world attached to the engine. By method: everything is drawn as one segment line of `@margoengine/lines`, which needs WebGPU: on the WebGL2 compatibility layer `attach` rejects with Lines' coded `webgpu` error, so pass a `sink` and draw `collect()`'s buffers yourself (one `gl.drawArrays(gl.LINES, ...)`). Lines are rebuilt each frame on the CPU from every source, so a large world costs a buffer copy a frame; no speed figure yet (speed phase). Shapes other than spheres, boxes, capsules, cylinders and cones draw as the box around them, as `physics.debugRender` does. |
| Character walk and jump (`CharacterController.walk`, `jump`, 2026-11-27) | Enforced: a positive finite jump speed, three finite numbers for a velocity, six for a state. By method: gravity is the world's, taken along `up` only (a gravity across `up` is left out); the walk velocity is followed in the air as on the ground (full air control, as Rapier's controller and the three.js example leave it), so ease it yourself for less; a jump is allowed only when the last move ended grounded (no grace time after leaving a ledge). Landing and a ceiling zero the speed along `up`; a platform rising under a jump adds its speed to the take-off step only. The controller's state is not in `physics.takeSnapshot()`: take `takeState()` with it. |
| Balance (`@margoengine/ragdoll/balance`, 2026-11-06) | By method: it stands on joint torques alone by default, every one a pair inside the body with the ankle held to what the sole answers; `carry` is an outside force, off unless set. It adds inertia to feet and shins (0.012 of the whole mass times the leg's length squared) brings the character's island to 8 solver passes at the least, and gives a hull foot a flat sole of four corners while it balances. Its torques are forces through the whole step, so a world set above 8 only helps: over 24 roundings at 8, 10 and 16 passes no figure steps late or falls, and no hips drift 0.0020 m. A stance knee takes its torque from the balance with a spring beside it that has no damper and grows with how far the knee is off its bend, full at 0.15 rad, so `motors.setStrength` does not reach it. It stands and steps at the heading it was added at: no turning or walking. Flat ground only, at the height of the feet; no stairs or slopes. `motors.hit` weakens a limb's motor, not the balance torques, which follow the global `strength` only. Measured over 24 hull roundings each at 8 passes: all seven figures settle with no step after the first second, at 0.0006 m/s at most. Worst drift of the hips over five seconds: Knight.glb 0.0009 m, Barbarian 0.0004, Ranger 0.0006, Rogue 0.0010, Mage 0.0003, Seed-san 0.0019, RiggedFigure 0.0005; no foot slides more than 0.0012 m. On 96 other roundings at 8 passes one Seed-san foot slid 0.0020 m and 8 of the 672 figure runs shook a bone over 0.005 m/s; at 10, 16 and 20 passes none did (known-bugs.md, "A standing figure can shake"). Pushes of 1.5 m/s in four directions over 32 roundings on Knight.glb: 125 of 128 pass the push test's reading and none fall; the old assist passed 122 and fell in none, holding about half the weight from outside. The other three are still stepping six seconds after the push and stand still by fourteen. Those 128 pushes at 8 / 10 / 16 passes, failing the reading / falling within four seconds: Knight 3/0, 1/0, 7/0; Rogue 1/0, 4/0, 2/0; Ranger 7/0, 8/0, 8/0; Mage 21/0, 25/0, 13/0; Barbarian 29/9, 36/14, 43/30; RiggedFigure 96/95, 92/88, 96/96; Seed-san 113/108, 121/120, 128/128. Falls in 128 pushes at 8 passes at 0.5 / 1 / 1.5 m/s: Knight, Ranger, Rogue and Mage 0 / 0 / 0, Barbarian 0 / 8 / 9, RiggedFigure 60 / 63 / 95, Seed-san 69 / 93 / 108, so only the first four stay up at 1.5 m/s and RiggedFigure and Seed-san do not reliably take 0.5 (known-bugs.md, "A push throws"). Not measured: speed, including the cost of the added passes. |
| Uneven bone scales in ragdolls (`@margoengine/ragdoll`, 2026-11-06) | Enforced: zero and mirrored bones are refused. By method: any positive scale is taken. Bodies are rigid and sized in world units when the ragdoll is built, so a scale animated afterwards does not resize them. A bone's own uneven scale costs nothing: a fall with a stretched spine matches the same rig built unstretched to under 1 mm. A bone turned under an uneven scale above it is skewed, so the bones drawn below it stretch as it turns, as in IK, while the bodies keep their joint distance; the pose holds exactly where the bone went limp and drifts from its body as it turns away. A hull fitted to a skewed bone takes the scales of the bone's axes and not the skew. Proved on Seed-san's own scales (`hair_E`, 0.9995, 1, 0.9986); scales as large as 0.1, 3, 40 only on a stand-in rig. |
| Swept collision (`@margoengine/kinematics-constraints/swept`, 2026-11-06) | By method: colliders hold still during a check, so a moving obstacle needs its own stepping. The path checked is the shortest arc per bone for a chain, and the shortest arc about the hull's origin for a hull; if your animation plays another path, this one is certified, not yours. A contact is any gap at or below `minClearance` plus `tolerance` (1e-4), and a motion that starts there stops at time 0, so keep `minClearance` below the gap the pose was solved with. A gap of `d` and a speed bound of `s` give a step of `d / s`, so a motion that grazes a surface for a long way takes many steps: past the budget of 4,096 poses it ends `exhausted`, which is not clear; raise `maxSteps` or `tolerance`. |
| Robot swept collision (`@margoengine/robot-planning`, `sweepRobot`, 2026-11-06) | By method: as the swept collision row above, on the straight line in joint space between the two poses; if your animation plays another path, this one is certified, not yours. Self collision is checked only with `selfCollision: true`, on the pairs `Robot.selfCollisionPairs` lists. |
| Physical optics (`@margoengine/optics`, 2026-11-27) | By method: geometric and scalar wave optics of non-absorbing media; complex indices (metals, absorbing films) are not taken. `multilayerReflectance` and `thinFilmReflectance` treat layers as coherent and perfectly flat. `cieXYZ` is the Wyman, Sloan and Shirley fit of the CIE 1931 observer, within about 0.03 of the tabulated functions, not the table. `besselJ` is accurate to about 1e-14 for \|x\| up to a few hundred. `hexagonalHaloProfile` takes rays in the principal section of 60 degree wedges only (no skew rays, no plate or column orientation). `traceGradedRay` is fourth-order Runge-Kutta with the step the caller gives, so the invariant n cos(theta) holds to integration accuracy, not exactly. CPU only; no GPU code yet. |
| Joint-limit solver (`@margoengine/robot-planning/limits`, 2026-11-06) | By method: a local solver, so a start behind an obstacle can stall with a way round it; that is reported as `blocked`, and the planner is the way out. Convergence is proved from starts near an answer, not from anywhere. Ranges are per scalar joint: a ball joint is three of them, so a cone limit is a box of angles. Obstacle gradients are finite differences, so each nearby pair costs one pose per joint per iteration, and at most 48 pairs count per iteration, the closest. |
| Motion planner (`@margoengine/robot-planning/plan`, 2026-11-06) | By method: sampling planners are probabilistically complete, so `no-path` means the budget ran out, not that no path exists, and a narrow passage can need far more samples. Paths are feasible, not optimal: shortcutting only shortens them. A continuous joint plans on the line of its value, not on a circle, and samples stay one turn each way of the start. Colliders hold still during a plan. `planToPose` picks the first clear pose at the target; if that pose cannot be reached it reports `no-path` without trying another. Nearest neighbours are a plain scan, so a tree's cost grows with the square of its nodes. `Roadmap.grow` and `query` run on the calling thread. |
| URDF import (`@margoengine/robot-planning/urdf`, 2026-11-06) | By method: a mesh collision shape becomes its convex hull, so a concave link reads fatter than it is. A cylinder is a prism drawn round it, 16 sides by default. Only collision meshes are fetched; visuals are data, for your own loader. `<transmission>`, `<gazebo>`, `<material>` and sensors are not read, and `xacro` is not expanded: pass the generated URDF. A floating joint is six plain joints, three of them rotations in a fixed order, so it has the gimbal lock of Euler angles. A package path not listed in `packages` is a guess at the folder above the document. Mesh units are as the file gives them; only `scale` applies. `/urdf` loads `@margoengine/loaders/xml` at once and the rest of the loaders and `@margoengine/geometry` only when a mesh is met. |
| Batched GPU clearance (`@margoengine/robot-planning/gpu`, 2026-11-06) | By method: f32, about 1e-6 of a scene of size 1, so it sorts poses and proves nothing; `Roadmap.addPoses` proves each survivor on the CPU. An overlap reads zero or less with no depth. Poses only, not the motion between them: edges still take the CPU swept check. The base, the shapes and the colliders are read once. A `MeshVolume` and a field that is a plain function are refused. One invocation walks every pair of a pose in turn, with no broad phase, so a pose with many shapes and hulls of many points costs in proportion. A field query keeps 48 or 64 cells on its stack and past that answers with the safe lower bound, as `maxCells` does. Run on the RTX A6000 only. |
| Concave obstacles (`@margoengine/kinematics-constraints/sdf`, 2026-11-06) | By method: `SDFVolume` is only as fine as its grid. A wall thinner than a cell may not be in the field at all, and the default margin of one cell's diagonal reads every obstacle that much fatter; a grid must hold the whole obstacle, because past its edge a reading is the distance to the grid. Both volumes take a rotation, one uniform scale and a move, no shear. A crossing segment reads minus its radius and an overlapping hull reads zero or less on a mesh, which ranks poses and is not a depth. Mesh queries prune with a box round the query, so a long diagonal link visits more of the tree than it needs. `/sdf` is the one entry that loads `@margoengine/bvh/inside`, for the sign of a solid mesh. |
| `p-morph` build plus first frame (accepted only for now, open in [known-bugs.md](known-bugs.md#build-plus-first-frame-of-100-morphed-copies-is-still-slower-than-threes-webgl-backend)) | 154 ms, or 125 to 143 with `PBRModel.compile()` (first frame 17), against three's WebGPU 217 and WebGL 54, busy-machine diagnostic. |
| `PBRModel.compile()` | Compiles for the canvas pass under the lights and effects set when it is called. A later change to either, a batched textureless mesh, and any pass other than beauty compile on the draw as before. |

## Browser matrix (batch 273, 2026-11-15)

Measured with `packages/webgl2-compat/scripts/browser-matrix.mjs` (the copy-paste command is in the
[webgl2-compat README](../packages/webgl2-compat/README.md#how-it-is-tested)) in the browsers that most often lack
WebGPU. Every case runs natively on WebGPU and through the WebGL2 compatibility layer in the same browser. A pass meets
the case's own bar (the compatibility check's 0.1% of pixels and 0.25 mean for the basic scene, float64 within 1e-5 for
inverse trig, the materials check's unlit colours within 3, the voxel traversal check's bar); a refusal throws a coded
`MargoError` with its help link; a difference is a measured gap that is not a bug; unmeasured is a row the browser
itself cannot give (no WebGPU adapter for a native row, or a screenshot that shows no WebGL2 canvas for a picture
row). Results only: no timings.

| Browser | OS | GPU (as the browser reports it) | Rows | Bugs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Firefox 157.0 | Windows 11 | NVIDIA RTX A6000; WebGL2 reports "ANGLE (NVIDIA, NVIDIA GeForce 8800 GTX Direct3D11 ...), or similar", WebGPU adapter info empty | 91 | 0 |
| Safari 27.2 | macOS 27.2.1 | Apple M6; WebGL2 reports "Apple GPU", WebGPU adapter vendor and architecture "apple" | 25 measured | 0 (4 rows not measured, below) |
| Chrome 124.0.6367.219 | Android 15 (Pixel_8 emulator, user build) | SwiftShader through ANGLE on Vulkan ("Android Emulator OpenGL ES Translator"); `navigator.gpu` present, no WebGPU adapter | 84 (native 8 refusals, 31 unmeasured; layer 33 pass, 12 unmeasured) | 0 |
| Safari, iOS Simulator | iOS 27.2 (iPhone 18 Pro) | the Mac's GPU (a simulator, not a device result) | pending | Remote Automation is still off in the simulator's Safari settings (no simulator holds the setting, checked 2026-11-15), so `safaridriver` finds no session host; the Mac's screen was also locked |

In Firefox and Safari every row not listed below passes, natively and on the layer: the basic scene (4x MSAA, exact
pixel, two views), the compatibility feature level (native only: the layer has no adapter to ask), 32 of the 33
feature probes, the eight materials scenarios, the gltf/pbr quad and the voxel path tracer traversal.

| Row | Browser | Native WebGPU | WebGL2 layer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| features: msaaAspects | Firefox 157 | pass | refusal `compatibility-layer`: sampling a stencil aspect needs `WEBGL_stencil_texturing`, which this WebGL2 lacks |
| features: bitmapCopies | Firefox 157 | pass | difference, 1,521 values: a straight-alpha copy of a pixel with alpha 0 keeps its colour on the layer ([11, 200, 7, 0]) where Firefox's native copy zeroes it ([0, 0, 0, 0]); the layer keeps both copy rules the probe checks, native breaks one |
| post: GTAO creases | Firefox 157 | pass | difference: 16 x 16 occlusion values, mean 0.938, largest gap 0.0225 and mean gap 0.00056 against native |
| features from canvasRead on (27 probes), materials, gltf/pbr, post | Safari 27.2 | not measured | not measured: the Mac's screen locked during the run, Safari then fired no animation frames, the canvasRead probe waited for one and the WebDriver session stopped answering ("fetch failed", then timeouts). A run earlier that day, before the lock, passed them all except bitmapCopies (a difference of 1,196 values, the same alpha 0 copy rule as Firefox) and the GTAO gap; its report was overwritten, so these rows are rerun with the screen unlocked. The matrix now refuses at the start when the browser fires no frames; a rerun later on 2026-11-15 was refused that way, the screen locked again |
| basic scene (3), gltf/pbr, post, voxel traversal, materials, compatibility feature level | Android Chrome 124 | refusal: `webgpu` for the basic scene ("WebGPU adapter unavailable"), `unsupported` for the others | basic scene, gltf/pbr and materials (12 rows) unmeasured: the emulator shows no WebGL canvas at all, a plain one cleared to red included (in [known-bugs.md](known-bugs.md)); GTAO and the voxel traversal, read back, pass |
| features (31 probes) | Android Chrome 124 | unmeasured: no WebGPU adapter | pass, judged alone (inverseTrig within 1e-5 of float64, bitmapCopies keeps both copy rules, the rest without an error or GL error); no native result to compare |

Found and fixed by the matrix: every pick in Firefox answered the first mesh, because Firefox clears an integer
target through float32 (KB-FX273 in [known-bugs.md](known-bugs.md)). Safari's WebDriver element screenshot of a
WebGPU canvas comes back black in Safari 27.2, so the matrix crops the canvas out of the page screenshot instead; that
is a WebDriver behaviour of Safari and not a Margo defect. The same run found that `DynamicInstances.pick` on the
layer could answer null right after the first frame, while the layer's CPU culling route was still loading (fixed, in
[known-bugs.md](known-bugs.md)). On Android the matrix found that it could not drive Chrome on a user-build image
(Playwright's command line is ignored there) and that its cases assumed a native adapter; both are fixed in the script,
which now drives Chrome through its own DevTools socket and runs the layer's probes alone (in
[known-bugs.md](known-bugs.md)).

### Rerun 2026-11-27 (Windows 11, packages built at b958f1a9b6)

The same script on the workstation (Ryzen 9 9950X with its integrated AMD Radeon graphics, and an RTX A6000). Results
only: no timings.

| Browser | GPU (as the browser reports it) | Rows | Bugs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Firefox 157.0 (Playwright's build) | NVIDIA RTX A6000 | 95: native 48 pass; layer 44 pass, 1 refusal, 2 differences | 0 |
| Edge 158.0.4370.33, `MARGO_GPU=amd` | AMD Radeon integrated (`amd`, `rdna-2`; ANGLE Direct3D 11) | 95: native 48 pass; layer 43 pass, 4 differences | 0 |
| WebKit 27.2, Playwright's Windows build (not Safari; no WebGPU, no `OffscreenCanvas`) | not reported | 81: native 8 refusals, 33 unmeasured; layer 37 pass | 3 reported, below |

- Firefox: `msaaAspects` refuses (`compatibility-layer`, no `WEBGL_stencil_texturing`); `bitmapCopies` differs in the
  same 1,521 values as on 2026-11-15 (the layer keeps both copy rules, Firefox's native copy breaks one); GTAO creases
  differ by at most 0.046 (mean gap 0.00084), against 0.0225 and 0.00056 on 2026-11-15. The cause of that growth was
  not traced; the row has no bar beyond 1/255 for a pass.
- AMD integrated: `implicitFootprint` and `mipFiltering` differ by the driver's compressed mip blend (accepted
  2026-11-10; `features-browser.mjs` holds the layer to native's LOD there), `derivativeBranch` by native's own error
  (KB-AMD-HELPERDERIV1), GTAO creases by at most 0.047 (mean gap 0.00083). Every step of the package's `test:gpu`
  (32 steps, WebGPU against the layer on the same GPU) passes on this GPU, at d88c50b716.
- WebKit, Windows build: `external` needs `VideoFrame` and the materials video case needs `captureStream`, which this
  build lacks. `bitmapCopies` is a wrong result on the layer there, from a browser defect: the build's 2D `drawImage`
  composites a `premultiplyAlpha: 'none'` bitmap as premultiplied, and the layer tells a straight bitmap from a
  premultiplied one by such a draw, so partly transparent straight bitmaps are copied wrong
  ([known-bugs.md](known-bugs.md), KB-WEBKIT-BITMAPALPHA1). Safari 27.2 on macOS kept both copy rules on 2026-11-15.

## Platform

| Limit | Starts at | Why | What you see | Escape hatch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Physics kernel download (`@margoengine/physics`, `Physics.load()`, 2026-11-24) | By size: the kernel is a deflated Wasm blueprint inside the entry's JavaScript, inflated and compiled by the first `Physics.load()`, once per app; no Wasm file, bundler plugin or peer install. Before 2026-11-24 the solver was Rapier, a 3,082,103 byte Wasm (1,176,707 gzip) with a 270,338 byte lazy chunk. | One file less for every app, and a solver that is Margo's own. | `Physics.load()` rejects with a `MargoError` (`failed`) when the blueprint cannot be compiled (a Content Security Policy without `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` among them); the next call tries again. | Allow `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` as `docs/csp.md` says. |
| Boundary-layer wind and Mann turbulence (ATMO-01) | Dyer–Paulson stability is a surface-layer closure for fixed roughness above flat ground. Positive L is stable, negative L is unstable and positive infinity is neutral. The finite Mann box advects with the sampled mean layer, tapers within one vertical cell at the boundaries and tiles horizontally. Shear and taper are algebraic, without projection. | Pinned scalar Weather and native Physics agree on the same grid and continuous queries. | Nonlinear and rogue waves (`@margoengine/physics/rogue`, 2026-11-26, SEA-03) | By method: second-order random waves (Dalzell's kernels over a finite set of equal-variance components, default 160 drawn up to 3 times the peak frequency), not a phase-resolved nonlinear evolution (no high-order spectral or NLS solver): four-wave focusing enters through the statistics and the rogue events they draw, not through the waves' own evolution. The kinematics are linear under Wheeler's stretching (the second-order potential of Sharma and Dean, as Alberello et al. restate it, carries a glyph the restatement leaves uncertain); the pressure takes the second order's rise as hydrostatic. Rogue waves are constrained NewWaves, each within a window of 8 zero-crossing periods and wavelengths (inside it, the components' amplitudes vary with the window, so the sea's local spectrum is the event's); drawn ones come at one wave per zero-crossing wavelength squared per zero-crossing period (Fedele's space-time extremes not used), at the rate four-wave focusing adds beyond the second-order sea's own. No breaking: a crest steeper than Barthelemy et al.'s (2018) onset is kept. Runs of high waves (the three sisters) by Kimura's first-order chain: lag-two correlation ignored, a point's record of linear Gaussian heights (Goda 1983 found observed runs of two to three waves longer in swell); kappa from the spectrum is biased toward short groups, and the corrected estimate raises the rate of three in a row about 2.6 times at 1.5 H_s, the main uncertainty; three sisters stand at one point, not along a crest. The default iron ore is 0.1 mm fines. A per-opening mixture can release 12 mm pellets and fines with separate mass carries. The scene supplies the mass fractions. The outflow port supplies one total cargo flux, with zero added jet velocity. | Mass is accounted for, plumes settle by grain size, slicks drift with the water and wind, and a breach's cargo follows the hull. | Finite instantaneous oil spills use Fay's three axisymmetric spreading regimes and follow the live sea. The transitions join the radius laws. Turbulence and advection act on the resulting parcels. Submerged parcels use the sea's depth flow and reflect from the moving waterline. Fin jets assume a circular steady nozzle above a flat submerged bed. They integrate Phares wall stress and van Rijn pickup at 96 stress evaluations per eligible impulse and release four parcels. Below one nozzle diameter or with the footprint option, stress is averaged. The 40 µm noncohesive silt option extrapolates the low-flow sand relation. The live bed option debits and deposits packed volume on a finite mobile layer. The layer must fit above bedrock with a single sediment writer. Each vertex limits its own contribution to its remaining mobile stock. The tracer ledger still records settled mass. Optional Stiver–Mackay evaporation assumes fixed slick temperature, air-side transfer and density, and uses the Fay area computed from the initial oil volume by default. A prescribed fixed area uses the initial volume divided by that area as its reference thickness. Fixed exposure has a cold-oil lab comparison. An independent expanding-slick evaporation comparison remains open. Vapour is accounted for separately. Optional emulsification reports water uptake, density, viscosity and thicker film with the footprint computed from the initial Fay release and its age. It assumes constant dry oil viscosity and maximum water fraction. Early uptake in the Troll field case is up to 36.74 percentage points low. An optional closed water pool exchanges each specified soluble component with its slick and permits first-order aqueous biodegradation. It uses the initial oil volume and a separate fixed water volume, with an independent partition coefficient and transfer velocity for each constituent. The dissolved pool moves with the slick. The model supports optional emulsion and a supplied fixed exchange area. Bulk evaporation and droplet dispersion use separate releases. A 24 h closed-tank naphthalene endpoint is 10.7% low, and measured biodegradation and open-water exchange remain open. Wave-averaged Stokes transport uses a fixed, uniformly spaced directional spectrum with still-water depth. Supply the Eulerian mean in the optional current field. Optional Delvigne–Sweeney dispersion uses up to the configured class slots, one centroid per diameter class, breaker exposure sampled at the slick centre, and a prescribed maximum diameter. Resurfacing rejoins the parent slick. Resolved bed wash requires a valid log-layer velocity sample and explicit roughness length. The rectangle supports up to 65,536 midpoint samples. It estimates mean tangent stress and omits the unresolved near-wall jets and vortices. Optional cohesive flocs have fractal dimension 2 and use a spherical drag correction up to particle Reynolds number 1,000. The flow supplies dry concentration and shear rate. Optional shear-limited breakup needs positive floc yield force below e^4 times water density times kinematic viscosity squared divided by 9. It predicts laboratory dilution sizes with 6.58 micrometres RMS error. Fin-jet parcels enter suspension at the van Rijn reference level below the free surface. The default and minimum are 1% of local water depth. Positive oil shear yield stress selects a coherent fixed-volume film. The film uses zero net spreading tension and omits evaporation, breaking dispersion and fracture. The thickness probe reports a nominal radial film. Bed pickup accepts one custom sinking grain size. The optional dense-sand damping was developed for clean packed sand of 51–562 µm at porosity near 0.4. The largest held-out wash retreat error is an underprediction by a factor of 2.81. | Cloth tethers (`setTethers`, long range attachments, 2026-11-27) | By method: each free particle is tied to one pin, its nearest by the shortest path through the structural and shear edges at rest; the tie is a sphere around that pin's current position, so a pin that moves far in one step drags its particles' spheres with it. Ties are rebuilt on the CPU (Dijkstra over the body's edges) when a tear, a pin change or a new stretch needs it, not every step. A particle tied to a pin that the cloth folds around (a geodesic longer than the straight line) may still reach any point within that geodesic, so tethers bound the stretch along the cloth, not each edge. Measured (`tests/soft-tethers.test.js`): a 2 by 10 m sheet at one pass a step stretches 0.65 percent without and none with; a particle inside its sphere moves bit for bit as untied. | Kim et al. 2012's unilateral projection, which removes the stretch few passes leave without stiffening a slack cloth. | Only pins anchor: a particle held by an attachment to a rigid body (`soft.attach`) is not an anchor; the rebuild walks every edge of a tethered body. | Pin the particles that hold the cloth, or attach it and pin the attached row. |

Measured (`tests/soft-skinned-cloth.test.js`): a cape on a character that runs, turns and bobs stays within its max distances and backstops to 1e-5 m over 240 steps, swinging out to its limits; free below its pinned row it moves bit for bit as a cloth pinned there. | Garments follow the body where they must and swing where they may, as character cloth is authored in games and DCC tools. | The skinned mesh is skinned on the CPU every frame; a GPU path (skinned in the vertex stage) is open, as for all soft solving. | Skin with the renderer's joint matrices; give the shoulders and waistband 0 and the hems the most. |

By method: symplectic Euler keeps a modified energy, and each strike hands the swing from a falling ball to a level one, so a hung cradle at e = 1 loses about g h^2 / l of its energy a strike, second order in the substep h: 0.019 percent at the standard tier's 8 substeps (the end ball's turning height 97.7 percent of the release after 60 s, 115 strikes), 0.0012 percent at the high tier's 32 (99.85 percent). Origin cells are a power of two of metres (default 4,096), so an f32 offset inside a cell keeps about 0.25 mm. Its work a step, counted in `stats.work` (each thread's share in `stats.threadWork`), is substeps x (particle updates + edge solves + particle-collider tests), and a slow frame steps up to 8 steps at once. Not timed (build phase). | Thousands of particles stepped and drawn with no readback or upload. | The WebGL2 layer and Node pay the whole step on the CPU, on one thread unless given more. | `soft.create(desc)` for self contact, tearing and two-way coupling; fewer particles or substeps on the WebGL2 layer. |

Presets are representative, not exact: the same named fabric measured elsewhere differs by up to ten times (shirting cotton G = 0.367 gf/cm/deg in Luible 2008 against 3.50 in Seo and Tamura 2017; wool gabardine 0.588 against 2.93; silk habutae 0.11 to 0.51 across three papers), and no KES-F measurement of canvas or sailcloth was found, so those presets are the nearest measured fabrics (jute and polyester plain weaves). Rows with no compliance are damped Levenberg-Marquardt style (contacts by sqrt(f32 epsilon) of their diagonal, edges and links by their violation squared up to that), so a contact set with no answer (a particle between surfaces closer than its thickness) is met as nearly as it can be, not exactly. A light body pinched by a cloth leaves no faster than the sides close while they pinch it; afterwards it rides the cloth. The two halves of a cut body separate once by their contact thickness (the particles' radius plus the faces'), up to 4 radii in a step. Measured cost, paired A/B against the sweep it replaces (this Mac, loaded, one process, per-round minimums of 7; quiet rerun before release): a 12 by 12 cloth of 1 kg particles pinned at its corners, 1.05 to 4.26 ms a step (4.1 times); the same cloth with a 1,000 kg box on it, 1.49 to 62.2 ms a step (42 times), where a thousand-to-one mass ratio needs hundreds of Newton steps in its hardest pieces (the sweep took none, and let the box through or threw it). By method: two copies, so a key takes twice the room; a write is two reads, a write and a read back, each of the whole save. A failed read of the newest copy counts as damage, so the write after it can go over that copy. CRC-32 finds accidents and is no signature: the 802.3 polynomial has Hamming distance 4 up to 91,607 bits (about 11 KB), and 3 at least to 131,072 bits (Koopman, DSN 2002), so on a bigger save every 1 or 2 bit error and every burst of 32 bits is found, and other damage slips past about once in 2^32. Not proved: power loss, which nothing here has tested, so that the fsync really orders the disk is taken from the system's promise. Checked in a real browser with WebGPU removed (`npm run check:no-webgpu`, part of `check:merge`: every site demo installs the layer without WebGPU, shows the message without WebGL2 too, downloads none of the layer with WebGPU, throws no uncaught error, and the preview draws two coloured boxes, read back as pixels) and in [gates-browser-tests.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/gates-browser-tests.json). The WebGL2 compatibility layer (`@margoengine/webgl2-compat`) is what the site runs without WebGPU, and the fuller fallback: it runs the WebGPU code of core and the packages as an optional download that WebGPU users never load ([webgl2-compat-roadmap.md](webgl2-compat-roadmap.md)). Compute entry points that store only their own texel run as fragment draws and those with a bounded number of stores as point draws, on the GPU. The rest (atomics, workgroup memory, barriers, stores in loops of unknown length) run on the CPU in JavaScript: a clustered-binning kernel over 3,456 clusters takes 1.5 ms with 16 lights, 2.8 ms with 64 and 9.4 ms with 256 (37 to 94 million loop iterations a second); a 64-wide workgroup reduction with 7 barriers runs 4.4 million invocations a second (65,536 in 14.9 ms). | WebGL2 has no compute shaders, storage buffers or atomics. | The same results as WebGPU (the layer's compute check compares both on one GPU), slower: GPU-written inputs of a CPU kernel are read back synchronously (counted in the device's `stalls`). A NaN that a CPU-tier kernel stores, bitcasts or packs is written as the one quiet NaN 0x7fc00000 (f16 0x7e00), so its sign and payload are not kept, which WGSL 15.7.2 allows (any value) and which keeps the bytes the same on every engine and on the interpreter. A CPU-tier dispatch stops at its work budget, 100,000,000 invocations plus loop iterations by default (`cpuWorkBudget`), and is reported as a `GPUInternalError` coded `failed` with nothing stored. Two numbers: the base, everything `install()` loads (device, GLSL back end, WGSL front end, the render path), is 70,274 B (235,884 B minified); the lazy part is 30,819 B (96,623 B minified): the compute runtime, which only a page that makes its first compute pipeline loads, about 6,000 B of it the interpreter chunk that only a page without `unsafe-eval` downloads, and the texture read-back chunk, which a page loads with its first `copyTextureToBuffer` or compute pipeline. All of it, as one file, is 100,514 B. A page on WebGPU downloads none of it. | The layer translates WGSL to GLSL and runs WebGPU's device model on WebGL2, so the base holds a full WGSL front end (check.ts 61 KB, parser, builtins) and the GLSL emitter. Property names are not mangled. | Accepted difference (Scott accepted, 2026-10-31; the limit itself was set 2026-10-30): the sizes gate holds the base to 73,000 B, not the 60,000 B target the roadmap once stated and no gate enforced. The base carries the full WGSL to GLSL translator and the WGSL checker, both needed on the first frame; native WebGPU always validates shaders, so a production build without the checker would behave differently. The lazy part is measured and gated separately. The five largest modules of the base by their share of the gzip bytes, before read-back left device/render.ts (2,080 B, 2026-11-06): device/render.ts 14.0 KB, glsl/emit.ts 13.9 KB, wgsl/check.ts 11.4 KB, device/resources.ts 5.0 KB, wgsl/builtins.ts 4.3 KB. | A page that never runs compute or reads a texture back pays the base only. [webgl2-compat-roadmap.md](webgl2-compat-roadmap.md) tracks the size work. |
| Content Security Policy | Enforced by the browser: core compiles its Wasm kernel, so `script-src` needs `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` (as do Draco and Basis). The standard WebGPU path and the other WebGL2 tiers need no `'unsafe-eval'`, workers included (the optional WebGL2 CPU compute tier of `webgl2-compat` builds its shaders with `new Function` where the page allows it, and without `'unsafe-eval'` runs the same kernels on an interpreter, 13 to 41 times slower, a diagnostic figure): the Draco/KTX2 decoder worker loads its Emscripten code with `importScripts`, and the build replaces the `new Function` wrapper generators in the Basis glue with closures, output byte-identical ([no-eval-workers.test.js](../tests/no-eval-workers.test.js)). No COOP/COEP. Checked with zero violations on Edge, one policy on the page and every worker ([csp-check.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/csp-check.json)). | Wasm is how the kernel stays small and fast. | Without `'wasm-unsafe-eval'`, `Engine.create` rejects (MargoError code `failed` naming the required `script-src` permission, with the browser compilation error as `cause` and a link to [CSP requirements](csp.md)) ([csp-check-negative.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/results/csp-check-negative.json)). | Headers for Cloudflare Pages, Netlify, Vercel and Nginx in [deploying.md](deploying.md). The tree opens cells by Barnes's 1994 test (d > side / theta + the centre of mass's offset), not the 1986 one, which kept one ring seed in ten (seed 3) crossed with edges 13 % uneven: on a 20,000-node graph that opens 10 % more cells on the first step in 2D (19 % in 3D) and 21 % (41 %) over the next 100 steps, counted. Enforced: a hull is a closed convex polyhedron with flat faces of at most 256 edges and no two neighbours that are one plane split in two, within about 0.8 degrees with every corner within half of FLAT, 1e-4 of the hull's size, of the other's plane (a mesh with such faces loses contact points, Gregorius 2015, so `addHull` refuses it); a real crease under 0.8 degrees between faces too wide to be one flat face is taken, as a hull of random points has them; its rows last for the world's life. By method: the separating axis test is linear in vertices per face and quadratic in edges, with no hill climbing or cached axis yet, so a hull of hundreds of faces costs a step more than it should until the quiet pass. By method: GJK stops after 64 descents, and the expanding polytope holds 96 vertices and 192 faces; a depth search that runs out gives no contact for that step and the next step tries again. By method: a point with a new id continues an old one within 2 cm on the first body, so a contact that jumps further starts its impulses from zero. By method: a contact's normal is found once a step and held for its substeps, and a point the body has not yet reached acts as a plane (Catto 2013's speculative point), so a fast body passing a corner can feel a ghost of that plane; not measured, batch 126 owns it. By method (2026-11-08): at one pass a substep a contact between two dynamic bodies that neither dominates is capped at an eighth of the substep rate (30 Hz at 4 substeps) while it carries under 50 times the lighter body's weight, as one pass settles no pile at a quarter; the ground, kinematic and dominant bodies and heavier loads keep the quarter. Measured at 4 substeps of one pass: the 20-row pyramid sleeps at 2.3 s, its top moved 32 mm, its bottom row 1.19 mm into the floor; 30 rows, whose bottom pairs carry about 40 times a cube's weight, sleep at 2.0 s and rest at 5.9e-4 m/s with sleeping off; the 1:100 and 1:1000 stacks keep the quarter and sag 14.4 and 137 mm. A deeper pile whose bottom pairs pass 50 times takes the quarter there; not measured past 30 rows. By method (2026-11-07): a substep relaxes as many times as it pushes, so 2 relaxing passes of joints and contacts at the defaults where there was 1: one pass left the friction anchors' push in a pile of 14 rows or more as speed, and it rocked for good. By method: a manifold's normal rows sweep until no impulse moves by more than rounding, at most 16 sweeps a pass, on the points' speeds alone; a relaxing pass settles in 3 to 8 sweeps on the 1:1000 stack. By method (2026-11-08): a manifold of four points ends each sweep with the exact step along the one pattern of its impulses that moves no body, the points' shares of one load among themselves, which the sweeps settled only by the leak (about 3 percent a sweep), so a soft pass ran all 16; it now settles in about 4 (perf-history 80). Friction keeps one sweep. By method (2026-11-08): inside the slop a biased pass closes a point rigidly to the slop's depth, (gap + slop) / h as a speculative row (Catto's Solver2D soft step), and the soft push acts only past it, so every point of a resting manifold rests at the same depth whatever its load: a cube released on a slope below tan t = mu holds under 1e-6 m from its first second (it moved up to 3.8e-5 m as its points sank at speeds that followed their loads). Measured on the harness, defaults and 4 substeps of one pass: creep 5.5e-5 and 5.9e-6 m to 0; the 1:1000 stack's top drifts 1.6e-8 and 1.4e-7 m (6.6e-7 and 3.7e-6 m before the exact step of the four points' shares); the 20-row pyramid at the defaults sleeps at 1.50 s (1.78 s before that step, 3.2 s earlier), and at 4 substeps of one pass, which fails its bars either way, moved its top 0.291 m (0.277) and its fastest box at 30 s 0.51 m/s (0.18); with the exact step of the four points' shares (2026-11-08) 0.270 m and 0.28 m/s, still awake until the eighth-rate spring of two movable bodies at one pass (above) let it sleep. By method (2026-11-08): a ball or a capsule meets the other surface at its core plus its radius along the normal, wherever it has turned to, so a rolling ball's point stays on the floor; its lever arm stays the step's contact point. By method (2026-11-08): a point struck while its gap is still open notes the speed it will meet the surface with, v^2 = v0^2 + 2 a d over the gap, gravity's gain added, so a ball from 1 m at e 0.5 peaks at 0.2487 m at the defaults and 0.2473 m at 4 substeps of one pass (was 0.2481 and 0.2432). By method: a resting contact sags by its load over its stiffness, which follows the lighter body, so a heavy box on a light one sits deeper: 3.9 mm at 1:100 and 3.5 cm at 1:1000 with metre cubes. A rolling ball slips 0.35 percent of its speed by 2.5 s, as friction is a stiff spring, and lands 0.13 percent over 5/7 g sin t. Enforced: a manifold holds four points. By method: the reduction always keeps the deepest point, so its area can fall short of the best four: 0.711 of the best at worst and 0.9915 on average over 3,000 random sets. Enforced: 536,870,912 pair rows and 32-bit offsets inside the block; a step throws when memory cannot hold the pairs. By method: pairs are found once a step over the motion expected at its start, so a body a contact turns round mid-step can leave its fat box until the next step; the margin is 0.04 m at any body size; a fixed body written by hand needs `touch`; a collider's row comes back only after a step. A single add or removal costs one pass over the lists, so adding one collider a frame to a very large world pays for the whole list. Until the narrow phase lands, two bodies touch when their fat boxes overlap, so islands run larger than they will. Writing a sleeper's columns does not wake it. A body at a steady pose with its energy under the threshold can go to sleep mid-air if nothing pushes it, as gravity is not a force the sleep test sees: a body at rest under gravity moves, so this needs zero gravity or `gravityScale` 0. A snapshot is the whole block, so its size follows capacity, not the bodies in use. By method: f32 state, as a far world needs `FloatingOrigin`. Needs Wasm SIMD, as core's kernel already does, so there is no second blueprint. `Physics`, `PhysicsBody` and `PhysicsCollider` of the entry serve free motion only: `setType`, `follow`, friction and the other contact settings, joints, queries, character controllers and `addModel` throw `unsupported` until their batch. `body.sleep()` and impulses take effect at the next step. | Own physics joints (`@margoengine/physics`, 2026-11-07) | By method: locks are exact along a path of joints, so a chain of 50 hung straight holds a 1000:1 end mass to under 1e-5 of its length, at rest and swung at 3 m/s. By method: a lock's turning arm is read at the start of a substep, so a light link under a large pull would turn as an explicit spring of stiffness about twice the pull times its arm; the pull of every taut lock of all three sliding axes therefore joins the inertia the joints' rows turn a body by (h^2 F . r across each arm pulled outward: the geometric stiffness of Tournier et al. 2015, taken into the mass on both sides of the step as Zhang and Skeel 1997 take a stiff force's gradient, so nothing is damped), and a link holds under any pull. A chain of 50 laid out level with a 1000:1 end mass, 1 kg links of a sphere's inertia (0.001 kg m2 at 0.05 m arms), holds 1e-4 of its length through its first swing, each joint included (0.084 mm and 0.024 mm to step 160, where it read 20 m long before; 100:1 and 10:1 hold it too). The price is frequency: a turn against the pull that a substep resolves is slowed by (h omega)^2 / 2 of itself (a 1.5 m bob's period by 1e-5), and one it does not resolve rings at a sixth of the substep rate. By method: nothing rings a snap down, so past the first swing, where the chain goes slack at each turn and snaps taut, the line reads 13 mm long and a joint opens 4.2 mm within 20 s (1,148 m before; `docs/known-bugs.md`). Sliding joints, ropes and the locks of the turning axes carry no such term. Where a branch or a ring ends a path, paths meet pass by pass: a grid under its own weight opens 0.18 mm at 8 by 8 and 0.95 mm at 30 by 30, a heavy hub with three arms 7.3 mm, and 5.3 to 8.7 mm with the hub started a micrometre to 0.3 mm aside, as the widest gap is the peak of a swing that rounding steers, but 1000 kg on the corner of an 8 by 8 grid of 1 kg links opens 69 mm and still moves at 0.2 m/s after 10 s (8 passes: 13 mm). By method: limits are one row at a time, so a long run of hinges on their stops carries its moment slowly: six links droop 48 mm, twelve droop 0.91 m and still move at 0.29 m/s in the last 5 s of 10. By method: a limit past its edge pushes back with the mass its row sees, as a contact does, so a limb a floor holds past its cone rests there: a hand of 0.36 kg comes to 0.02 rad past its cone, one of 3.6 g stays 0.49 rad past it under its 1.5 kg arm. At the edge a limit holds any load: a link of a hundredth of the mass carries a full one 0.008 rad past a cone of 0.2. By method: a rope is one row at a time, so two ropes under a 1000:1 end mass rest 35 mm long, 1.7 percent, and stay there. By method: a spring is implicit Euler, so with no damping one of 5 rad/s loses 23 percent of its amplitude in 10 s. `/articulation` (batch 128) is where branches and limits go exact. By method: one walk over every joint row a step, and rows and factors refreshed twice a substep, which the quiet pass may halve. By design: 2 passes at least for joints, so `iterations: 1` adds a settling pass for them; `generic` is not served yet. By design: a sensor reads the pose a step starts from, so an event comes up to a step after the overlap; two fixed bodies never meet, sensor or not; a disabled collider keeps its mass; dominance acts in contacts, not in joints. By method, four limits on the lock solve, each with a test that fails without it. (1) A row with under n u of its size left after the rows before it depends on them and carries nothing, n the rows of its path and u f32's epsilon (Higham 1990, stop 4.3 at his n u), read off Householder QR of M^-1/2 J^T so the doubles round each row only by its own length: a body held by ten rows on six freedoms stands still where it used to reach 18,904,462 m/s, and a path with 13 rows on 12 freedoms no longer keeps its dependent row (4e-7 of its size by elimination of J M^-1 J^T, 1e-32 now). Cost: a row within about sqrt(n u) radians of depending, 1.3e-3 rad on a path of 14 rows, is dropped too; and the kernel grew 4,449 B deflated (125,328 to 129,777 B). (2) A lock closes a gap at 3 m/s plus what the turning carries its anchors, the clamp of Buss and Kim 2005, whose D_max,i = d_i + D_max this is. A valid scene reaches it when a body is moved by hand off its joint or a hub turns at 8 rad/s at 100 m. Pairs are found once a step, so without it a joint 6 m open jumps a body past a wall in one substep. Cost: a wide gap takes more steps, and on the proof scenes it acted on 5 rows of 6,960 in the limb and moved no figure. (3) Where rows nearly depend on each other a push is a Gauss-Newton step outside its model, so a body's turn may rise by at most 0.2 rad a substep times N / M, and its centre by that much of its arm, N what the path asks and M what its bodies would each move (Buss and Kim 2005, section 4; they use 0.79 rad for inverse kinematics, here 0.79 lets a taut chain reach 39 m/s and 0.1 starts to cut the chain of fifty). A valid scene reaches it when a chain is pulled straight between two points further apart than it is long, the same pose as an arm reaching past its reach. Cost: what is cut stays open into the next substeps, and the whole path's push is cut, not only its bad direction, as a path has no singular value decomposition. It cut nothing in any scene of `kernel/tests/joints.rs`. (4) A warm start that would add more than a push's energy, half the island's mass times 3 m/s squared, is taken only as far as the minimum of the quadratic the passes descend. A valid scene reaches it when a limit catches a swing, as what the row holds is an impact and no load: once per catch on the proof scenes, keeping 0 to 7 percent. Cost: that row starts its substep cold, and no figure in `kernel/tests/joints.rs` moved. No paper does this; the line search is standard, its use here is our own. By method: a lock is exact and a contact is a capped spring, so a joint stretched through a wall drags its body through at about 1.5 m/s. By method: a turn past about 1 rad a substep leaves rows nothing to read, so a lock on a hub at 77 rad/s holds with 2 substeps, to 13 m on a radius of 10, and with 1 substep runs away and is refused after 59 steps. By design: a body past 1e15 in position or speed stops the world with `failed`, checked at the end of a step: a run away faster than that within one step would get past it, not seen in 200 random webs of 10,000 steps. Their top, 1.3e8 m/s for one step, is a kinematic turn of 77 rad/s forcing locks near a toggle, where the exact speed is one over the angle: only the pushing pass's bias is cut, after its speeds are solved in full, so a speed is answered in full. Scenes with no answer are only kept in the numbers: 60 random webs of unsatisfiable joints stay under 1e5 m/s, seed 45 spins under the 18,400 rad/s its kinematic turns can carry (2,559 rad/s; a cut of the whole solve once gave 162,278), and which seed is fastest changes with any constant; seeds 1 and 35 spin under 18,400 rad/s and hold every joint under the 56.85 m the scene's cube allows (956 rad/s and 38.0 m to step 400, 1,354 rad/s and 40.9 m to step 600), but near a toggle a row that does not yet depend is answered in full, so seed 49 reaches 10,991 m/s and a joint 165.8 m open and the 60 webs have no gap bar yet (`docs/known-bugs.md`). By method: each joint of the chain of 50 hung straight opens under 2e-5 m at rest and swung, under the same 1e-4 of its length as its stretch; laid out level and let fall, a joint opens 6.1 mm at 1:1, 6.2 mm at 10:1, 3.1 mm at 100:1 and 4.2 mm at 1000:1 within 20 s, from rows that turn within a substep once a snap has set the links turning (`docs/known-bugs.md`) | A joint in a branch, a loop or on its limits settles over passes, so its gap under a far heavier load is the price; a chain is exact. | A grid or ring of joints under a far heavier load opens a gap (0.95 mm at 30 by 30; 69 mm for 1000 kg on the corner of an 8 by 8 grid), and a long run of hinges on their stops droops. | Use a chain, which is exact. By method: one manifold of up to four points for each triangle a shape touches, each a pair row of its own, so a box across a crease holds both normals and a large box on a fine mesh solves a manifold per triangle under it.
