### Prefiltered IBL metadata capacity (2026-11-10)

The optional environment/prefiltered encoder refuses KTX2 key/value data above 4,294,967,295 bytes with RangeError before reading cube mips or allocating output. The total includes the metadata length word, key, payload and padding. A complete 8192-edge source cube needs at least 4,294,967,548 metadata bytes, even with a 1x1 BRDF LUT; 8192 and 16384 source edges cannot be saved in this lossless embedded-source format. Source edges through 4096 remain representable with every supported LUT edge (1..4096); this is a format capacity statement, not a promise of available memory or device support. Specular level byte offsets remain u64.

### Indexed cache variant deletion (2026-11-10)

The optional cache/eviction index coalesces removals in the same object-store transaction: each key is counted once, and byte/file totals are read and written once for the batch. AssetCache.delete(url) removes all Vary representations and associated records while preserving unrelated entries and exact usage. Repeated deletion does not subtract absent entries. Public interfaces and cache schema/version are unchanged. Evidence: packages/cache/test/eviction.test.js and the real IndexedDB evictionVariants browser case.

Live volume materials (review5, 2026-11-10): attenuation edits invalidate parsed optical-depth caches per channel; replacing the array invalidates all channels. Equal numeric assignments are not observable, so replacing an underflowed zero with explicit opacity requires array replacement or explicit infinite optical depth. Pointer animation retains authored logarithmic precision. Exact slab evidence and the unchanged mesh-slab/range limitations are documented in live-volume-materials.md.

Transmission activation from zero (2026-11-10): the physical parser retains medium state for an authored KHR_materials_transmission extension even when its factor is zero or omitted. Pointer playback activates tint for positive factors and restores the opaque path at zero. Native capture registration remains inactive until transmission is active. The existing scalar-thickness, screen capture and display-space blending limits still apply; this change adds no optical model.

### Range-cache response transit age (2026-11-10)

RangeCache includes elapsed request time together with the Age header when calculating the freshness deadline after a miss or a 304 response. For max-age=10, Age=3 and a four-second request, three seconds of freshness remain when the response arrives; Age=8 with the same transit is already expired. The controlled-clock regression checks the next cache session revalidates in both cases. Existing once-per-instance checking and offline fallback policies are unchanged; this is clock correctness, not a speed result. No public API or schema change.

## Review 5 refused HDR restoration

DOF, Bloom and SSAO require native WebGPU or at least the half-float compatibility tier. A restoration setup failure disposes and detaches the effect; a refused HDR PostStack detaches its children too. The engine reports the original coded error once through onError. Create fresh effects after capability recovery. Ten RTX A6000 cases use masked capabilities, not physical lower-tier devices. [Methods](review5-effect-restoration.md).

Locked-toolchain root entry measurements for this repair: DOF 9529 to 9538 gzip bytes, post 42105 to 42126; existing ceilings unchanged. Core plus stage remains 24209 gzip bytes.

SSGI exact one-bounce round trips on RTX A6000 / ANGLE D3D11 can differ by one display level despite identical GL commands. The first differing target is the ray trace; native WebGPU and ANGLE Vulkan pass this fixture. This separately recorded driver case leaves the exact assertion unchanged. See [raw values and reproduction](review5-ssgi-angle.md).

### Ambiguous flat pen tilt (2026-11-10)

When a pen event lacks spherical angles, a tilt pair with both components nonzero and either at +/-90 degrees maps to altitude zero and azimuth zero, following the informative Pointer Events Level 3/4 fallback convention. This cannot recover the pen's physical direction from ambiguous readings. The four flat axis directions and explicitly supplied altitude/azimuth retain their values; raw tilt samples remain unchanged. Evidence uses synthetic legacy events on the CPU and in the native/compatibility input browser gate, not a physical stylus. No public API change.

### Validated cache policy retention (2026-11-10)

AssetCache and RangeCache persist Cache-Control and Expires with their metadata. A 304 retains either omitted field, replaces any provided value and calculates freshness using the current response's Date/Age and request transit. An explicit no-cache therefore remains effective on later 304 responses that omit lifetime fields. Freshness updates require matching stored validators. Older records without saved policy remain conservatively revalidated until a response supplies it; their offline bytes remain usable. Public API and schema version are unchanged. Root and ranges entry sizes remain within their existing ceilings.

### Asset-cache delayed hit bookkeeping (2026-11-10)

An already-read response may still finish after its stored copy is evicted or replaced. Its background last-use update cannot recreate missing metadata, overwrite a newer file's size, type or validators, or move last use backwards. A 304 freshness update requires matching stored validators. The same four delayed-response cases run with plain and indexed eviction on the CPU stand-in and real IndexedDB; after a 150-byte-budget eviction only one 100-byte file remains, and replacing that file with an 80-byte response retains the new response's headers. Public API and schema are unchanged. This does not add global request coalescing or change the documented offline fallback.

Batch 162 raycast world-sphere reads: the sphere rejection reads each matrix and sphere value once; a matrix or sphere with impure index getters sees fewer reads. Spheres are unchanged bit for bit (NaN by value). Candidate gathering and traversal are unchanged and no world-sphere cache is kept. The claim covers read counts only, with timing pending the quiet rerun. [Evidence](whitepaper/batch-162-workcounts.md#row-161-world-sphere-reads).

Batch 162 Euler conversion: setFromEuler reads each angle once, so an EulerLike with impure getters sees 3 reads instead of 6; values are unchanged bit for bit. It costs +13 B gzip on math/quaternion. Matrix4.multiplyMatrices keeps its 80-read loop: a read-once version was bit-identical but cost +91 to +369 B gzip per bundling entry. The claim covers operation counts only, with timing pending the quiet rerun. [Evidence](whitepaper/batch-162-workcounts.md#row-19-euler-conversion).

Batch 162 hull eye and parametric samples: each hull face stores its farthest outside point and distance (two numbers). Hull vertices, faces, indices, UVs and normals are unchanged. parametricGeometry reads each coordinate of a returned point once; a result with impure index getters sees one read per coordinate instead of two. The claim covers operation counts only, with timing pending the quiet rerun. [Evidence](whitepaper/batch-162-workcounts.md#row-47-hull-eye-and-parametric-samples).

Batch 162 mergeVertices hash factors: two 12-byte Int32Array scratch arrays per call; nothing survives the call. Cell size, neighbor order, collision checks, attribute comparisons and output bytes are unchanged. The claim covers hash operation counts only, with timing pending the quiet rerun. [Evidence](whitepaper/batch-162-workcounts.md#row-45-mergevertices-hash-factors).

Batch 162 lathe/tube angular reuse: per-call Float64 tables add 16 bytes per angular column (2,064 bytes for the p-extrude lathe, 272 bytes for its tube). Frames, curve samples, normalization, closed seams, extrusion and output stream bytes stay unchanged; no cache survives a call. The claim covers angular operation counts only, with timing pending the quiet rerun. [Evidence](whitepaper/batch-162-workcounts.md#row-42-lathe-and-tube-angular-reuse).

Batch 162 primitive angular reuse: sphere/cylinder/capsule/torus allocate a temporary Float64 sin/cos table of 16 bytes per angular column including the seam (at most 1,040 bytes per affected p-primitives builder). No cache survives a call. Geometry buffers and groups match the parent byte for byte on the same JavaScript runtime; cross-runtime transcendental bit identity is not promised. Operation counts are not a runtime or competitive speed claim. [Evidence](whitepaper/batch-162-workcounts.md).

### Terrain clipmap triangulation error (batch 169, 2026-11-10)

`TerrainQuery` answers the bilinear heightmap surface exactly (66049 of 66049 samples equal
the source). The clipmap draws each ring as two triangles per cell at that ring's spacing,
so the drawn surface differs from the bilinear one. On a 257 x 257 fbm fixture spanning 100
height units, the measured max error is 2.27 at the finest ring and 8.14, 15.97, 27.17 and
62.39 at 2, 4, 8 and 16 cell spacing (RMS 0.22 to 12.89). Coarse rings sit far from the
camera by design. [Values](whitepaper/batch-169.md#job-5-terrain-uniform-uploads).

Entry size: @margoengine/terrain 13,295 to 13,310 B gzip (+15 B) for the changed-only
uniform uploads; recorded as deliberate growth in the sizes baseline. Core and stage
unchanged.

### Subdivision face counts against Blender (batch 169, 2026-11-10)

`subdivideMesh` keeps every face planar, so each curved quad of the result is stored as
two triangles; Blender's Subdivision Surface modifier keeps curved quads. Vertex positions
match Blender 5.3 within its Float32 storage (largest 1.52e-7 on the tested cube, cylinder,
wedge and open grid), but curved results hold twice Blender's faces (cube level 1: 48
against 24). Flat results are equal. Accepted work difference: planar faces are a
mesh-edit invariant. [Values](whitepaper/batch-169.md#job-3-mesh-edit-subdivision-edges).

### Text measurement reuse and oracle scope (batch 169, 2026-11-10)

`layoutText` reuses logical kerning only when visual neighbors retain their original
source adjacency; shaped prefix advances remain raw until the same scaling and
spacing operations run. A deterministic measurer is required within a call.
Four Source Sans 3 advance widths equal Canvas, while external Troika 0.52.4
selection widths differ by up to 8.900960288826809e-6 em. Numeric differences are
retained; glyph pixels and full Unicode equivalence were not measured. This is not
a runtime speed claim. [All values and commands](whitepaper/batch-169.md).

### UI layout measurement contract (batch 169, 2026-11-10)

`arrange` retains content sizes by node and available inner width only during one
call. Custom measurers return stable values for a width during that call. Direct
edits between calls require no dirty flags. On the nested-row oracle, two different
width constraints require two callbacks, versus Yoga 3.2.1's one; fully explicit
grow/shrink fixtures require zero callbacks on either side and yield equal
rectangles. [Evidence and reproducible scope](whitepaper/batch-169.md). No cross-call
cache, competitive timing result or full CSS/Yoga conformance is claimed.

## Native pointer lock on a locked Mac (lane L, 2026-11-10)

Chromium grants `requestPointerLock` only to a page whose view has operating-system focus. On macOS that is a view in
the key window of the front application. The Apple silicon Mac runs the browser checks unattended with its console locked:
`ioreg -n Root -d1` reports `CGSSessionScreenIsLocked` true and `lsappinfo front` names `com.apple.loginwindow`. No
browser window can be key, so Chromium 156.0.8078.4 rejects every request with `WrongDocumentError` ("The root
document of this element is not valid for pointer lock."). Measured 2026-11-10 for the headless shell, new headless
(`channel: 'chromium'`) and headed, with and without `page.bringToFront()` and CDP `Emulation.setFocusEmulationEnabled`;
`document.hasFocus()` was true, the page visible and the click a real user activation in every case. No launch flag or
harness change can make a window key while macOS shows the login window, so the cause is outside Margo.

What the checks do instead (`scripts/support/pointer-lock.mjs`): `packages/input/test/input-browser.mjs` and
`packages/worker/tests/browser-check.mjs` first try native lock in a scratch page. If it works, they run unchanged. If
it is refused with `WrongDocumentError` on macOS while the console is locked or a non-browser app is in front, they
print a `NOTE ... native acquisition not proven on this machine` line naming the error and the front app, and run
their lock steps (request, `pointerlockchange`, locked movement into rendered pixels or worker controls, release)
against a stand-in for the platform's lock state written to Pointer Lock 2.0 (W3C Working Draft,
https://www.w3.org/TR/pointerlock-2/). Any other refusal, on any platform, still fails the check. What this does not
prove: that Chromium on macOS acquires a native lock for Margo's elements. That needs a run with the console unlocked
and the browser in front (finish-later "132 | worker"); the Windows workstation runs the native path. Regression for the
classifier: `tests/pointer-lock-harness.test.js`.

## webgl2-compat footprint check per platform, and explicit gradients on ANGLE Metal (lane L, 2026-11-10)

`packages/webgl2-compat/test/bias-browser.mjs` compares the layer's raw f32 sample bits with native WebGPU on each
ANGLE backend. It forced `d3d11` and `vulkan`, which macOS does not have, so Chromium fell back to SwiftShader and
the harness refused the run. It now takes the platform's real backends: Windows `d3d11` and `vulkan`, macOS `metal`,
Linux `vulkan` and `gl` (the Linux rows have not been run yet; finish-later).

The first Metal run found a real difference, fixed in the same commit. `textureSampleGrad(t, s, uv, dpdx(uv),
dpdy(uv))` on the oblique map read 0.4205882 (LOD about 1.77) through the layer and 0.3563725 (LOD about 1.86)
natively, on the Apple silicon Mac (Apple M-series GPU, Chromium 156.0.8078.4). A probe of the same texture showed why:
natively, gradients written as `dpdx(uv), dpdy(uv)` give exactly the implicit `textureSample` value, but the same
gradients passed as constants give 0.4205882, so the native result is the implicit footprint, not the generic
explicit-gradient path. ANGLE Metal's GLSL `textureGrad(c, dFdx(c), dFdy(c))` takes the generic path (0.4205882
for both forms). The layer now emits implicit sampling for `textureSampleGrad` whose gradients are `dpdx`/`dpdy` (any
coarse or fine form) of the very coordinate it samples, which is the implicit footprint by definition (WGSL,
https://www.w3.org/TR/WGSL/#texturesamplegrad and #texturesample). Any other explicit gradients still use
`textureGrad`; on Metal they matched native in the probe (constant gradients, axis-aligned and diagonal gradients:
identical bits). Regressions: `packages/webgl2-compat/test/glsl.test.js` (emission, and the cases that must keep
`textureGrad`) and `bias-browser.mjs` on the Mac (1280 f32 words identical to native after the fix, 128 words differed
before).

Accepted difference seen in the same probe and not part of this check: `textureSampleLevel` at a fractional LOD
(1.7679) reads 0.4264706 natively and 0.4248279 through the layer, because the layer blends levels with the exact
float fraction while the Metal sampler snaps it to 8 bits. That is the layer's documented exact-mip design
(`emit.ts`, `exactMip`).

### Materials wireframe compatibility replacement

ANGLE D3D11 can retain retired index storage across a VAO element-buffer replacement. The optional backend detaches the old element binding before selecting a different buffer; unchanged draws retain their cache hits. Exact indices and pixels are preserved, with no GPU wait or changed resource count. Raw replay and 285-check native/compat 1x/4x material grids are documented in whitepaper/materials-compat-hunt.md. This closes wireframe replacement failures, not the historical dispersion reset defect.

## Root dev server file watching (2026-11-10)

The root Vite server (`npm run dev:examples`, `npm run modern:dev:extensions`, `npm run dev:ik`) watches only the
files it has served: each page's html, its modules and the package builds they import are added to the watcher when
the server first transforms them (`servedFilesWatch()` in vite.config.mjs). Vite's default watches the whole root,
and chokidar opened one native watch per file before the first page was served: 62,864 paths in a lane checkout,
where three sciviz tabs are served 137 files. Measured on the workstation (busy machine, diagnostic): three sciviz tabs
requested the moment `npm run dev:examples` prints its URL, cold dependency cache, all loaded 56.4 s after the start
before and 1.2 to 1.7 s after (the first page with the watcher off: 2.4 s). Regression: `tests/dev-servers.test.js`
("watches only what it serves": paths watched against files served, and an edit of a served file still reported).
Limit: a file the server has not served yet is not watched, so a new page or an unrequested file causes no reload
until it is first requested; editing or rebuilding anything an open page loaded reloads it as before.

## Water caustics: limits, scale and the WebGL2 range fix (2026-11-10)

`@margoengine/post/caustics` (`SurfaceCaustics`, 2026-11-25): any surface mesh, copied as six floats per triangle corner;
`size` 0.1..100,000 m, `resolution` 32..2048 (power of two, 256), `layers` 2..32 (12), `refractiveIndex` 1..3 (1.333),
`intensity` 0..100 (1), absorption and colour 0..100 per channel. One refracting interface: the receivers are inside the
medium (a pool floor, a tank bottom), not under a closed glass object, which ProductCaustics of studio traces. The sun only
(`engine.lighting`), one map square: light that lands outside it is lost. Its beams and projection are the shared shaders
water/caustics now draws with (the same numbers: water's project, energy, caustics and scale checks pass unchanged).
`@margoengine/water/caustics`: `size` 0.1..100,000 m (default 100), `resolution` 32..2048 (default 256, power of two),
`layers` 2..32 (default 12), `heightRange` finite, `refractiveIndex` 1..2 (1.333), `intensity` 0..100 (1), absorption per
metre [0.38, 0.1, 0.045], `color` [1, 1, 1]. The surface is Water or FFTOcean (Water `segments` up to 512). There is no
dispersion option: every channel refracts at one index. The rivals have no real-time caustics to match (three.js,
Babylon.js, PlayCanvas; community demos project a normal-map texture). A per-channel
split needs three beam footprints, so three times the beam work, and is not built without a demand for it.
Entry size 9,140 B min+gzip under its 9,230 B ceiling (was 9,042 B before the range change below); core plus stage unchanged.

Work and measured numbers (`node packages/water/test/caustics-scale.browser.mjs`, RTX A6000, busy machine, diagnostic only):
flux maps `3 * resolution^2 * layers * 8` B, beam triangle instances `2 * segments^2 * layers`.

| case | segments / map / layers | beam triangles | flux maps | native GPU | WebGL2 layer wall |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| default | 128 / 256 / 12 | 393,216 | 18 MiB | 0.52 ms | 19 to 23 ms (water alone 12 ms) |
| medium | 256 / 1024 / 16 | 2,097,152 | 384 MiB | 3.3 ms | 26 ms |
| limit | 512 / 2048 / 32 | 16,777,216 | 3,072 MiB | 21 ms | 49 to 58 ms |

The limit case needs 3 GiB of GPU memory and misses a 60 fps budget; it is a validated upper bound, not a recommendation.
Bug found and fixed here: the per-frame range (scale) pass used a 64-lane workgroup reduction, which the WebGL2 layer runs
in JavaScript, so the default size cost 214 ms a frame there (0.5 ms native). The pass is now three kernels with no
workgroup memory or barrier (per-triangle weights, 512 chunk sums, the scale), which the layer runs on the GPU: 19 ms a
frame at the default size, the same energy errors (relative error 4.76e-6 and 1.49e-4 on both backends). Regression:
`packages/water/test/caustics-scale.browser.mjs` fails when any range kernel plans onto the `cpu` tier.
## Compute distance fields (jump flooding)

`@margoengine/compute/distance` floods the nearest seed over a 2D mask (2 to 4096 per side) or a 3D mask (2 to 512 per side)
in log2(longest side) + 1 passes (+2 for `jfa+2`), two u32 buffers ping-ponging and no readback on the GPU. Each buffer
holds one u32 per cell, so the device's storage binding limit also caps the field: native WebGPU here reports 2 GiB (a
512^3 field runs), the WebGL2 layer 128 MiB (up to 4096^2 in 2D, 320^3 in 3D); a larger field throws a coded `rangeError` naming the
limit. Steps start at the power of two over the longest side, so sizes need not be powers of two. Squared distances are
exact u32 integers (at most 33.5 million in 2D, 786,432 in 3D) and ties go to the lower cell index, so WebGPU, the WebGL2
layer and the CPU backend produce the same nearest-seed buffer; distances agree to the last bits of sqrt only. A cell no
seed reaches (no seeds at all) holds `NO_SEED` and `NO_DISTANCE` (the largest f32).

Measured error rates (cells whose flooded seed is not a nearest one, against the exact transform; 1024^2 in 2D with 1, 10,
1,000 seeds and a thin sine curve, 128^3 in 3D with the same and a helix; identical on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer):
`jfa+1` (default) at most 0.0024 percent wrong cells (2.4e-5), farthest excess 0.64 cells in 2D and 1.94 cells in 3D
(10 seeds); plain `jfa` at most 0.012 percent wrong, excess up to 1.30 cells in 2D and 2.40 cells in 3D. The plan's
"at most 1 cell" holds for `jfa+1` in 2D only; the 3D excess is the known weakness of flooding with sparse seeds, so use
`distanceTransformExact` or `jfa+2` where 2 cells matter. The 3D flood checks all 27 neighbours (no slice-by-slice
variant). `signedDistance` runs two floods and puts the zero set half a cell from the cell centres (`edge` option).
The CPU backend runs the same passes in JavaScript (about 0.5 s for 256^2 with four masks); use the exact transform there.
Entry size 5187 B min+gzip (ceiling 5443 B); the plan's 3,500 B estimate left out the CPU-backend flood, the exact
oracle shared with text and the signed and Voronoi code.

## Audio offline spectrograms

`@margoengine/audio/spectrogram` takes frame sizes that are powers of two from 32 to 65536, hops from 1 to the size, and
refuses a result of more than 134,217,728 spectrum values (frames x bins) per array. Spectra are Float32; the transforms
run in double precision on the CPU (radix-2, two real frames per complex FFT) and in f32 on the GPU path, which batches
frames of at most 4,194,304 samples through `compute/fft`. Measured: STFT then ISTFT of 3 s of noise plus a chirp at
48 kHz (size 2048) has a largest error of 2.98e-8 at hop 512 and 5.96e-8 at hop 1024 (bar 1e-6). GPU against CPU on 2,109,457 samples (4,121 frames): 1.75e-7 of the peak on WebGPU
and on the WebGL2 layer, round trip through `istft` 1.8e-7. `istft` and `resynthesize` need the summed squared window to be even enough (smallest over largest
at least 0.1, `overlapRatio`): Hann passes at hop size/4 and size/2 and fails at 3/4. Without centring the first and last
window-length samples where the window is 0 cannot be recovered. Uses `Math.cos` for twiddles and window values, so the last bits can
differ between JavaScript engines.

Griffin-Lim (fast variant, random start, 1 s chirp at 48 kHz, 32 iterations), magnitude SNR of the returned signal: size
2048 hop 256 reaches 21.6 dB with momentum 0.99 and 16.8 dB without; 75 percent overlap reaches 18.0 dB (size 1024 hop 256)
or 19.0 dB (size 2048 hop 512), so the 20 dB bar needs 87.5 percent overlap or more than 32 iterations. Spectral
convergence never worsens without momentum (tested); with momentum it can rise for an iteration. Memory is about 7 Float64
arrays of frames x bins values. The phase vocoder is the `/vocoder` entry (below). A Rust/Wasm FFT was not
built: the paired A/B is a timing run and timing runs wait for the speed phase (the speed-phase inventory); the
TypeScript FFT does 11,264 butterflies per 2048-point frame and 4,121 frames took 132 ms on a busy machine.


## Planet recipes (lague plan 8, 2026-11-10)

`@margoengine/terrain/planet-recipes`, 3,216 B min+gzip (new entry; the planet entry is no larger: the shared noise moved to an
internal module). Defaults, each with its source in the README: crater density 1,000 per 10^6 km^2 of diameter `dMin` or more,
`dMin` radius / 20,000, `dMax` radius / 4 (at most the radius), cumulative exponent 2 (1 to 3), depth 0.196 D^1.01 from rim crest to floor and rim 0.036 D^1.01
(D in km, Pike 1977; the coefficients are taken from the plan and were not re-read from the paper, which could not be opened
here; only depth over diameter about 0.2 under 15 km and the 3,400 m depth ceiling were confirmed against its abstract),
ejecta 0.14 R^0.74 (r / R)^-3 m (McGetchin et al. 1973, coefficients as in the plan), rim uplift (r / R)^-4 and the fade from 2.5
to 3 radii are authored, as are the preset numbers and the blend rule.
Work bound: one lattice per octave of diameter (about 13 on the Moon by default), 27 cells each, at most 256 craters in a
cell (a denser setting throws). Measured on the CPU (Node, busy machine, diagnostic): a moon preset sample costs 6.6 us at
full detail and 3.8 us at a coarse patch against 1.0 us for `planetNoise`, so a 1,089-vertex patch is about 7 ms; 0.001 craters
reach a default sample on average (one at most in 100,000 samples). Placement is a jittered 3D lattice, not the equal-area
cube-sphere cells of the plan: no face seams, 27 cells instead of 9. Diameters pass a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test under 0.02 and the
crater count matches the density within 5% (24,627 craters on a 10 km test body).
Built 2026-11-27: complex craters, rays and secondary crater chains, 3,226 B to 5,848 B min+gzip for the entry
(the planet entry 7,512 B to 7,636 B for its brightness input). The complex size laws (Pike 1977: depth, rim, floor, peak
height), the terrace width (Pearce and Melosh 1986), ray length and count (Elliott et al. 2018) and secondary sizes
(Singer et al. 2020) were read in secondary sources or search summaries where the paper itself was not open: Pike 1977
and Pearce and Melosh 1986 were not read. Authored, not measured: the ramps between onset diameters, the peak's width
and outline, four terraces with their benches, wander and gaps, the fade of peaks from 140 to 200 km, the spread and
shape of rays, chain spacing, a secondary's half depth and 1.25 stretch, and the Mars (7,000 m) and ice (3,000 m)
transitions. Not modelled: peak rings and multi-ring basins above about 175 km (they stay flat-floored with no peak),
oblique impacts (rays are symmetric about the great circle fan), secondaries below 1 km primaries, and fresh-ejecta
colour other than one brightness. Rays are placed per sample against every rayed crater, so their cost grows with the
count (at most 64). A floor is still bounded by `maxDepth` below the ground.

Steady-frame work counts (Scott's 60+ fps rule, 2026-11-10). Planet recipes: the render path is untouched, so draws, buffer writes, bind groups and allocations per frame are unchanged; heights run only when a patch is built (at least one patch a frame, about 6 ms of the 16.7 ms frame with the moon preset, the rest spread by `budget`). A miss against a 2 ms patch target is listed in the speed phase list.
Water caustics after the range fix (commit c741c965a4): per frame one more compute pass (3 instead of 2: weights, 512 chunk sums, scale) and one more bind group; no buffer write and no allocation added (the weights buffer, 2 * segments^2 * 4 B, 128 KiB at the default and 2 MiB at 512 segments, and a 2 KiB partials buffer are created once); draws unchanged (one per depth slice plus the projection). Default size 0.52 ms native GPU timestamps; the WebGL2 layer 19 to 23 ms wall (water alone 12 ms), within 60 fps on the A6000, mid laptop iGPU not measured here.

## AMD Direct3D 11 trilinear blend under the WebGL2 layer
On AMD GPUs through ANGLE Direct3D 11 the driver blends mip levels with clamp(1.25 f - 0.125) instead of the LOD fraction f, for explicit and implicit sampling; native WebGPU on the same GPU blends with f. The WebGL2 layer keeps the hardware footprint and cannot query the LOD, so implicit-sampled images there differ slightly from native on AMD (batch 160 IOR: 2,423,682 against 2,421,894 native). Control and evidence: docs/known-bugs.md, "AMD Direct3D 11 steepens the trilinear blend". For explicit-LOD sampling the layer blends two integer levels by the full float fraction, while a sampler snaps the fraction to its own mipmap precision, which WebGPU leaves to the implementation (Khronos, Vulkan 1.3 Specification, 2022, `VkPhysicalDeviceLimits::mipmapPrecisionBits`, at least 4 bits: https://registry.khronos.org/vulkan/specs/1.3-extensions/html/vkspec.html#limits-mipmapPrecisionBits). Native WebGPU on the Radeon 680M rounds it to the nearest 1/256 (2026-11-15, the raw page of `scripts/reference-rendering/mip-blend-control.html` at 1,001 explicit levels from 0 to 1: every weight the nearest 1/256, worst 0.0019 from the float fraction), so a fractional explicit level there can differ from native by up to 1/512 of the two levels' difference. A level on the 1/256 grid is snapped to itself there, but the RTX A6000's native sampler still blended such a level apart from the layer (the one-sample DOF `focus` case, mean 0.00053), so a sampler's blend differs in its arithmetic as well as its precision; `@margoengine/dof` reads its near-field chain at whole levels and blends the two in the shader instead.

### Lague plan 1: particle liquid (water/liquid)

ParticleLiquid draws 0 to 4,194,304 particles, all of one radius (0.001 to 100 world units, default 0.05), from a Float32Array (stride 3..64 floats, offset >= 0; uploaded at creation and on update()) or a STORAGE GPUBuffer or GpuArray (count required; the buffer must hold offset + (count - 1) * stride + 3 floats). Option ranges: ior 1..3 (1.333), absorption 0..100 per unit ([0.38, 0.1, 0.045]), color 0..10 ([1, 1, 1]), smoothing 0.0001..100 (0.7 * radius), maxFilterRadius 1..64 px (32), filterRange > 0 (10 * radius), filterClamp 0..filterRange (radius), thicknessScale 0..1000 (1), resolutionScale 1 or 0.5, shininess 1..100000 (2000). A frame is 6 render passes and 6 draws with one 320 B uniform write; memory is three r32float and one depth32float frame-size targets plus an r16float thickness target (about 36 MiB at 1920 x 1080 with resolutionScale 1). Thickness is the sum of sphere chords cut at the scene depth, so overlapping particles count more than once: scale it with thicknessScale. The surface writes no scene depth (effects after it see the scene behind), casts and receives no shadow, and refraction reads the current frame only, so what is off screen refracts as the nearest edge texel. Perspective cameras only. Whitewater (with particles.velocities and options.whitewater): pool 1..4,194,304 (default 65,536), one step per update(); a neighbour bucket holds 8 particles, so a cell h / 2 wide with more (packing denser than 8 per (h / 2)^3, or two cells G apart sharing a wrapped bucket) drops its highest indices from the neighbour sums; at most 255 diffuse particles per fluid particle per step; when a step emits more than the pool they are subsampled evenly; thresholds are the paper's in SI units with particleMass 1000 * (2 * radius)^3, so small scenes need a lower kineticEnergy range; sprites are discs, not the paper's volume rendering; whitewater neither casts nor receives shadows. Step cost (busy A6000, wall): 3.8 ms at 65,536 fluid particles, 9.0 ms at 262,144; WebGL2 layer 6.9 and 12.0 ms (docs/water-liquid.md). Narrow band (narrowBand, default false; bandVoxel 0.0001..1000, default 4 * radius): rebuilt only on update(), so particles that move without one keep the old band; the voxel grows by 1.25 until the grid fits the band atlas (max(64, fluid side) texels square), so a very spread-out cloud gets coarser voxels and a thicker band; thickness is one volume-preserving ball per voxel, not per particle. Not built: anisotropic kernels (Yu-Turk, ruled out: a solver-side cost) and screen-space meshes. Busy-machine cost on the RTX A6000: 1.05 ms GPU at 32,768 particles and 1280 x 720, 8.06 ms at 4,194,304 and 1920 x 1080 (docs/water-liquid.md).

### GPU particle liquid (GPULiquid)

`GPULiquid` (`@margoengine/water/liquid`, FLUID-02 and FLUID-03, parity bar P13) steps 1 to 1,048,576 particles (80 B
each) on a grid of at most 4,194,304 nodes (32 B each, and 16 B more with surface tension), 8 to 256 cells along the container's longest side and at least
4 on every side. What it does not do, and what was measured:

- Two profiles. `'accurate'` is incompressible to its solve's tolerance: the grid's velocity is projected each substep
  with a pressure per grid cell (the trilinear-velocity, constant-pressure pair, whose pressure can show a checkerboard
  that leaves the velocity unaffected) by Jacobi-preconditioned conjugate gradients from zero, at most
  `pressureIterations` (128) to a residual of `pressureTolerance` (1e-4) of the first; a solve that hits the cap leaves
  the rest of its divergence (`stats.pressureResidual`). The Jacobi preconditioner converges slowly on the grid's
  long-wave and checkerboard-like modes: still water converges within the cap, but a column falling round a sphere in a
  0.8 m tank (32,768 particles, about 26 cells a side) reaches the cap with 6.4e-4 of its divergence left on the GPU
  (4.5e-4 with free-slip walls); a multigrid preconditioner cuts the iterations by 2.5 to 3 but not the work, because of the pressure pair's null modes (KB-LIQUID-MGPCG1). A cell is liquid at half its rest density or more (the free surface lies within a cell of
  the particles' edge, first order) and solid when all its corners lie inside colliders, so a collider's surface is
  placed to the grid's nodes. Measured on the CPU twin (`gpu-liquid.test.js`): a 0.2 m layer on a floor collider holds
  its centroid within a quarter particle spacing over 1.5 s, its cell pressure is rho g d within rho g h, and the floor
  carries its weight within 1%; 0.6 s into a dam break of 8,192 particles the liquid at the floor reads 1.006 times rest
  density, where the fast profile reads 1.028. The GPU's projection matches the twin's to 3.2e-7 m and 2.7e-5 m/s over a frame of 32,768
  particles and their floor's force to 0.002% (`gpu-liquid-check.mjs`). The pressure enters G2P only through the
  projected grid velocity, so a particle reads it with the B-spline's 27 nodes while the projection holds the
  divergence of each cell's 8; the cells' density correction (half a cell's excess a substep) keeps the volume across
  that gap. Each substep costs 7 + 5 * pressureIterations dispatches (the ones past convergence have no workgroups);
  speed is measured in the speed phase.
- Walls (`walls`, default `'smooth'`): a smooth wall is no-slip under the liquid's own `viscosity`, by Launder and
  Spalding's (1974) wall function (the viscous sublayer below y+ = 11.2, the smooth-wall log law, kappa = 0.4187 and
  E = 9.793, above it) read from the speed of the grid's node on the wall at the B-spline weights' mean (13/32 cell,
  sublayer) or geometric mean (0.2751 cell, log law) distance from it, and pushed back as the MPM traction condition on
  the three node layers at the wall (shares 1/8, 3/4, 1/8, over the part of the wall inside the container). It is an
  equilibrium boundary layer: no roughness (a rough bed slows liquid more), no developing layer at a front, no
  separation; the wetted area is resolved to the grid, so the edge of a sheet wets up to 1.5 cells too much wall (a slab
  32 cells long slid 6.5 to 7.8% more than the closed form dU/dt = -u*^2 / d, under the 3 h / L = 9.4% bound,
  `gpu-liquid.test.js`). Each node's friction is explicit, at most its own speed along the wall a substep. `'slip'`
  holds only the motion into a wall. The walls take no force back (they are fixed); the colliders keep their Coulomb
  `friction`.
- Dam breaks against measurements (`gpu-liquid-dambreak.test.js`, the CPU twin, both profiles, nothing fitted, smooth
  walls): Martin and Moyce's (1952) two-dimensional collapses on a smooth bed between free-slip side walls, each
  station's T inside the spread of their own runs at that Z widened by the timing errors of both sides (about 0.2 to
  0.3 in T), in table 2 (n^2 = 2) to Z = 12 and, held out, table 1 (n^2 = 1) to Z = 13 and table 3 (n^2 = 4) to
  Z = 7.67, at a / 8 cells; and Lobovsky et al.'s (2014) three-dimensional tank, the front's mean speed along the bed
  after t* = 1 inside the 1.14 to 1.74 sqrt(g H) their Table 1 gathers from the measured dam breaks: the accurate
  profile reads 1.632 at H = 300 mm (3 cm cells; theirs 1.56) and, held out, 1.502 at 600 mm (4 cm; theirs 1.34), the
  fast profile 1.672 and 1.528 (with free-slip walls both ran faster, 1.668 and 1.758 at 300 mm, the fast one past the
  measured range). With free-slip walls the late run-out ran ahead of the runs (table 1, Z = 13: T = 7.80 against 9.21
  to 9.72; the gap did not close as the cells shrank); the bed's friction closes it: table 1 reads T = 9.56 (accurate)
  and 9.58 (fast) at Z = 13 and 10.60 at Z = 14 (where only the 4 1/2 in column has runs, 10.5 and 11.0), the same at
  a / 12 within 0.3. Past Z = 12 in table 2 the simulated front lags the runs by a little more than the bound: T = 8.94
  at Z = 13 against 8.60 to 8.73 (bound 8.97, inside) and 9.62 to 9.64 at Z = 14 against 9.26 to 9.36 (bound 9.60), the
  same at a / 12; the friction there is from the equilibrium log law, which does not know the layer is still developing
  behind the front. The impact pressures Lobovsky et al. measured on the far wall (sensors 3 to 80 mm above the bed,
  4.2 mm across) are not checked: a sensor is a tenth of an interactive grid's cell.
- The fast profile is weakly compressible: the Tait equation lets the liquid compress by about g d / c^2 at depth d. With
  the default speed of sound 2 sqrt(g H) a 0.6 m column in a 1 m tank reads 1.04 to 1.13 times rest density from its
  surface layer to its floor (CPU twin, 6,000 particles, 2.5 s), within 0.02 of the closed form (1 + 6 g d / c^2)^(1/6)
  while the column still rings from its start (rms speed 0.13 to 0.25 m/s after 1.5 to 2.5 s; the APIC transfers damp
  little, raise `viscosity` to settle sooner). The top layer reads under rest density and carries no pressure, so a free
  surface sinks into the liquid by about a cell. A stiffer liquid needs a higher `speedOfSound` and proportionally more
  substeps.
- Up to 4 emitters and 4 drains, and at most `capacity` particles alive (1,048,576); an emitter adds nothing while the
  liquid is full. An emitter is a disc nozzle that places its particles at the jet's velocity; it is not a pressure
  inlet (it does not hold a flow rate against the liquid's back pressure) and a drain is not an outlet with a pressure:
  it removes what the flow carries into it, so the efflux through a drain is set by the liquid's own motion, not by an
  orifice law. Each frame with a drain runs four compaction dispatches and copies the particle buffer once
  (`capacity` * 80 bytes). Empty slots hold NaN positions, which the surface and debug view draw as nothing.
- Up to 4 liquids, each with its own density, viscosity and colour, all at one speed of sound and on one grid; no
  two-phase air, no spray or foam of its own (the surface's `whitewater` can draw them from the particles' velocities).
  The liquids do not dissolve into each other: a particle keeps its liquid's density and viscosity, and `mixing` blends
  only colours (each relaxes towards the weighted mean colour round it, which is not exactly conserving: the mean colour
  drifts by the fixed-point rounding, under 4.2e-4 a step). Between two liquids there is no interfacial tension of its own
  beyond `surfaceTension`, which acts on the liquids' shared free surface. Each liquid's start box rounds to whole
  lattice columns, so their particles start a few percent apart in volume and the rest density is the volume-weighted
  mean. Two liquids of 1000 and 3000 kg/m³ press on a floor with their summed weight to the fixed-point rounding
  (`gpu-liquid.test.js`).
- Surface tension is the continuum surface force on the grid, so it acts over the cells the surface's density falls
  across (about one), not on a sharp surface: a feature under a few cells across (a thin jet, a small drop) is rounded
  by the grid's curvature, not its own. Measured: without gravity a 0.2 m cube at sigma = 10 N/m pulls into a ball and
  holds 150.8 Pa inside against Laplace's 2 sigma / R = 161.2 Pa (WebGPU, 32,768 particles, cell 0.0125 m, averaged
  over 2 to 3 s; the check's bound is 2 sigma / (R + h) to 2 sigma / (R - h)), and 146 to 177 Pa on the CPU twin at a
  0.025 m cell; the spurious currents round that drop stay near 0.004 m/s. It is explicit, so it is refused above
  density * cell³ / (2 pi substep²) (Brackbill et al.'s capillary step limit). Nodes under a quarter of rest density
  (the far edge of the particles' spread) take its push as nodes at a quarter, which keeps them from being flung and
  slightly softens the force there.
- Adhesion is a pull towards the walls and colliders with a set acceleration within one cell (fading out at two), not a
  contact angle: the angle a drop makes with a wall follows from adhesion, gravity and surface tension together and is
  not set directly. A film thinner than a cell hangs from the ceiling exactly when adhesion is above gravity
  (`gpu-liquid.test.js`); liquid on a side wall is pulled sideways only, so it still runs down the wall.
- Colliders are up to 8 spheres, boxes, capsules, planes and triangle meshes, moved by the caller or by a linked body
  (`link`). A mesh is a distance field of at most 64³ samples (`bakeLiquidMesh`, all mesh fields together at most
  2,097,152 samples), so detail finer than its sample spacing is rounded off (a baked cube's edges by up to one spacing)
  and a mesh thinner than about a grid cell lets liquid through; the bake tests every sample against every triangle, at
  most 2^30 pairs (simplify the mesh past that). The liquid's force on them is exact in total (a floor collider's impulse
  matches the column's weight and momentum change within the fixed-point rounding, `gpu-liquid.test.js`), but on a
  small submerged body the grid's cells blur the surface: held in a 0.4 m layer (WebGPU, 65,536 particles, cell
  0.037 m, averaged over 1 to 3 s, smooth walls) a sphere of radius 0.1 m took 36.5 N of lift against Archimedes' 41.1 N
  (0.89), a capsule of radius 0.07 m and length 0.2 m 35.9 N against 44.3 N (0.81), and a baked mesh cube of half size
  0.08 m 33.0 N against 40.2 N (0.82): each between rho g V of the shape a quarter cell smaller and larger, the bound
  `gpu-liquid-check.mjs` holds. A linked box of 500 kg/m³ and half size 0.1 m floated with a mean draft of 0.077 m against
  Archimedes' 0.100 m (bob 0.014 m over the last 2 of 4 s; 0.090 m with free-slip walls; the free level is read
  from the corner columns beside the walls), inside the check's bound of 0.025 m. On WebGPU the linked body takes its impulse when the force
  sums are read back, usually the next frame: every impulse arrives exactly once, but a frame late, and when the read
  lands depends on the GPU, so a run with linked bodies repeats bit for bit only on the CPU twin. The coupling is
  explicit (the body's motion this frame, the liquid's push a frame later), so a body much lighter than the liquid it
  displaces can oscillate; give it damping. The moment a linked body takes is about the collider's centre at the last
  step of the read window, which differs from the exact sum by the centre's travel over that window times the impulse.
- The pointer blends node velocities towards its own inside a sphere; it is not a solid and takes no force back.
- No node moves more than one cell a substep: faster liquid (a violent pointer, a body faster than cell / substep,
  15.6 m/s at the defaults) is slowed to that speed. A frame advances at most 1/30 s and takes at most `maxSubsteps`
  substeps; past that it runs in slow motion (`stats.realTime` false).
- Fixed-point sums: a node's mass or momentum sum past 32,768 particles' worth (2^31 / 65,536), or a collider's frame
  impulse past 2,097,152 particle-mass m/s (2^31 / 1,024), wraps; the pressure is taken at most at 3 times rest density.
  Neither happens in a liquid that is not already failing.
- Deterministic on one GPU and driver (the same options and steps give the same bits, also after a restore); another GPU
  may round its f32 arithmetic differently, so two GPUs agree to rounding, not bit for bit.
- Large worlds: the liquid lives in one world cell (`originCell`, cells of `originCellSize`, a power of two up to 2^20 m)
  and keeps every position in that cell's frame, so a tank anywhere in the world steps with the precision of one near
  the origin; `shiftOrigin` moves the world's origin by whole cells and changes no bit (`gpu-liquid.test.js`: 20 steps
  across a shift of 1,000 cells of 4,096 m repeat 20 steps without it, hash for hash; `gpu-liquid-check.mjs`: the
  surface and debug view draw the same picture before and after a shift, within 1% of the lit pixels, which round
  differently in the camera's f32 matrices). The container itself does not follow anything: one liquid is one tank of
  at most 256 cells a side, and the cell only places it. Positions the caller gives (box, colliders, pointer, emitters,
  drains) are in the liquid's frame; a linked body's are in the world's (origin cell 0), converted in f64 each frame.
- On the WebGL2 compatibility layer the CPU twin steps it on the main thread: 4,096 particles took about 120 ms a frame
  on a loaded laptop (180 frames in 22 s), so keep a few thousand there.
- Speed against three.js's `webgpu_compute_particles_fluid` is not measured yet (speed phase, `scripts/speed-phase.json`).
  The like-for-like scene, recorded now so nothing in the design is tuned to it afterwards: the rival example run as
  published, in its own folder outside this repository (docs/benchmarking.md, "Comparing engines"), at each particle
  count it offers, against `examples/gpu-liquid.html` at the same count with the fast profile, a grid of the same cells
  per particle and the same substeps a frame as the rival takes, the pointer still and the surface drawn; 120 frames to
  warm up, then GPU time a frame from timestamp queries and wall time over 600 frames on a quiet machine, both
  published. The accurate profile is measured in the same scene and published as an accepted difference (it adds the
  pressure solve, 7 + 5 * iterations dispatches a substep, that a weakly compressible rival does not do). Nothing in the
  fast profile's design is known to cost more than the rival's method: one substep is the same scatter, grid update and
  gather of MLS-MPM (Hu et al. 2018) in five dispatches with no readback, its sums integer atomics (WGSL has no float
  atomics on storage, so a GPU scatter takes integer or compare-exchange atomics either way), and `stats.dispatches`
  counts them.

## Sciviz volume filtering precision (2026-11-11)

The volume marches (`figure.volume`, `@margoengine/sciviz/bricks`) read voxels through the GPU's trilinear filter.
WebGPU leaves the filter's weight precision to the implementation; desktop GPUs keep 8 fractional bits (the D3D11 and
Vulkan `subTexelPrecisionBits` figure), so each axis weight of each fetch can be off by up to 1/256 and a fetch by up to
3/256 of its largest neighbour difference. Where the same voxels sit at other texel positions (one texture against a
brick atlas) the weights round differently, so two correct marches of the same maths differ in the last steps.
Shading amplifies this through the normalised gradient, which has no finite closed-form bound where the gradient is
small, so the bound is measured on the picture from that error model.

Measured on the 40^3 lit one-brick check (`packages/sciviz/tests/bricks-browser.js`, 480 x 360, RTX A6000, native
WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer):

| Comparison | Largest difference (of 255) | Pixels differing |
|---|---|---|
| whole against bricked, both exact float trilinear (test-only `filterMode` 1) | 1 native, 0 WebGL2 layer | 2, 0 |
| whole against bricked, both hardware filtered | 3 | 41, 39 |
| each hardware march against its exact march | 6 | 1198 to 1202 |
| model: every weight one full 1/256 step off (`filterMode` 2) against exact, one sign pattern (former `sin` hash) | 8 whole, 3 bricked | about 2,100 |

The model's sign pattern is exact integer arithmetic (2026-11-15): the position floored to the 1/256 sub-texel grid,
hashed with pcg3d (Jarzynski and Olano, "Hash Functions for GPU Rendering", JCGT 9(3), 2020), one pattern per pipeline
constant `filterSeed`. The former `fract(sin(...) * 43758.5453)` sign took `sin` near 5,000 radians, where WGSL sets no
accuracy (2^-11 absolute only inside [-pi, pi]) and GLSL ES 3.00 none at all, so each GPU drew its own pattern and its
own bound (3 on a Radeon 680M and on the WebGL2 layer of an Apple M6, failing hardware 4). The check now takes the worst
over 16 patterns. Apple M6, native WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer alike (identical per pattern):

| Comparison (40^3 lit one-brick check, Apple M6) | Largest difference (of 255) | Pixels differing |
|---|---|---|
| each hardware march against its exact march, Apple M6 | 4 | 841 whole, 843 bricked |
| model, worst of 16 sign patterns against exact | 8 (whole), 7 (bricked) | |
| model, each pattern alone | 3 to 8 whole, 3 to 7 bricked | |

Across six cameras the hardware-to-hardware difference was 1 to 3 and the exact-to-exact one 0 to 1 (the atlas offset
rounds border + v in float). The check requires exact-to-exact at most 1 and each hardware march within the model's
worst difference; the multi-brick checks keep their hardware bound of 2. Rounding the weights to nearest or down to an
8-bit grid moved the picture by 2 and 3 only, so the hardware also rounds elsewhere (likely in its half-float filtering
arithmetic); the full-step model is the one that bounds it. The filter mode is a pipeline constant that tests set; it
is not an option, and the normal path builds with the hardware branch only.

## Repeatable pictures of folded translucent surfaces on NVIDIA (KB5700f, 2026-11-11)

A translucent surface (any opacity below 1, blended, no depth write) that covers a pixel more than once in its one
draw, such as a sciviz `figure.surface` whose hills fold over each other on screen, is not byte-repeatable on NVIDIA
GPUs at the default 4x MSAA: on the RTX A6000 two unchanged captures differ by one level in a few dozen bytes, on
WebGPU (D3D12) and on the WebGL2 layer (ANGLE D3D11) alike. A raw-API page with no Margo code shows the same
(`scripts/reference-rendering/fold-blend-repeat.html`: 23 of 23 repeats differ, up to 62 and 86 bytes), while an AMD
RDNA 2 iGPU on the same PC and an Apple M6 (Metal) repeat it exactly; the upstream draft is
docs/upstream-reports/KB5700f/report.md. Opaque surfaces and translucent surfaces that cover each pixel once repeat
exactly everywhere (`packages/sciviz/tests/surface-repeat-browser.mjs`, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer). For byte-exact
captures of a folded translucent surface on NVIDIA, draw it at opacity 1 or capture at one sample (`exactSize`); the
sciviz look (no depth pre-pass, no forced OIT) is unchanged.

The same holds for glTF models with BLEND parts (KB1824, 2026-11-11): Khronos GlassVaseFlowers at 4x differs in 4 of 5 rebuilds on the RTX A6000 (up to 28 pixels, up to 10 levels at 270 degrees) and repeats exactly on the AMD RDNA 2 iGPU of the same PC, at one sample everywhere, and on the A6000 with its BLEND glass made OPAQUE (`packages/oit/test/gpu/repeat-check.mjs`). For byte-exact captures of such a model on NVIDIA, capture at one sample.

## Shot tool masks (tools/shot, 2026-11-14)

The `sky` and `water` masks of `tools/shot` (docs/shots.md, Masks) split the pixels with no geometry at a flat plane
(`shot.horizon.y`, the mean sea level), not at the displaced sea: a crest above the mean level near the horizon counts
as sky. The tool takes masks from textures the page gives; Storm Light gives `geometry` and `depth`. There is no
`foam` mask yet: `@margoengine/water` keeps the foam it draws in a private per-view history, so a foam mask needs a
read accessor in the water package first (with its WebGPU and WebGL2 checks). Masks are single-sample reads of
single-sample textures (SceneTargets draws at one sample); a supersampled shot takes them down by coverage, so at the
1.5x default an edge pixel holds the share each mask covers, and at `supersample` 1 every mask pixel is all in or out.

## Shot tool capture (tools/shot, 2026-11-14)

`supersample` is 1 to 2 and no rendered side may pass 8,192 pixels. The canvas is enlarged through the window at a
pixel ratio of 1, so effects sized in pixels (bloom and depth of field radii, contact shadow steps) cover a smaller
share of the frame than in a live page at the same size: tune a shot's look at the scale it renders at. `msaa` forces
1 or 4 scene samples through what core reads (`globalThis.margoLow`), which is also core's pixel-ratio cap; at the
shot's pixel ratio of 1 the cap changes no size. Sub-frames are drawn on the page's own frame loop: a page whose
effects keep history across frames (TAA) carries it from sub-frame to sub-frame, and a closed shutter (`shutter` 0)
averages only what changes between draws. The resolve (mean, area filter, dither) runs on the CPU in the page, one
pass a kept frame.

## Look checks (headless/look, shorts P4, 2026-11-14)

The optional `@margoengine/headless/look` entry is 10,650 B min+gzip (new, previously absent; ceiling 10,970 B). Core
plus stage is unchanged. Frames are 8-bit sRGB RGBA; masks are one byte or four per pixel with 128 and above inside;
frames, masks and still frames of one probe must be one size. The `nan` check needs the float frame (Float32 or
half-float RGBA): NaN does not survive into an 8-bit PNG. `horizonSeam` needs the camera's view-projection at the
probe frame and the `sky` mask (it measures only columns with sky 3 rows above the line; until 2026-11-14 it measured
every column, and Cabin Hearth's mantel across the line of an interior read as a 15.8-code seam), `waterSeam` the `water` mask, `foamEdges` a `foam` mask (none exists yet: see "Shot tool masks"), `crush`
reads declared dark areas from a `dark` mask, `flicker` and `shimmer` need 3 or more still-camera frames, `backends` the
WebGL2 compatibility frame and `reference` a 16-sample reference frame. The shot tool (`tools/shot/look.mjs`) gives
each probe its masks and the view-projection core drew it with (the last sub-frame's, when a shot averages
sub-frames), so with a `sky` mask `horizonSeam` runs and with a `water` mask `waterSeam`; it does not write `dark`, `foam`, still,
float, compat or reference inputs yet, so those checks are left out; a check named in `lookBounds` without its input
fails as not run. FLIP is the paper's 8-bit (LDR) form at 67 pixels per degree by default; `hdrFlip` (HDR-FLIP, 2026-11-27) takes float frames and costs one FLIP per exposure, max(2, ceil(stop - start)) of them (about 10 for a lamp-lit interior), and its tone curves are the ACES fit, Reinhard and any curve of Equation 1's rational form (Hable's Uncharted 2 curve is not built in: pass its coefficients). It rejects negative, NaN and infinite light, and a reference whose largest or median luminance is 0 unless both exposures are given; the checks and `checkProbe` do not run it yet (a probe's `hdr` frame has no float reference beside it). `blocks` looks for
steps repeating at one pitch (default 8 pixels) in tiles 8 pitches across, so blocks smaller than a tile, one-code
block steps and blocks masked by strong texture are not seen. `flat` needs a constant 65 x 65 window, `banding` flat
runs of 6 pixels or more. `lights` counts bright discs by shape (fill 0.6 to 0.95 of the box, aspect within 1.5) from
24 pixels up; the scene's own lights (lamps, a moon) set its bound. Default bounds are starting values, not
calibrated against viewers.

Sky coverage (`sky-coverage`, the pixels `@margoengine/sky` drew, KB-HEARTH-CLIP1) limits only `skyClip`, and only
on a shot with no page `sky` mask whose page has that sky; on any other page `skyClip` still counts the whole frame. It
is where the sky drew against the frame's depth: what is drawn over the sky later without writing depth (snow flakes,
glass, particles) still counts as sky, and a pixel gap in a mesh counts as sky because the sky shows through it. Views
drawn into a target of their own are not recorded. The record is read on probe frames only.

Storm Light's tour (`tools/shot/shots/storm-light-tour.json`) sets only `lights`, per probe (`probeLookBounds`): [2, 4]
on climb, gallery and west, which face its lit windows, lamps and lantern, and [0, 0] on open and strike. Measured with
its masks on the RTX A6000 (2026-11-16, `--production --encode`), every other check passes at its default, the
horizon included (`horizonSeam` open 0, strike 0, climb 0, gallery 0.936, west 0 codes; `waterSeam` 1.85, 1.27, 0.197,
0.973 and 0 codes; before the far-air fog the horizon was 38.5, 0, 40.4, 37.6 and 2.11 and the gallery water 37.4,
KB-STORM-HORIZON1). It exits 3 on one check: gallery counts 1 light disc, the lantern seen through its lattice, where
the earlier render counted the same glow as 2 parts; that bound waits for a ruling. Storm Light is held from the
videos until mid December.

### Points style entry (batch 228 job 2)
`@margoengine/points/style` evaluates Potree attribute filters and OGC 3D Tiles point styles (show, color, pointSize, defines, conditions) on the CPU, once per `evaluate`, `bindPointStyle` or `update` call: about one pass over the used columns per call, so a slider restyles on change, not every frame. Bound styles hide points through the cloud's selection mask in filter mode: hidden points draw nothing and are unpickable but still count against the point budget (use `createStyledCloud` to drop them), and the binding owns the mask while it lives. Margo's choices against the specification: a colour whose conditions all fail keeps the point's own colour, not white; `pointSize` is in the material's units (pixels by default), clamped by `minPixelSize` and `maxPixelSize`; column names match exactly, then ignoring case, `_`, `-` and spaces. `styleSource` drops hidden points from each octree node as it loads and ignores `pointSize`; a node's `count` (used for budget planning) stays the source's count; a new style needs a new wrapped source and `OctreeCloud`. Swizzles such as `.rgb` are not part of the language (single components `.r`, `.x` and `[0]` are).

Batch 228 job 2 size: points/style is a new optional entry, 0 to 14,025 B min+gzip (bare imports external), ceiling 14,446 B; it holds the 3D Tiles interpreter, the filters, binding, extraction (PointCloud construction, as points/clip) and octree node styling. The interpreter moved from tiles into packages/shared, so tiles/style went from 10,052 to 10,058 B (ceiling raised from 10,057). Core + stage unchanged.

Batch 228 job 3 (transparent points): already present. `addEffect` from `@margoengine/oit/vfx` brings a `PointsPlugin`'s transparent clouds and sprites into the weighted blended and moments OIT passes, and on native WebGPU the exact per-pixel one (packages/oit/README.md, "Particles, splats and points"; GPU proof packages/oit/test/gpu/vfx-check.mjs). The points README limit line now says so instead of "use alphaTest or additive blending".

### Parity 245.4 DragonBones reader

`@margoengine/sprites/dragonbones` reads DragonBones 5.x JSON (`_ske.json`) with its `_tex.json` atlas and converts each
armature onto the `sprites/spine` runtime. Limits, each with a coded error or a `warnings` entry, never a silent change:

| Case | Behaviour | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Binary `.dbbin` | Refused (coded `failed`) | The public binary description leaves timeline tags and frame layouts undefined; export JSON |
| 4.x documents and pre-5.5 bone or slot `frame` timelines | Refused | Not described by the 5.5 format page; re-export as 5.5 JSON |
| Rotated atlas regions | Refused | The rotation direction is not documented; export without rotation |
| `curve` with more than four values | Refused | The format shows one cubic only; its multi-point form is not described |
| Colour offsets (`aO`, `rO`, `gO`, `bO`) | Multipliers drawn, offsets not; one warning | The shared runtime tints by multiplication and a dark colour, not an additive offset |
| Blend modes other than normal, add, multiply, screen | Drawn as normal; one warning | Those four are the modes the skeletal layer draws |
| `inheritTranslation: false` | Read as true; one warning | The shared runtime always inherits translation |
| Bone timeline `scale` and `offset` | Read as 1 and 0; one warning | Their meaning is not described |
| Ellipse bounding boxes | 64-sided polygon; the exact `subType`, `width` and `height` stay on `attachment.data.dragonBones` | Bounding attachments are polygons |
| Nested armatures | Flattened in place of their slot; they play their default (or display `actions`) animation on the top clock | Their own events are not reported, and the host slot colour does not tint them |

Readings the format page leaves open are listed with their sources in docs/clean-room.md (degrees, the skew axes,
weighted bind spaces, FFD offsets per vertex, the classic ease blend for non-zero `tweenEasing`, `clockwise` rings and
string booleans). An absent `tweenEasing` with no `curve` holds the key (no tween), as the page gives null.
Size: 25,259 B gzip (budget 26,017 B), of which the reader is about 10.8 KB and the rest is the shared Spine runtime chunk it builds on; the Spine entry alone loads no DragonBones code.
Default budgets as the skeletal JSON reader: 1,000,000 JSON values and vertices, 64 nesting levels; the converted
document may use up to eight times those, for repeated nested-animation cycles. Evidence:
packages/sprites/tests/dragonbones.test.js (14 tests, five real exports) and dragonbones-check.mjs (exact pixels of
images, a weighted FFD mesh and a nested armature, a real file posed and seeked back, native and compatibility).
Speed not measured (build phase).

## Committed Wasm blueprints (2026-11-15)

`npm run check:wasm-repro` rebuilds the blueprints only where rustc matches rust-toolchain.toml (1.99.0); elsewhere it
prints why and builds nothing, so the byte-for-byte proof comes from the machines that have the toolchain (local CI on
the dev PC). A deflated or gzip TypeScript blueprint is compared without its checkout line endings. Cross-system
equality has been shown on Windows only; no Linux or macOS rebuild is on record yet.

## Job 185.1 push 3: GLSL functions in node graphs (`@margoengine/shader/glsl`, 2026-11-15)

`glslFn(code, {name, defines, flipY, strict})` turns one GLSL ES 3.00 or 1.00 function, with the helpers, structs and constants it uses, into a node function; `glslToWGSL` returns its WGSL, entry name, parameters and result type; `toGLSL(target, translator, options)` returns the GLSL ES 3.00 program and binding tables the WebGL2 layer makes from a NodePass, a NodeMaterial that has drawn, or `{vertex, fragment}` WGSL, through the translator the caller passes (`await import('@margoengine/webgl2-compat/glsl')`). Defaults: the last function defined is called, no defines, `flipY` false, `strict` false (translated functions carry `@diagnostic(off, derivative_uniformity)`, so an implicit lookup in a per-pixel branch compiles as GLSL allows; `strict: true` keeps WGSL's rule). A source without `#version` reads as GLSL ES 3.00. Lookups read level 0 in vertex and compute nodes and use implicit derivatives in fragment and post nodes, as `texture()` does; each stage is translated once per source and options (cache of 256 translations). Refused, with MargoError `failed`, `line`, `column` and a help link: syntax errors, a uniform or a `gl_` built-in inside the source ("pass it as an argument"), an `out` or `inout` parameter on the called function, a parameter that is not a scalar, vector, square matrix or `sampler2D`/`samplerCube`/`sampler3D`/`sampler2DArray`, and a non-value return. Lines count from the source as written; a backslash line continuation joins two lines, so lines after it count one less, and columns after a macro expansion are those of the expanded line. Errors found while typing the translation (an unknown function, mismatched operands) carry no position. Limits are the shared front end's: 65,536 code units, 32,768 tokens, 128 nested statements and expressions, 64 macro rounds. Not in this entry: whole GLSL programs with `main`, uniforms and varyings (a raw GLSL material), and a Shadertoy `mainImage` wrapper; both are separate rows for Scott to decide. Sizes: shader/glsl 17,206 B min+gzip (new, ceiling 17,723 B); it bundles the GLSL front end that transitions/glsl also bundles, because two packages cannot share a chunk. Shader root unchanged at 18,664 B, transitions/glsl 19,656 B within 20,083 B, core + stage unchanged. Evidence: `packages/shader/test/glsl.test.js` (pinned WGSL for five fixtures, each checked by the layer's WGSL checker, toGLSL for a NodePass and a NodeMaterial, positions, options, hostile input) and `packages/shader/test/glsl-check.mjs` natively and with `--compat` on an RTX A6000 (Chrome, ANGLE Direct3D 11 for WebGL2): every pixel of five fixtures at two parameter values equals the browser's own WebGL2 compiler (maximum difference 0 levels on both legs, bound 1), NodeMaterials from GLSL equal their WGSL and `texture()` twins, and six toGLSL programs compile and link in raw WebGL2.

## Process tree kills

Scripts and tests end a process tree on Windows only through scripts/support/shutdown.mjs (KB-TEST-FILEEXIT1;
tests/process-kill.test.js fails on a raw `taskkill` or a `ParentProcessId` walk anywhere else). A child process is
ended by `killChildTreeSync` (`taskkill /T /F` while Node still holds its handle; 1.2 s measured on the loaded
workstation); a bare pid by `killOwnTree`, which reads the whole process table first (4 to 20 s there, up to the 30,000
ms shutdown budget) and ends the pid only if it is below the caller. Accepted difference: below a live child,
taskkill finds the tree by `ParentProcessId`, which Microsoft documents may name a newer process that took a dead
parent's pid, and does not say whether taskkill compares creation times; a process orphaned by an earlier holder of
the child's pid could be taken in. Pass a pid instead of the child to get the checked walk, at its cost. A child whose
exit was seen is never ended by pid; anything it left running is not ended either.

## Browser close limit

A hosted browser close (`launchBrowser` in `scripts/lib/browser.mjs`, KB-P3h, 2026-11-15) has a hard limit,
`CLOSE_LIMIT_MS` (20,000 ms). A close still open then (a host that never acknowledges the end, a client close that
never returns) kills the host and the browser with their process trees (on Windows `killOwnTree` in
`scripts/support/shutdown.mjs`, which ends a pid only while it is below the suite's own process, KB-TEST-FILEEXIT1; the
process groups elsewhere), waits up to `CLOSE_KILL_MS` (8,000 ms) after the kill for them to be gone, releases the host
and fails with `SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT`, listing the open steps (`open`), the killed pids (`killed`) and any still running
(`survivors`). On Windows the kill itself reads the whole process table: 4 to 20 s measured on the loaded
workstation (it may take up to the 30,000 ms shutdown budget), against 1.2 s for the `taskkill /T` it replaced, which could end another run's process through a reused pid. Measured closes: 0.25 s alone, 0.28 to 2.03 s beside two GPU suites and ten CPU hogs; the close's own
bounded waits add up to about 7 s. Before the limit a close past the budget threw but left the host and its
browser running and the host referenced, so a suite that went on after the error never exited. Firefox and WebKit
run without a host and close the ordinary way, inside the 30,000 ms budget, with no kill. `check:readme-run` closes each example's browser after the example's 20 s deadline,
under this limit, and fails the example only when the close itself fails (2026-11-21, docs/known-bugs.md KB1703).

## GLSL programs as materials, push 1 (`@margoengine/shader/glsl-material`, 2026-11-15)

`new ShaderMaterial({vertexShader, fragmentShader, uniforms, defines, glslVersion, flipY, clipSpace, strict, builtins})` takes a whole GLSL ES 3.00 or 1.00 program with `void main()` in each stage, as three.js `RawShaderMaterial` does, and is a `RawShaderMaterial` drawn by a `RawMesh` in `RawShaders`; `glslProgramToWGSL(source)` returns the two WGSL stages and the uniform, texture, attribute and varying tables. Defaults: `flipY` true (2D lookups and `texelFetch` read a Margo texture as GL reads one uploaded with `UNPACK_FLIP_Y_WEBGL`), `clipSpace` 'gl' (clip z from -1 to 1 onto Margo's reversed depth; 'webgpu' leaves it), `strict` false (`@diagnostic(off, derivative_uniformity)` on the module), `builtins` false (the only accepted value in this push: the program declares every uniform and attribute it reads), no defines. Uniform types: `float`, `int`, `uint`, `bool`, their vectors, `mat2`, `mat3`, `mat4`, and `sampler2D`, `samplerCube`, `sampler3D`, `sampler2DArray`; values are live (`material.uniforms.x.value`, no translation), booleans are stored as 0 or 1, a string is a colour for a `vec3` only, and any other non-number value throws RangeError. A missing uniform starts at zero; a missing sampler reads opaque white (GL reads black), as raw materials do. Missing attributes read (0, 0, 0, 1) and narrower ones are widened that way, as GL's generic attribute default does; integer attributes keep their kind. Varyings link by name; refused at link, with MargoError `failed`, `stage`, `line`, `column` and a help link: a type or interpolation mismatch, a varying read but not written, a non-flat integer varying, mixed versions, a uniform with two types, a type outside the list above (`mat2x3` and other non-square matrices, structs, arrays and blocks came in push 3, below), more than one colour output and `gl_FragData` above 0. Built-ins: `gl_Position`, `gl_PointSize` (accepted and ignored: WebGPU points are one pixel; sized points are push 3), `gl_VertexID`, `gl_InstanceID`, `gl_FragCoord` (rows from the bottom, GL depth, `w` as 1/w), `gl_FrontFacing`, `gl_PointCoord` ((0.5, 0.5), the centre of a one-pixel point), `gl_FragColor`, `gl_FragData[0]`, `gl_FragDepth` (stored as 1 - d, clamped to 0..1), `gl_DepthRange` and the `gl_Max*` constants at the WebGL 1 and 2 minimums. Accepted difference: a flat varying takes the first vertex of a primitive on WebGPU and the last in GL (WebGPU's `@interpolate(flat)` default `first`; OpenGL ES 3.0 section 2.18 provoking vertex), so the two agree only where flat values are equal across a primitive. Translations are cached per source, defines and options (64 programs; `defines` and `needsUpdate` translate again, uniform values never do). Limits are the shared front end's: 65,536 code units a stage, 32,768 tokens, 128 nested statements and expressions, 64 macro rounds. Not in this push: `builtins: 'three'`, 'babylon', 'playcanvas' (the engine's matrices and attributes under each engine's names), `shaderMesh`, includes, instancing helpers and the extra raw state (depthCompare, depthBias, alphaToCoverage) are push 2; uniform blocks, structs, arrays, integer and shadow samplers, sized points and wireframe push 3; ShaderPass and Shadertoy pushes 4 and 5; lights and fog uniforms push 6; Shadertoy sound, VR and cube maps push 7. Pushes 2, 3 and 6 and ShaderPass and Shadertoy have since landed (their sections below); what still stays refused is listed under push 3. Sizes: shader/glsl-material 23,792 B min+gzip (new, ceiling 24,503 B; shader/raw on its own is 14,369 B, +14 B for the `RawShaderMaterial<U>` uniform type parameter, within 14,662 B); it bundles the GLSL front end that shader/glsl and transitions/glsl also bundle. shader/glsl 17,310 B (ceiling 17,723 B) and transitions/glsl 19,756 B (ceiling 20,083 B) after the two optional `GLSLHost` hooks (`samplerOf`, `yUp`), core + stage unchanged at 24,837 B. Evidence: `packages/shader/test/glsl-material.test.js` (pinned WGSL for eight programs, each stage checked by the layer's WGSL checker, the tables, live uniforms, the work count, a defines change that changes the uniform layout, every link fault with its position, the GL conventions) and `packages/shader/test/glsl-material-check.mjs` natively and with `--compat` (RTX A6000, Chrome, ANGLE Direct3D 11 for WebGL): eight original programs (every uniform type, GLSL ES 1.00 attributes and varyings with texture2D and a perspective w, gl_FragCoord, gl_FrontFacing and derivatives on both faces, gl_FragDepth with the depth test and a flat int varying, discard and defines, a vertex-stage lookup with a uniform both stages share, attribute widening and absent attributes, gl_FragData with mat3 and int uniforms, a loop and a sampler helper) over 32 x 32 pixels, with their first uniform values and defines and again after a live change, equal the browser's own WebGL compile (WebGL 1 for 1.00, WebGL 2 for 3.00) within the bound of 1 level: 15 of the 16 draws differ by 0 levels on both legs, and the perspective-w program differs by 1 level in one channel of one pixel (mean 0.0003) on both legs; uniform changes translated nothing and the defines change translated once.

## GLSL programs as materials, push 2 (`@margoengine/shader/glsl-material`, `@margoengine/shader/raw`, 2026-11-15)

`builtins` (default `'auto'`) supplies the engine's matrices and vertex streams under one convention's names: `'modelViewMatrix'` (`modelMatrix`, `viewMatrix`, `modelViewMatrix`, `projectionMatrix`, `normalMatrix`, `cameraPosition`, `isOrthographic`, attributes `position`, `normal`, `uv`, `uv1`, `color`, `tangent`, `instanceMatrix`, `instanceColor`, all usable undeclared), `'worldViewProjection'` (`world`, `view`, `projection`, `worldView`, `worldViewProjection`, attributes `position`, `normal`, `uv`, `uv2`, `color` as vec4), `'matrix_model'` (`matrix_model`, `matrix_normal`, `matrix_view`, `matrix_viewInverse`, `matrix_view3`, `matrix_projection`, `matrix_viewProjection`, `view_position`, `camera_params`, `screen_size`, `viewport_size`, `view_index`, attributes `vertex_position`, `vertex_normal`) or `false`. `'auto'` takes the one convention the program's names show and refuses names of two with MargoError `failed` and a help link; a name listed in `uniforms` is the caller's. A declared built-in of the wrong type is refused. docs/porting-glsl.md maps the engines onto these names. `shaderMesh(geometry, material, options)` builds a `RawMesh` from `{positions, normals, uvs, uvs1, colors, tangents, indices}` or a core `Geometry`, with extra attributes and instances by GLSL name; mismatched counts throw RangeError. `RawMesh` and `shaderMesh`'s result are generic over the material, so `mesh.material.uniforms.x.value` keeps its type. Includes: `#include <name>` or `"name"` from `includes`, 8 deep, plus the built-in fragment chunks `tonemapping_fragment` (PBR Neutral when Margo displays the frame) and `colorspace_fragment` (sRGB encode when the target expects it). `outputColorSpace` 'srgb' (default) or 'linear'. GL state names on ShaderMaterial: `side`, `depthFunc`, `polygonOffset` with factor and units, `blending: 'custom'` with source, destination and equation for colour and alpha. On RawShaderMaterial: `depthCompare` (default 'greater-equal'), `depthBias` and `depthBiasSlopeScale` (triangle topologies only; WebGPU allows no bias on points and lines), `alphaToCoverage` (multisampled colour passes only), `blending: 'subtractive'`, and textures with `sampleType: 'depth'` (2d, cube and 2d array; 3d is refused) with a comparison sampler defaulting to `compare: 'less-equal'` and a far depth of 1 when no texture is set. By method: `isOrthographic` and the orthographic flag of `camera_params` read `projection[3].w > 0.5`, as the camera block's projection is rebuilt in float32 from the view projection and a perspective `[3][3]` is near 0 but not exactly 0; `camera_params` assumes Margo's reversed-Z projections and reports a far of 3.4e38 for an infinite far plane; an absent matrix attribute reads the identity's column, where GL's generic attribute reads (0, 0, 0, 1) for each column; an sRGB output (`outputColorSpace` 'srgb') is decoded to linear in an HDR capture, so captures of a GLSL program and a core material agree, and a colour above 1 is clamped there as GL clamps it; the GL projection is derived from Margo's reversed-Z projection per column as `z' = w - 2z` and the vertex entry turns `gl_Position.z` back the same way, so the depth written is Margo's to within float32 rounding of that step, and a program that reads clip z sees GL's range. Sizes: shader/glsl-material 32,127 B min+gzip (from 23,792 B, ceiling 24,503 to 33,091 B): ShaderMaterial alone is 27,427 B, and the rest is `RawMesh`, which `shaderMesh` builds and every drawing app imports anyway (ShaderMaterial with RawMesh and RawShaders 34,406 B, the whole entry with RawShaders 35,358 B). shader/raw 14,769 B (from 14,369 B, ceiling 14,662 to 15,212 B) for the depth state. shader/serialization 20,015 B (from 19,296 B, ceiling 19,875 to 20,616 B): it bundles RawShaderMaterial, and its raw material codec now saves `depthCompare`, `depthBias`, `depthBiasSlopeScale` and `alphaToCoverage` too. ShaderMaterial itself had no codec in this push; since then `glslMaterialCodec(ShaderMaterial)` of `@margoengine/shader/serialization` saves one (`packages/shader/test/glsl-material-data.test.js`). shader/glsl and transitions/glsl unchanged; core + stage unchanged. Evidence: `packages/shader/test/glsl-material-builtins.test.js` (each convention, implicit names, `'auto'` and its refusal, type mismatches, matrix attributes, instancing, the geometry mapping, includes, the output colour space, the state names, every fixture's WGSL through the layer's checker), `packages/shader/test/raw.test.js` (the depth state, bias and coverage rules, depth texture layouts and fallbacks, the typed material), and on the GPU (RTX A6000, Chrome, natively and with `--compat` on ANGLE Direct3D 11): `glsl-material-check.mjs` draws six original programs (each convention, four instances, includes with both chunks, a linear output) against the browser's own WebGL with the same engine values computed in double precision, 0 levels on both legs, first and after a live change, and a GLSL quad in front of and behind a core box sorts by depth both ways; `raw-check.mjs` draws a depth texture compare, an equal depth test and a biased draw.

## GLSL programs as materials, push 3 (`@margoengine/shader/glsl-material`, `@margoengine/shader/raw`, 2026-11-15)

Uniform blocks, structs, arrays of structs, scalar, vector and matrix arrays, non-square matrices, sampler arrays, integer and shadow samplers, sized points, flat varyings and `wireframe` are supported, each proved against the browser's WebGL compiler within 1 level natively and on the WebGL2 layer (`packages/shader/test/glsl-material-data-fixtures.js`). Limits that stay:
