- A struct or array uniform is copied into a private variable of each invocation that reads it (WGSL uniform structs need 16-byte aligned members, GL's need not), so a large array of structs costs a copy per vertex or fragment. Arrays of vec3, vec4, mat3 and mat4 are read in place.
- Integer textures read the nearest texel of level 0, clamped to the edge (WGSL has no sampler for integer textures); integer cube lookups (`isamplerCube`, `usamplerCube`) are refused with a coded error.
- Shadow lookups compare at level 0 in the vertex stage or when the call names a level or gradients (`textureSampleCompareLevel`); a bias argument is not applied to the compare.
- A sampler array indexed with anything but a constant reads every element and keeps one (a `select` chain), so its cost grows with the array; passing a sampler array, or an element indexed by a variable, to a function is refused.
- Sized points: `shaderMesh` refuses per-instance attributes on a sized point list (each point is already an instance). In a multi-view frame a point is sized in pixels of its view, as GL sizes it in its viewport (KB-GLSLP1, fixed 2026-11-15: shader/raw 15,178 to 15,217 B min+gzip, ceiling 15,212 to 15,673 B, for the 16-byte view rectangle in the camera block, which every raw pipeline binds; splitting it into its own block would add a binding to every raw pipeline for the same 16 bytes).
- Wireframe lines are 1 pixel wide (WebGPU has no line width) and each edge is drawn once.
- Flat varyings: `shaderMesh` rewrites the index so each primitive starts at GL's provoking (last) vertex; a `RawMesh` built by hand keeps WebGPU's first-vertex rule.
- Saving a ShaderMaterial needs `glslMaterialCodec(ShaderMaterial)` in the codecs; the textures in its uniforms follow the material library's texture rules.

Sizes (min+gzip, measured before and after): shader/glsl-material 32,149 to 35,623 B (ceiling 36,692), shader/glsl 17,310 to 18,220 B (ceiling 18,767), transitions/glsl 19,756 to 20,658 B (ceiling 21,278), shader/black-hole 24,095 to 24,480 B (ceiling 25,215), shader/raw 14,780 to 15,178 B (ceiling 15,212), shader/serialization 20,015 to 20,271 B (ceiling 20,616). Core and stage unchanged.

## GLSL programs as materials, push 6: lights, fog and motion vectors (`@margoengine/shader/glsl-material`, 2026-11-15)

`lights: true`, `fog: true` and `velocity` are proved against the browser's WebGL compiler at 0 levels natively and on the WebGL2 layer (`packages/shader/test/glsl-material-scene-fixtures.js`, `packages/shader/test/glsl-velocity-check.mjs`). Limits that stay:

- Light lists hold as many lights as the declared array (`pointLights[N]`, `spotLights[N]`), in list order; the rest are left out, with `pointLightCount` and `spotLightCount` saying how many arrived. The lights are not culled per tile, as Clustered culls them; a program loops over its own array.
- The names are Margo's own, not three.js chunk names (`directionalLights`, `fogColor` of its chunks): three.js chunk text is not a public specification, so a three.js program that uses `lights: true` renames its uniforms (docs/porting-glsl.md).
- The fog and lights come from `shaderScene(raw)` per RawShaders; the sun and ambient light always from `engine.lighting`. A uniform of those names given in `uniforms` is the caller's.
- `velocity` runs the vertex stage twice in TAA's velocity pass (the cost of a second vertex shading per vertex in that pass). Uniforms named in `velocity: {}` are scalars, vectors or matrices; a struct, array or texture the motion reads is not followed. Last frame's `isOrthographic` and `camera_params` are this frame's (a switch between projections is a cut). A vertex shader that reads textures or `gl_VertexID` gives the same value both runs.
- ShaderPass and Shadertoy carry no scene code: `toy.material()` refuses `lights`, `fog` and `velocity` with a TypeError naming `shader/glsl-material`.

Sizes (min+gzip, measured before and after): shader/glsl-material 36,514 to 39,715 B (ceiling 36,692 to 40,907) for the scene uniforms, `shaderScene`, the linker's scene part and the velocity entry. The scene code lives in `glsl/scene.ts` and the entry only, so shader/glsl-pass went 41,275 to 41,632 B (within 41,657), shader/shadertoy 46,809 to 47,217 B (within 48,214) and shader/raw 15,230 to 15,266 B (within 15,673); before that split they were 44,068 B, 49,694 B and 15,775 B. The bytes left in those three are the hook call sites, the velocity entry name and `drawnBy`. Core and stage unchanged.

## PostStack changes after setup (`@margoengine/post/stack`, 2026-11-15)

`stack.addEffect(effect, index?)`, `stack.removeEffect(effect)`, `stack.moveEffect(effect, index)` and `PostStack.join(engine, effect, index?)` change a live stack (GAP-POST-ADD1). Limits, enforced: one PostStack per scene (join reuses it); the order rule (HDR, at most one display, then LDR; SMAA or FXAA, never both; distinct names) holds after every change, and a refused call changes nothing; changes are made between frames (core throws `'state'` while the frame graph runs, the stack while it composes); `removeEffect` always disposes the effect, as `scene.removePlugin` does (switch it off with its `enabled` option instead); an effect refused for its place has joined that stack and can only be added to it again; `stack.effects` is a frozen copy replaced on every change. Cost, by deterministic work count on the recording mock GPU (`packages/post/test/stack-dynamic.test.js`): adding Bloom to `[SSAO, Tonemap, FXAA]` creates 4 pipelines and 3 textures on its first frame, exactly the difference between constructing the two lists; moving or removing it creates none; removing Tonemap after Bloom creates 1 pipeline (Bloom's tonemapping output) and no texture; 50 add and remove rounds leave no live GPU object. A ping-pong target that no effect wrote in a frame is freed at the end of that frame. Real GPU: `packages/post/test/stack-dynamic-browser.mjs` compares a changed stack with one constructed with the same final list, natively and with `MARGO_COMPAT=1`.

## GLSL post passes (`@margoengine/shader/glsl-pass`, 2026-11-15)

`NodePass.attach(engine, node, options?)` and `ShaderPass.attach(engine, shader, options?)` are async: they load `@margoengine/post/stack` when called (an optional peer of shader, so neither the shader root nor shader/glsl-pass imports it), add the pass to the scene's PostStack after the last effect of its kind (`PostStack.join`), or run it in a new PostStack when the scene has none, and return it; `pass.dispose()` takes it out of that stack, and a stack made for it goes with it (KB-NODEPASS-ATTACH, GAP-POST-ADD1; evidence `packages/shader/test/pass-attach.test.js` and the attach leg of `packages/shader/test/glsl-pass-check.mjs`, native and `MARGO_COMPAT=1`, 0 levels from the inverted scene).

`ShaderPass` draws a full-screen GLSL program as a PostStack stage over one triangle; the stack's colour is bound to the first of `tDiffuse`, `textureSampler` and `uColorBuffer` the fragment declares (or `input`). By method: a pass reads 8-bit display colour in `'ldr'` (after tonemapping) and linear rgba16float in `'hdr'`; the built-in matrices are the identity (`projectionMatrix` the GL identity, held in Margo's projection as clip z (w - z) / 2), `cameraPosition` is the origin and `time` the camera block's clock; the scene's depth is not bound. In a view of a multi-view frame the pass draws inside the view and keeps the views drawn before it; its uv then names the input pixels under the fragment, so `vUv` runs over the view's part of the target rather than from 0 to 1 (a vignette spans the target). A pass without a vertex stage gets one that writes `vUv`, `vUV` and `vUv0` only when the fragment declares them as vec2. The pipeline is created synchronously so the first frame draws (as NodePass); a WGSL error then reports through the engine's uncaptured error, not `material.error`. Sizes: shader/glsl-pass 40,447 B min+gzip (new, ceiling 41,661 B; it bundles ShaderMaterial, RawMesh and RawShaders), shader/raw 15,217 to 15,230 B (within its 15,673 B ceiling) for colour-only pipelines, shader/glsl-material 35,640 to 35,656 B (within 36,692 B), core and stage unchanged. Evidence: `packages/shader/test/glsl-pass.test.js` (the supplied vertex stage for 1.00 and 3.00, the input names, every fixture through the layer's WGSL checker, the colour space per kind, the stack contract) and `packages/shader/test/glsl-pass-check.mjs` natively and with `--compat` (RTX A6000, Chrome, ANGLE Direct3D 11): six original programs (each convention's input and coordinate names, a vertex stage of its own with the identity matrices, a vec2 position attribute through `attributes`, a pass-through and a gl_FragCoord pass with no input) as the second stage after a pass that draws a known image, against the browser's own WebGL drawing the same program over its own drawing of that image: 0 levels at every pixel on both legs, first and after a live uniform change.

## Shadertoy programs (`@margoengine/shader/shadertoy`, 2026-11-15)

`Shadertoy` runs the Image tab (`mainImage`) with Shadertoy's documented inputs as a GLSL ES 3.00 program through the
GLSL front end of `shader/glsl-material`; 46.8 kB min+gzip on its own (ceiling 48214 B), as it bundles that front
end, RawMesh, RawShaders' pipeline builder and ShaderPass. By method: a pass's `iResolution` is its target and
fragCoord the target pixel from the lower left, so in a multi-view frame the image spans the whole target and each
view shows its part, as a screen-space effect (draw `toy.texture` per view for one image each); `toy.texture` is
rgba8unorm at `resolution` (default 512 x 512), values as mainImage writes them, not sRGB decoded; on a mesh fragCoord
is uv times `resolution`. The image's alpha is written as 1. An unbound channel reads opaque black (GL's unbound
unit), and so does a plain GPUTexture or view channel after a device restore (reported once, #borrowed-lost, until
`toy.setChannel` gives a new one); a `(device) => texture` channel is made once per device and is a sampler2D unless
its `type` says otherwise. `setChannel` keeps a channel's kind and sampler type, which the program is built with. `iChannelTime` is a video's `currentTime`, an audio context's, else 0. `iMouse` and `iDate` are what the caller sets (`toy.mouse`,
`toy.date`; the date defaults to the local clock, month from 0). `vflip` is fixed (2D channels read upright, as
Shadertoy's flipped uploads). Buffers A to D are rgba32float at the image's size (the target's for a pass,
`resolution` for the texture and materials, each consumer with its own set), start at zero, and start again at zero
when the size changes; Shadertoy offers half floats too, Margo keeps 32 bits. A linear or mipmap buffer channel is
filtered by `textureLoad` taps in the shader (four a level, eight for trilinear) on every device, so the result does
not depend on `float32-filterable`; this costs more loads than one hardware sample, and the level of detail is GL's
reference formula (OpenGL ES 3.0.6 equations 3.17 to 3.21), where hardware may approximate it. Mip levels of
buffers, videos, keyboard and audio are made each frame by a 2 x 2 box (GL leaves generateMipmap's filter to the
implementation; an odd size clamps its last texel). Work per frame: one draw per buffer, one more draw per mip level
made, and one bind group per program reading a buffer, as the two textures of each buffer take turns. The keyboard
channel uses `keyCode` as Shadertoy does; video frames are copied with `copyExternalImageToTexture` each frame, an
image or ImageBitmap once. A channel passed to a GLSL function as `sampler2D` reads both the device's sample and the
taps and keeps the one its mode names, so such a lookup costs both. Paused, the buffers and channel feeds hold until
`toy.frame` is set. Pointer input for `iMouse` is the app's (set `toy.mouse`). Cube A is rgba16float (Shadertoy's
is half float too), a power of two from 1 to 2048 a face (default 1024: 48 MiB for the atlas and 48 MiB for the cube,
a third more each with mip levels), drawn after the buffers and before the image, and starts again
at zero when the image's size changes; its `rayOri` is zero and `rayDir` is normalized. Work per frame: one draw and
six copies, one more draw and six copies per mip level when a channel asks for mipmap. At a face seam the level a 2 x 2
quad picks is the GPU's, as in GL. mainVR's pass rays start at the camera's position and go through the pixel's point
on the near plane, so an orthographic camera gets wrong origins; no real XR device or pose has been tested, only a
fixed pair of eye cameras. `toy.sound()` renders one 512 x 512 block (262,144 samples, 4 MiB of readback) a frame
while the toy is attached, so 180 seconds at 44,100 Hz take 31 frames; seconds are at most 600; samples are clamped to
-1 to 1 and kept as 32-bit floats; the Sound tab's channels read textures only, and the render starts again on a new
device. A channel whose filter is not `'mipmap'` reads only the base level of a texture with mip levels (GL's rule).

### Procedural stone, soot and brick close-ups (fire step 5, 2026-11-15)
`@margoengine/procedural/textures-pbr` adds `stone` (Worley cells with mortar, per-stone height and tint) and `soot` (a plume mask from the middle of the v = 0 edge, not periodic: use clamp addressing), and two options: `tint` (0..1, per-cell colour of bricks, tiles and stone; default 0.25 for stone, 0 otherwise) and `chip` (0..1, chipped bevelled edges; default 0). With both at 0 bricks and tiles bake the maps they baked before. Stone searches 3 x 3 cells, so with jitter 0.1 to 0.9 a rare second-nearest point outside that block is missed and the mortar there is slightly too wide. No photograph match or close-up quality is claimed; the kettle close-up check of the fire plan decides whether CC0 scans are needed. Entry size: textures-pbr 4,915 to 5,448 B min+gzip, ceiling 5,171 to 5,704 B: the bytes are the two pattern bodies, the chipped-edge helper and the option checks, which every bake shares; a split would compile a second pipeline for two patterns. Core and stage unchanged.

### Soot and material presets (fire step 6, 2026-11-15)
`@margoengine/materials/soot` `soot(source, surface)` returns a `layered()` layer whose mask is the plume density over one flat face, baked on the CPU (default 64 x 64 texels, at most 1024); a curved surface or a face whose UVs are not one affine map of its world rectangle needs one mask per flat part or a decal. The plume ignores walls in its way, draughts and the flue: smoke that would leave up the chimney still darkens a face placed in its path. `sootDecal` returns one multiply decal shaped for `@margoengine/post/decals` (no post import) that needs a soot atlas to fade; without one it darkens its whole box evenly. `/presets` are colour, roughness and metalness only, no maps: copper and iron F0 are measured values (Hoffman 2013); the rest are art defaults. Entry sizes: soot 0 to 11,045 B gzip (ceiling 11,377), nearly all of it the Texture class it returns, shared with the materials root; presets 0 to 278 B (ceiling 534). Core and stage unchanged.

`@margoengine/audio/wav` (2026-11-16) holds a whole file in memory: `decodeWav` makes one Float32Array per channel (4 B a
sample, whatever the file's width) and `encodeWav` one Uint8Array of the file, so a 10-minute 48 kHz stereo 24-bit file
is 173 MB as bytes and 230 MB decoded. It reads PCM (8, 16, 24, 32 bits) and IEEE float (32, 64 bits) only, and refuses
files of 4 GiB or more (RF64 and BW64 are rejected by name). 32-bit PCM and 64-bit float lose bits in Float32 channels
(a Float32 holds 24 bits of a 32-bit sample, and 64-bit float is rounded to 32), so reading then writing those two
formats is exact only for samples a Float32 holds. Integer output has no dither: 1.0 writes the largest value and
values past 1.0 clamp.

### glTF root after the physical-material merge (2026-11-16)

`@margoengine/gltf-pro` is now part of `@margoengine/gltf`: its root is `@margoengine/gltf/pbr`, `/model` is
`/pbr-model`, `/instancing` is `/pbr-instancing`, `/extended` is `/extended-materials` and `/coordinates` is
`/texture-coordinates`; the other subpaths keep their names under `@margoengine/gltf`. The `@margoengine/gltf` root
measures 7,651 B gzip, 1 B over its earlier 7,650 B, because its error texts now name `@margoengine/gltf/pbr` (Scott,
2026-11-16). The sizes budget rises with it; a split would only move the same strings into another entry. Core plus
stage stays 24,859 B gzip (61,056 B raw before and after).

### Core plus the glTF root below 30 KiB gzip (2026-11-27)

A full build stops when core plus the `@margoengine/gltf` root reaches 30 KiB (30,720 B) gzip, a gate never raised.
Core's snapshot rendering and multi-draw (+156 B, 22,369 to 22,525 B) took the pair to 30,848 B. The glTF root now
takes the shared error helpers from `@margoengine/core/extension` (it is on `SHARED_HELPERS`) and throws coded errors
with `margoError` instead of bundling math's `MargoError` class: 8,323 to 8,191 B, so the pair is 30,716 B. Errors keep
their names, codes and messages, and `instanceof MargoError` still matches. `tests/modern-core-budget.test.js` now checks
the pair, which only a full build checked before.

2026-11-28: node-named errors and their how-to text (KB-GLTFA A1, A4 to A6, 343e5d9ece) took the root to 8,459 B and
the pair to 30,984 B. The root's throws now carry a short message ending in a link to margoengine.com/errors
(`#gltf-invalid`, `#gltf-light`, `#gltf-transform`, `#gltf-url`), where the how-to text moved; node names, error codes
and error types are unchanged, and gltf/pbr gives the same short transform messages. Root 8,459 to 8,114 B, the pair
30,639 B. `scripts/errors/check.mjs` checks these two files (`ERROR_FILES`) like the listed packages.

## IFC and BIM data (2026-11-16)

- Class inheritance (`@margoengine/ifc/query` `isSubtypeOf`, `subtypesOf`, `supertypesOf` and `findElements` class
  filters) comes from the IFC4 ADD2 TC1 and IFC4X3 ADD2 EXPRESS schemas, whose terms allow use in software with
  attribution. The IFC2X3 TC1 EXPRESS file reserves all rights, so nothing is derived from it and no IFC2X3 tree
  ships. Instead `readIFCData` records an IFC2X3 model's inheritance from the open web-ifc runtime (`IFCData.inheritance`):
  for every entity type the runtime's schema lists (`GetIfcEntityList`, 653 for IFC2X3 in web-ifc 0.0.78) it makes one
  inherited `GetLineIDsWithType` lookup and keeps the classes present in the model that it returns. It reads a lookup
  through only when the lookup returns no more lines than the model has object definitions and its first line is one
  (a class is either below IfcObjectDefinition or holds none, IfcRoot aside), so the lines read add up to the elements
  times their inheritance depth and no geometry or relationship list is walked; the 653 lookups are the fixed cost on
  top of the 16 the rest of `readIFCData` makes. `findElements` class filters, the BCF visibility rules and
  `isSubtypeOf(data, ...)` follow that record, so IFC2X3-only classes (IfcBuildingElementComponent, IfcEdgeFeature,
  IfcElectricalElement and the like) match their subtypes and every class keeps its IFC2X3 parents (an IFC2X3
  IfcReinforcingBar is an IfcBuildingElement). The record covers the classes present in that model only.
  `isSubtypeOf`, `supertypesOf` and `subtypesOf` given the schema name `IFC2X3` still use the IFC4 tree: an
  IFC2X3-only class matches only itself there, and `subtypesOf` an IFC2X3 class can list IFC4-only subtypes such as
  IfcWallElementedCase, which an IFC2X3 file never holds.
- IDS 1.0 checking (`@margoengine/ifc/ids`) agrees with all 334 official test cases. Where the cases and the prose
  differ, the cases win, as the IDS developer guide requires: a specification whose `ifcVersion` does not list the
  model's schema is still checked (the cases check IFC4 files against IFC2X3 specifications) and the report notes it
  in `warnings`; a value on the exact edge of the tolerance band (v -/+ (|v| 1e-6 + 1e-6)) passes, within 8 units in
  the last place of the edge's rounding; a simple value checks a bounded property's lower, upper and set point values
  for equality, while a bounds restriction needs its whole range inside. An applicability with a `maxOccurs` of 1 (the
  XML schema's default when the attribute is absent) reads as unbounded. A specification whose applicability has no
  entity facet tests every entity of the model, which reads every line once. IFC2X3 generic occurrences
  (IfcFlowTerminal and the other classes the IFC2X3 occurrence-type mapping table pairs) take their type object's
  name. BCF 3.0 viewpoints from `bcfTopicsFromIDS` need the caller's `camera`; without one, write BCF 2.1.
- The GPU scene (`@margoengine/ifc/scene`): a geometry placed `instancing` times or more (default 2) by opaque
  placements draws as one `createInstancedMesh`; the rest goes into `BatchedMesh` draws of at most `batchVertices`
  (default and maximum 1,000,000) vertices, and a single geometry larger than that draws as its own instanced mesh of
  one. Translucent surfaces (file alpha below 1) are batched, never instanced, so their per-surface alpha holds.
  Ghosted elements and opacity overrides draw as translucent copies in the translucent batches (a batch that has no
  room grows to at least 65,536 vertices) while the element itself is hidden, so a ghost costs a copy of its vertices. A hidden
  instance keeps its slot with a zero matrix. Picking a batch needs `@margoengine/selection/hit-details`: the element
  slot is written into UV0 (exact below 2^24 elements), which plain `Picking` does not read; instances resolve by
  `instanceId` with either picker. Clipping is the materials' `clippingPlanes`, at most 16 planes (a section box
  uses six; up to 8 cut in the rasterizer with the `clip-distances` feature, more discard); a BCF viewpoint with more
  than 16 planes is refused with a coded error.
- Section caps and cut edges (`@margoengine/ifc/section`, 2026-11-16) are computed on the CPU from every shown
  element's triangles, once per plane per `update()` that sees a change (planes, shown elements or their colours), so
  the cost grows with the triangles of the elements each plane crosses (elements whose vertices all lie in front of a
  plane are skipped after one pass over their vertices). Caps need closed surfaces: an open chain of segments (a
  surface that is not closed, after joining ends closer than `tolerance`, default 1e-5 m) draws as cut edges with no
  cap. Hidden and ghosted elements get no caps. Caps are one batch drawn with their own material (roughness 1, not
  clipped: they are trimmed on the CPU instead) and are not picked through `scene.elementAt`; points that lie on the
  straight line between their neighbours are dropped from the loops. Cut edges need a `@margoengine/lines` plugin.
- Georeferencing: IfcMapConversion `Scale` defaults to 1 when the file leaves it out, in every schema (IFC2X3's
  ePSet_MapConversion and IFC4's and IFC4X3's IfcMapConversion); IfcMapConversionScaled's FactorX, FactorY and FactorZ
  default to 1 too.
- BCF viewpoints carry no camera target: `viewFromBCF` places `target` `targetDistance` meters (default 10) ahead of
  the camera along its direction. A topic's snapshot and a viewpoint's bitmaps are read and written as the bytes the
  caller gives; Margo does not render a snapshot when it writes a viewpoint (capture one with `@margoengine/headless`
  `readPixels` and pass it in). `storeyPlan` takes the storey's elevation from IfcBuildingStorey.Elevation (project length units to meters,
  rebased by the scene's origin), which ignores any building placement offset; pass `elevation` when the model places
  its building away from 0. Materials default to roughness 0.8, metalness 0 and double sided, because IFC
  tessellations often mix windings. Colours from the file and overrides are sRGB and are converted to linear.
- Streaming (`streamIFCMeshes` in `/scene`, `streamIFCInWorker` in `/worker`): chunks of `chunk` elements (default
  256, 1 to 1,000,000). Streaming starts once web-ifc has indexed the whole STEP file (OpenModel reads it all; web-ifc
  0.0.78 has no partial open); tessellation, most of a load, is what streams. The elements are every IfcProduct except
  IfcOpeningElement (and IfcSpace unless `spaces: true`), the same set web-ifc's StreamAllMeshes reads (checked on the
  test models); `readIFCMeshes` reads the same list in the same order, so its element order is the streaming order
  (shell classes first by default, `order: 'file'` for expressID order). Each element is read with GetFlatMesh,
  because web-ifc 0.0.78's StreamMeshes wrapper passes its browser build one argument more than that build's binding
  takes. `IFCScene.add` keeps a streamed scene equal to a whole load: a geometry crosses `instancing` over all adds and
  its batched parts move into one instance group; a full group or batch is rebuilt at twice its size (up to its
  limit, items packed, state kept), so a streamed model costs about twice its batch and instance uploads once and
  ends with the same draws. Rebuilding replaces meshes, so `scene.meshes` read during streaming goes stale. Placement
  counts are kept per geometry key; a different geometry object under a known key (another model) starts afresh.
  `streamIFCInWorker` has no back-pressure: chunks the loop has not taken yet wait in memory, at most the whole
  model. Its `timeoutMs` is the longest silence between messages, not a whole-load deadline.
- Property write-back (`@margoengine/ifc/write`) writes through the caller's web-ifc 0.0.78 and saves with its
  SaveModel. The file header (FILE_NAME, FILE_DESCRIPTION) is kept as read: web-ifc 0.0.78 has no call to write it.
  Reals web-ifc writes as `1E-07` get the decimal point ISO 10303-21 requires (`1.E-07`). Values in SI are written in
  the project's (or the given) unit rounded to 15 significant digits, so 0.2 m in millimetres is 200, not
  200.00000000000003. Shared sets, relationships and properties are told apart by counting references from property
  sets, quantity sets, complex properties and quantities, relationships defining by properties or template, type
  objects, extended (material and profile) properties and the property dependency, constraint and approval
  relationships; another kind of line referencing a property is not counted, so such a property may be rewritten in
  place. Enumeration attributes (PredefinedType and the like) are checked as upper-case EXPRESS identifiers, not
  against the schema's enumeration, which web-ifc does not expose; enumerated properties are checked against their
  IfcPropertyEnumeration when they have one. A plain number is an IfcReal (pass `{type: 'IfcInteger', raw}` for an
  integer). Only the optional IfcRoot text attributes can be cleared with null. With several sets of the same name on
  one element (a malformed file), the first is edited. Lines deleted through `/write` stay listed by web-ifc's
  GetLineIDsWithType until the model is saved and reopened; this package's readers skip them, other code calling
  web-ifc directly on the edited model must too. An editor indexes the model's property sets and relationships when
  `editIFC` is called; changes made around it afterwards (by a second editor or direct web-ifc calls) are not seen,
  so use one editor at a time and create a new one after outside changes.
- The buildingSMART test cases under `packages/ifc/tests/fixtures/` (CC BY-ND 4.0) are kept verbatim: their NOTICE.md
  records each file's SHA-256 and `tests/fixtures-verbatim.test.js` fails on any change.

## Offline resampling (GAP-FILM-RESAMPLE)

`@margoengine/audio/resample` works on whole decoded signals in memory; there is no streaming form. Its response with
the defaults (32 zero crossings, rolloff 0.92, 90 dB Kaiser window) is flat within 0.1 dB to 0.86 of the lower Nyquist
frequency and at least 90 dB down at and above it, so content between 0.86 and 1 of the lower Nyquist frequency (19.0
to 22.05 kHz for 44.1 kHz to 48 kHz) is rolled off. Samples past either end count as silence, so the first and last
`zeroCrossings / rolloff` input samples (about 1.5 ms at the defaults) see the edge. Channel mixing follows the Web
Audio speaker rules for 1, 2, 4 and 6 channels only; other counts are copied in order.

## Offline time-stretch (GAP-FILM-STRETCH)

`@margoengine/audio/stretch` is WSOLA, tuned for speech: it keeps pitch by lining up periods, so strongly percussive or
dense polyphonic music can show doubled or smeared transients at large factors; use `@margoengine/audio/vocoder`
(below) for such music. Factors run from 0.25 to 4; the tests pin pitch within 0.2 % and level within 2 % from 0.8 to 1.25.
It works on whole decoded signals in memory, with no streaming form.

## Audio clipping and silence scans (KB-FILM-AUDIOSCAN1)

`@margoengine/audio/scan` works on decoded samples. `findSilences` finds edges to within one window (10 ms by default)
and reports the loudest window's level, not a per-sample envelope; a trailing partial window counts by its own samples.
`scanClipping` reads sample peaks only: a run of inter-sample overs that never reaches the level in any sample is not a
clip here (true peak is `@margoengine/mixer/loudness`). Both read the whole signal in memory; there is no streaming form.

## Water surf (KB-WATER-SURF1, 2026-11-16)

`@margoengine/water` turns a swell into breaking surf on any terrain-coupled open sea, with no options (README, "Surf on
a beach"). Limits:

- Travel time is solved on the coastal heightmap's cells (an eikonal relaxed over the eight neighbours, one sweep per
  row and column), so a bay narrower than a few cells gets no diffracted swell, and the surf field is rebuilt only when
  the flow starts, the heightmap is replaced or the device is restored.
- The surf takes each component's direction from the travel-time gradient (Snell's law) and its height from linear
  shoaling with a 0.78 depth cap. There is no ray-spreading coefficient, so swell focused or spread by a canyon or a
  headland keeps the height of a straight beach.
- Outside the heightmap the seabed is unknown: cells at the map edge deeper than 0.7 of the deepest edge cell, or
  deeper than half the longest swell wavelength, are taken as deep water.
- Swell components (wavenumber up to 2.5 times the field's) shoal and break; shorter wind waves stay deep-water waves,
  damped where the swell breaks.
- Seaward of 0.9 m of depth the surface is analytic; the flow carries the inner surf and the swash (KB-WATER-SWASH1,
  2026-11-18). Measured on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer (packages/water/test/surf.browser.mjs): the 1 m, 60 m swell runs
  0.126 m up the 1:50 beach on 0.78 m cells, against 0.155 m from Hunt's 1959 law for regular waves and 0.238 m
  significant run-up from Stockdon et al. 2006 (a random sea). By method: the run-up rises with finer cells (a 1D replica
  of the beach, frictionless, the highest of six periods: 0.24, 0.31 and 0.37 m at 0.78, 0.39 and 0.2 m cells), the step is second order along a face
  and first order across it, and the surf's hand-over gives the flow no wave setup. Bed friction is Manning n = 0.02 on
  every cell (sand); there is no infiltration, so backwash on a coarse beach is too strong.
- The waterline of the coastal flow lies where the wet cells' level meets the bed (KB-WATER-SHORESAW1), so it is as fine
  as the flow's front: on the dune coast's 0.78 by 3.9 m cells the run-up still steps a few pixels far along the beach
  where it reaches one cell further in one row than the next. A finer heightmap along the shore makes it finer.
- The shoreline foam band and foam lines are held off by the steady share of breaking waves (Battjes and Janssen 1978,
  KB-WATER-FOAMPATCH-KH1), not by each instant's breaking, so a wave group's lull keeps the surf zone's look; the surf
  foam itself still follows the breaking crests, so a lull shows open water between them.
- Spin-up: the flow runs the surf's last 40 s before its first frame, in 1/45 s steps, so it starts in the swash it would
  have reached. That covers beaches down to about 1:100 below the 0.35 m hand-over (a long wave crosses it in
  2 sqrt(0.35 / g) / slope s: 19 s on 1:50, 38 s on 1:100); a gentler beach still fills its swash during the first
  frames. It costs 1,800 steps on the first frame and after every rebuild of the flow (heightmap replaced, device
  restored): on the 512 x 82 test map the first frame went from 812 to 1,256 ms on WebGPU and from 4.2 to 7.1 s on the
  WebGL2 layer (this workstation, diagnostic, other jobs running).
- Memory: 32 bytes per heightmap cell more than the connectivity buffer (two travel-time fields of four words), and
  8 bytes for the spin-up clock. Still water and `water/rivers` allocate none.
- Measured on the 1:50 beach of `packages/water/test/surf.browser.mjs` (1 m, 60 m swell): breaking starts at 1.54 m of
  depth (H/d 0.67 near the 0.78 cap), height 0.86 m offshore and 1.04 m at 2 m of depth.
- Size (`npm run quality -- --gate=sizes`): the water entry went from 21,933 to 25,433 B gzip and water/rivers, which
  shares the coastal chunk but not the surf, from 3,198 to 3,371 B. Core + stage unchanged.

### Wind-blown sand (vfx/blown-sand, scenes `blownSand`, 2026-11-17)

`BlownSand` (`@margoengine/vfx/blown-sand`) is one optional entry, 10,823 B min+gzip, new from 0 B (core plus stage unchanged). Enforced: `limit` 1 to 1,048,576 particles (default 32,768), `range` 10 to 2,000 m around the camera (default 250 m; nothing is drawn beyond it), `amount` 0 to 1, `grainSize` 0.06 to 2 mm, `windHeight` 0.5 to 100 m, `streak` 0.05 to 5 m, `height` 0.02 to 3 m; options outside these throw. By method: the sand is a function of the clock, the seed, a downwind profile of the ground and a gust field frozen in the mean flow (Taylor's hypothesis), so grains neither collide nor pile up, move no sand, change no ground and never run out; nothing is drawn below the threshold of motion (6.6 m/s at 10 m for 0.25 mm sand), and above it the flux saturates (Owen, Duran and Herrmann). The speed-up over a dune uses A = 3 and B = 0.3 chosen for the look of a crest, not the values of Kroy et al. 2002. Lighting: the grains take the sky's diffuse light and the sky behind them only through the `sky` hook; without it they take the engine's ambient term. Under a clear sky the scene's sky is nearly as bright as sunlit sand (measured on the dune-coast crest view: sky sRGB 167, 190, 229 against sunlit ground 171, 167, 157, the sun at about 117 degrees phase angle), so single-scattered sunlight cannot lift a grain above the sky and plumes over the skyline read as faint grey-blue smudges; under an overcast sky they read as a light tan veil. This is a known weakness in the look, not a measured error, and the scenes setting `blownSand` is off (0) by default until the whole film scene is judged.

The dune-coast scene loads `@margoengine/vfx/blown-sand` by `import()` only when `blownSand` is above 0 (KB-SCENES-BLOWNSAND-STATIC1, 2026-11-19), so a scene without sand never downloads its 10,823 B; the `scenes/dune-coast` entry went from 6,204 B to 6,475 B min+gzip for the on-demand load. `attach` stays synchronous and the sand joins when `scene.ready` settles: frames drawn before that have no sand, so a film awaits `scene.ready` before its first kept frame. Until the sand arrives a clock plugin records every frame delta and `advanceTime` call in order and the sand replays them, so its clock (and so its picture) equals the one it would have had from `attach`.

## Clean-frame checks and look families (headless/look, 2026-11-17)

`headless/look` grew from 11,368 B to 14,638 B min+gzip: eleven checks (T1 penumbra, T3 stairs, T4 shimmerMoving, T5
silhouette and silhouetteShape, T6 bounce and shadowTint, T7 colourEdges and the two night checks, T8 motionBlur), the
motion reprojection and the look family table, which share the luma, mask, Lab and bound helpers; splitting them into
a second entry would repeat those helpers and give `checkProbe` an async import. The shot tool reads `lookFamily` and, with `shot.moving`, writes the `moving` inputs (the next frame and the camera's
motion from the page's depth mask, so `shimmerMoving` and `motionBlur` run on real probes; the motion reads the mask's floats, so the page draws it as
`r32float`, a silhouette pixel takes its nearest surface's distance, and the motion is the camera's alone, so rain,
sea and cloud leave a residue). The `penumbra`, `subject`, `lit` and
`shadow` masks are page masks drawn by `SceneTargets` from the sun's shadow visibility (`penumbra`, `subject`,
`litGround` and `shadedGround` values, 2026-11-17, KB-LOOK-SHADOWMASK1), so `penumbra`, `silhouette*`, `bounce` and
`shadowTint` run on real shots (`tools/shot/test/look-masks-check.mjs`). Limits of those masks: the visibility is the
sun's alone (local lights' shadows do not count), a coloured shadow counts by its luminance, ground is a normal within
45 degrees of up facing the sun with a cosine of at least 0.2, and only gltf/pbr models and materials meshes can be the
subject (core meshes draw in one pass). `chromaSmear` (2026-11-24) measures the 4:2:0 loss on any frame without an encoder: BT.709 full range Y'CbCr, 2 x 2 chroma averages, bilinear read back; real players and encoders differ in filters and quantisation, so it bounds the loss from subsampling alone. Colour edges against a real decoded master are still unwritten. `stairs` and `colourEdges` read the frame alone. Their first test judged a step against the climb along its own row and
read 15 percent on a 16 sample per pixel frame (an antialiased edge near a pixel axis has one partial pixel per row); they
now look for a value between the plateaus (KB-LOOK-STAIRS-REAL1). Storm-light at 720 x 1280, whole frame: msaa 1 5.70 (30.6 by the old test)
percent, msaa 4 at supersample 1, 1.5 and 2 0.10, 0.00 and 0.01 percent, the 16 sample reference 0.00 percent, against
the bar of 1. `banding` read 0 to 0.1 percent on every real probe measured (bound 1, family 0.2): it did not misread.
The flood draft shots are msaa 1 at supersample 1 and read 2.7 to 22.7 percent `stairs`, which is real aliasing. The `motionBlur` allowance of 5 percent is a chosen
tolerance. Measured on a moving probe (2026-11-26, KB-LOOK-TV-MOTIONBLUR1): the timber-valley rail-line shot (8 sub-frames,
180 degrees, 1920 x 1080) reads 0.55 and 0.60 percent; its edges' 10 to 90 percent widths sit at 0.3 to 0.5 of their
travel and none under 0.1, the smear a 180 degree shutter gives (half the travel). The check calls an edge sharp under
half the shutter's smear, a quarter of the travel at 180 degrees, and takes the shot's angle from `manifest.render`
when it drew sub-frames; a frame drawn without them is judged at 180 degrees. `detailKept` (T7) is wired into the family: `detailKeptFloor` gives 0.5 for `natural`, 0.6 for `animatedFeature`, and a
shot naming a family fails its master below the floor (`tools/shot/encode.mjs`); `natural` keeps the warning.

T1 in penumbras (2026-11-26, KB-LOOK-TV-PENUMBRA2): `penumbra` reads the ground only (the penumbra mask less the page's
`plants` mask), and `penumbraPlants` holds the plants in the penumbra to the plants out of it in the same frame (ratio,
bound 1), because Immerkaer's estimator reads foliage texture detail as grain. Both need `PENUMBRA_MIN_PIXELS`, 2,055
interior pixels (5 percent relative standard error), and report the check as missing below it. A shot without a
`plants` mask reads the whole penumbra and does not run `penumbraPlants`; the plant check compares plants to plants, so
a frame whose plants are all in the penumbra, or that holds plants of very different detail in and out of it, cannot
be judged by it.

## T6 within blocks (headless/look `GROUND_BLOCK`, KB-LOOK-TV-POOLFAILS1, 2026-11-28)

`bounce` and `shadowTint` compare lit and shadowed ground only inside the same block of the frame, a tenth of its
shorter side (108 pixels at 1080p); a shadow with no lit ground in its block is left out, and a frame with none on both
sides in any block reports `missing`. A frame under 30 pixels on its shorter side has blocks of 3 pixels or fewer, too
small to hold both sides' interiors, so T6 reads nothing there. Light that changes within a block still counts.

## T6 like surfaces (headless/look, KB-LOOK-TV-TINTMATCH1, 2026-11-28)

With an albedo, `bounce` and `shadowTint` compare only ground of like albedo, 16 levels per sRGB channel (16 codes); a
surface lit or shaded alone is left out, and ground in no shared stratum makes the check report `missing`. Distance
is not stratified, and a small shadow interior (54 pixels on the blowup) cannot resolve a floor of 0.0448 b*
(standard error 0.14 b*, KB-LOOK-TV-TINTRES1). headless/look measures 18,518 B min+gzip (ceiling 18,587 B).

## T6 limits that follow the light (headless/look `lightBounds`, KB-LOOK-TV-PALL1, 2026-11-26)

`bounce` and `shadowTint` keep 10 to 35 percent and 3 to 100 b* for a probe whose light is a clear sun (diffuse fraction
d at most `CLEAR_SUN_DIFFUSE`, 0.3336) and for a probe with no recorded `light`; above it `bounce` is the base x d /
0.3336, at most 100, and the `shadowTint` floor the base x (1 - d) / (1 - 0.3336). By method: d is taken on level
ground (the sun's beam at its elevation against the sky's irradiance straight up), not at each pixel's normal, and the
model is linear in d with one anchor, so it holds a shadow's sky view and bounce in fixed proportion; local lights and
a `HemisphereLight` are not in d. `Sky.irradiance()` reads back 160 bytes from the GPU per call. `headless/look` measures
16,911 B min+gzip with `lightBounds` (quality budget 16,825 B raised to 17,419 B; a second entry would repeat the Lab and
bound helpers), `@margoengine/sky/base` 11,170 B with `irradiance` (budget 11,026 B to 11,506 B).

## Horses: horses (2026-11-18)

- Enforced: `withers` 1.2 to 2.1 m, `condition` 0.8 to 1.25, `speed` 0 to 25 m/s, `detail` 0, 1 or 2, `maneLength`
  0.02 to 0.8 m, `tailLength` 0.1 to 1.6 m, a crowd of 1 to 65,536 horses baked at 10 to 120 frames a second, coats from
  the six named ones, a rider of 1.4 to 2.1 m. Unknown setting names throw TypeError, values out of range RangeError.
- By method: the legs swing in the side plane only (no abduction or limb rotation), so a turning horse does not cross
  its legs. The gallop is the transverse gallop on the left lead, the canter the left lead. The mane and tail are hair
  cards shaded as strands (Kajiya-Kay), not simulated hair, and do not swing. `ground` sets the height under the
  horse's root only: the hooves are posed for flat ground and the body does not pitch with a slope. A crowd horse plays
  clips baked at 30 frames a second (`fps`), and near a gait boundary two clips blend, so a hoof may slide a little there.
- Proven (`packages/horses/test/horses.test.js`): masses from the girth equation inside the published group ranges
  (riding 488, cavalry 459, draft 859 kg); stride length from Alexander and Jayes inside measured horse ranges; gait by
  Froude number; footfall order, pairs, duty factors and suspensions per gait; trunk rises twice a stride at walk and
  trot and once at canter and gallop; a stance hoof keeps within 3 cm of where it struck, and rises under 3.5 cm before
  breakover, through every gait and type at 0.8 to 1.25 times the clip speed; across each stride the tested limb joints
  follow continuous paths with the expected carpus and hock bend directions; the rider seat keeps segment lengths and
  clears the barrel; the rider hip follows the saddle damped and a little behind; speed eases, the gait changes with
  hysteresis and `seek(t)` equals playing. On the GPU (`test/horses-check.mjs`, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer): a horse
  covers 17 percent of the frame, the saddle rises 0.058 m through a stride, seeking equals playing in chunks, and 60
  horses in a wedge and a line draw in one crowd call.
- Not done: no rider is drawn in the package's checks or examples (a `@margoengine/humans` person rides through
  `mountRider`; riders in crowds are seated by `@margoengine/armies` on the herd's saddles). Weak spots seen on real frames, not yet worked: the upper legs
  meet the body as visible cuffs, the legs read thin, the mane barely shows, the bay coat reads as chestnut. Not
  measured: speed.

## Formations: navmesh/formations (2026-11-18)

- Enforced: 1 to 4096 members a formation, march speed above 0 to 25 m/s, a non-zero finite wheel angle, a pivot of
  `'left'` or `'right'`, a `field` with a `direction(position)` method.
- By method: members are discs (on foot) or capsules (mounted) on flat XZ; `ground` only gives heights, nobody climbs or
  falls. Members avoid each other and `addObstacle` posts, not navmesh walls: march them down a path or field that keeps
  them on the mesh. A cavalry capsule turns but cannot step sideways. The overlap projection stops at 40 passes, so a
  body may sit up to 2 cm inside another for a step when a cavalry wedge charges through a crowded gap (the test bound).
- Proven (`packages/navmesh/test/formations.test.js`): slot layouts for line, column, square and wedge; a two-deep line
  of 80 holds its files and ranks within 10 percent over 30 m; a 90 degree wheel on the left flank holds spacing with the
  outer flank at marching speed; re-forming line to square and column fills every slot; a wedge through a gap and two
  columns passing head on overlap no more than 2 cm; a field march goes round a wall to its goal; `seek(t)` equals
  playing, forward and back; the settings rows. Not measured: speed (the build phase defers timing).

## Armies: armies (2026-11-18)

- Enforced: a crowd budget of 0 to 65,536 near and 0 to 1,048,576 far members and 0 or more vertices a frame,
  `nearScreen` above 0 to 10, `cullScreen` 0 to below `nearScreen`, `hysteresis` 0 to below 1; `farTriangles` 12 to
  1,000,000; strides above 0 to 20 m, `runAbove` 0 to 20 m/s with `blendBand` and `standBelow` below it, `stature` 0 to
  0.3, `step` `'cadence'` or `'route'`, atlas `variants` of two-number offset and scale; a rider `pitchShare` 0 to 1,
  `seatHip` 0 to 1 m, `hipHeight` 0 to 5. A far texture past 8192 rows of 2048 texels throws and names the fix. Unknown
  setting names throw TypeError, values out of range RangeError.
- By method: one person bake a crowd (variety from heights, outfits and phases; several bakes need several crowds). The
  far level plays one clip, the one with more weight, on a simplified mesh; the near level blends two. Riders follow the
  saddle rigidly (no damped spring as `mountRider`), about the few millimetres of lag a crowd rider leaves out. Members
  are culled by bounding sphere against the frustum and by screen size only, not by occlusion. With no herd
  (`horses: false`) riders are not drawn. A core Camera is brought up to date by `update` (its planes otherwise lag a

  skinned near mesh stands within 1e-5 m for every clip and time; the far mesh keeps its triangle budget with only the
  source's vertices and their own skin; levels by screen size, nearest first, inside every budget, culled off the
  frustum, with hysteresis only when asked; a camera that has not rendered or has turned is planned where it is now;
  a quarter stride is a quarter cycle at any speed (no foot slide), walk and run blend across 2 m/s; heights spread
  about 4 percent; a model facing +X walks and rides with +X ahead; riders on the seat frame with 0.4 of its pitch;
  an army seeks to the frame play reached. On the GPU (`test/armies-check.mjs`, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer): 300 foot
  and 40 riders on horses drawn in their levels inside a near budget of 64 (47 near, 147 far, 146 culled), a seek draws
  the same frame pixel for pixel, and 24 men all near and all far differ in 0.02 percent of their silhouette (bound 0.5;
  a quarter cycle off reads 19.7).

## Direct3D compile size of layer-compiled kernels (KB-COMPAT-FXCTIME1)

Every corpus entry point outside the voxel path tracer stays within what fxc, the Direct3D compiler under ANGLE's
WebGL2 on Windows, links in seconds: at most 250,000 characters of function body once every call is inlined and every
loop of constant start and bound (up to 64 trips) unrolled, and at most 2 copies of a function holding an open loop
and an array of its own (`packages/webgl2-compat/test/corpus-inline.test.js`, counted by
`scripts/support/wgsl-inline.mjs`). Cold links after KB-COMPAT-FXCTIME1 (RTX A6000, Edge, busy): robot-planning's
clearance kernel 6.3 to 7.2 s, lightmap's bake 6.7 s, sciviz's mapped volume 11.9 s.

## Water planar reflection coverage

`WaterReflection` uses a finite planar capture and an atmospheric reflection fallback.
Near a capture edge, the filter and distortion determine the width of the transition.
Reflected objects beyond the captured extent are unavailable to the planar adapter.

## Orbital mechanics and disk motion (SPACE-01)

The simulator uses a single inertial Cartesian frame. Registry coordinates move between origin cells
while local orbital positions and velocities stay unchanged. Force work is proportional to the product
of body count and the count of positive-mass sources. With all bodies massive, force cost is O(n²).
Serial uses one separation for both sides of a massive pair. Worker partitions independently compute
the target's acceleration in the same summation order, so they compute massive–massive separations twice.
Massless pairs contribute no gravity. Work receipts count geometry and the ordered contributions.
Use fixed steps small relative to close-approach and orbital timescales. Optional Plummer
softening changes the near-field force. A positive J2 models one body's axial figure. The exponential atmosphere
is a prescribed rotating background with dissipative drag, so its combined integrator is second order.
It models atmospheric deceleration without heating, ablation, aerodynamic lift, surface contact or a mission
atmosphere. The Cartesian solver uses Newtonian gravity and provides a bound-ellipse helper. Catalog orbit
elements continue to use the SGP4 entry. The scaled force path avoids overflow in squared distances
and isolated force factors. A singular or unrepresentable candidate is refused before accepting the
tick or its work counters. The helper is limited to ellipses. It uses direct residual arithmetic for
nearly parabolic periapsides and rejects out-of-range states. Step refinement resolves some close
encounters, but adaptive encounters, collisions and merging remain open.

The lensed disk uses circular Kerr angular velocity and a prescribed radial drift. The angular integral is exact
for zero spin and a two-point quadrature for spinning disks. The model covers slow radial drift of the emitter
texture. Full relativistic gas dynamics, disk thickness and angular momentum transport are separate work.

The orbit entry is 6,820 B gzip under a 6,947 B ceiling. The optional plain and shared Rust Wasm
assets are 14,124/14,212 B raw and 6,091/6,146 B gzip. Core and Stage gain zero bytes. The black-hole entry grows from 25,293 B to 25,814 B within its 26,010 B
budget. Core and stage together measure 24,820 B.

The independent October 2020 Apache Point normal points give geometric range residuals of
−9.86, +71.97, +218.18 and +60.78 m with a Newtonian eleven-body run initialized once from DE440.
Additional reductions for the atmosphere, relativity and geophysics are needed for precision
laser ranging. A comparison using DE440 centres still differs by about 10 m because it uses the
same geometric observable. APOLLO's millimetre instrumental scatter does not bound the omitted
adjustments. The reproduction is `packages/physics/scripts/space01-apollo-measured.mjs`.
[Colmenares et al. (2023), APOLLO archive](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7818557)

## Underwater acoustics (SOUND-03)

The medium is stationary with sound speed varying only with depth. Each ray and beam propagate in a
two-dimensional vertical plane. Speed is continuous and piecewise linear. The surface, bottom and layer
interfaces are flat. Reflection coefficients are signed pressure factors and attenuation is one constant
in dB/km for the column. Exactly tangent rays that would leave the medium follow the surface or the
sound-channel minimum. The Gaussian solution describes a high-frequency wave near each central ray.
It omits range-dependent bathymetry, rough-interface scattering, lateral spread and broadband waveguide
modes. Its pressure is relative to each beam's launch amplitude, with no automatic combination of independent
launches into a calibrated point source. The path, delay and pressure ports can feed a downstream audio graph.

Nonuniform columns visit each resolved interface. In a uniform column with many repeats, the straight path
folds into the column with one beam drift and integer powers of the reflection factors. The total reflection
count must remain exactly representable as a float64 integer. The solver refuses an unresolved layer-crossing
time or a tick that would leave the path or beam outside representable range. The previous accepted ray and
ports remain available. The world holds 384 bytes per ray for state, outputs and scratch, plus the field
registry's output copies, and 24 bytes per profile knot. The optional entry is 8,163 B gzip under an 8,284 B
ceiling. Each optional Wasm variant is 10,911 B raw and 4,846 B gzip. Core and Stage gain zero bytes.

The loaded native path operates on the same ray and output regions as the synchronous constructor.
Each worker writes a disjoint run of complete candidate rows. The world publishes those rows only
after all partitions and the beam outputs pass their checks. Worker stacks and the work receipts
are scratch. Counters report the previous accepted tick and do not enter snapshots. Browser workers
need an isolated origin with shared memory and a world hosted on a Worker, since the main page
cannot block at the worker join. Plain or shared serial native tracing works on the main page.
The registry origin cell can be shifted exactly without changing the local range or depth coordinates.

Published arrival timing was checked separately with `sound03-arrival-measured.mjs`. One of the four
ocean echoes matches within the timing resolution and published rounding. Three match when the reported
variability of individual arrivals is also allowed. Both nominal tank echo predictions differ by more than
the reported timing resolution. The tank paper does not give independent sound-speed or placement uncertainty.
The comparisons exercise geometric timing only. Receiver pressure, transmission loss and waveguide modes
remain open. [Chitre, 2007](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.2782884) ·
[Viegas, Zabel and Silva, 2023](https://doi.org/10.3390/s23104931)

## Ice thermodynamics (ICE-05)

Ice sites are independent vertical columns, porous frost layers or axisymmetric icicles. The ice slab and
prescribed snow are quasi-steady and omit lateral conduction, internal heat storage, brine redistribution,
and snow accumulation or ablation. Specify conductivity and snow depth for the represented layer. The surface
freezing-point formula is measured at practical salinity 4 to 40 and extends to the fresh-water point at 0.
Frost uses the Murphy–Koop ice curve above 110 K and through 273.15 K. The area and transfer coefficient describe
the resolved layer. Icicle cells approximate the side and tip areas by a cylinder with a fixed-radius attachment
when no ice remains. The solver updates heat rates and phase changes at 60 Hz and holds each boundary field for
the tick. The surface grow-and-thaw model uses conductive resistance below freezing and the supplied warm-side
transfer above freezing. The default 10 W/(m² K) is representative of a moderate neutral wind. The snow term is
prescribed cold-side insulation. It has no independent snow meltwater ledger. Basal and external heat follow the
boundary update, and no part of the same forcing is used for both stages. The steam calculation uses an
atmospheric-pressure water pool that contains the current tick's melt, with a constant liquid heat capacity.
Unfrozen feed and meltwater drain at the end of that step. Returned rates follow the layout-1 site order.

Each site uses 144 bytes of world state and geometry scratch plus another 104 bytes for the staged phase
inputs and results. An explicit warm transfer profile adds eight registered settings bytes per site. Registry
copies and native stack and helper setup are separate. The native phase budget can evaluate 1, 2 or 4
participants, with scalar site-specific boundary preparation retained.
The optional entry is 6,912 B gzip with a 7,168 B ceiling. Each Wasm asset is 1,300 B raw and
803 B gzip, with Brotli sizes of 741 B plain and 743 B shared. Core and Stage gain zero bytes.

### ICE-05 freshwater flow over a cold plate

At 120 minutes the two modeled cold-plate histories give 27.57 and 27.48 mm of ice for Re 474 and
1118 at either sampled point. In Kaaks et al.'s independent optical measurements, inlet and center
thicknesses are 13.47 and 20.69 mm at Re 474 and 9.68 and 19.08 mm at Re 1118. The temperature-forced
columns miss all 16 thickness observations across four samples in time, both locations and both flows.
The thermocouple and plate-resistance sensitivity also misses all 16.

Adding a uniform water-side heat estimate from independent inlet/outlet temperatures and flow gives
14.05 and 8.84 mm at 120 minutes. This still misses 15 of 16 observations. The uniform exchange
cannot resolve the local inlet heat transfer or changing geometry–flow feedback. The 0.25 mm comparison
allowance includes the reported 0.2 mm replicate spread and figure reading.
[Kaaks et al. (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.expthermflusci.2025.111417) ·
[Reproducible comparison](../packages/physics/scripts/ice05-channel-freezing-measured.mjs)

## Celestial ephemeris and rotation (SPACE-02)

The built-in analytic orbital elements are fitted to 1800–2050. For other dates or higher accuracy, provide a complete NASA/JPL SPK planetary/lunar kernel with J2000-frame type 2 or type 3 coverage, including the Sun's retarded epoch. The reader supports both IEEE byte orders. With SPK, the solar/lunar angles include geocentric stellar aberration and light time. Site rotation uses the ellipsoid and geometric horizon, with uniform discs for eclipse flux and the Danjon lunar-shadow enlargement. Atmosphere, solar limb darkening, observer-motion aberration and lunar limb relief are outside this geometric model. Tide values are direct astronomical forcing in Earth-fixed coordinates. Bathymetry, ocean response and solid-Earth compliance are supplied by their own models. Tracker shading is for adjacent parallel rows with equal widths and a shared rotation, and accepts the local row's slope and rotation offset.

The optional physics/celestial entry ships independently of the physics and sky roots. With the native orbit route it measures 13,117 B gzip against a 13,511 B ceiling. Each lazily fetched Wasm variant is 6,846 B raw and 2,755 B gzip. This change adds zero bytes to core and stage.

Native work at each accepted analytic epoch is eight planet rows, eight SIMD-paired lanes and 48 Newton updates. Four participants each run two rows. The fixed native tables take 768 B, the trial result 192 B, and the job 24 B plus 24 B per participant for its work receipt. Stack storage is 65,544 B per participant plus the shared pool control block. The optional native path evaluates the Standish elements only. The lunar series, Earth rotation, SPK polynomial lookup, and local site and tide calculations run in JavaScript.

### SPACE-02 measured eclipse contacts near the edge of totality

The circular-disc analytic mode uses the reported sites, independently measured Earth orientation and 0.25 s scan brackets. Cape Range Site 1 in 2023 yielded 65.75 s in the model and 18.1 s in the observer's GPS-clock flash-spectrum record. Contact errors were +41.225 s and +88.875 s. Stephenville in 2024 yielded 168 s in the model and 13.7 s in the GPS-clock record. Camera frames independently bounded that totality to 9.9–15.9 s. Both modeled contacts miss their respective camera windows. Shifting the site by 0.001° or 50 m gives 167.5–168.5 s. At Gunter, photographs show beads through maximum while the model gives 162 s of totality. These cases quantify the limits of the analytic ephemeris and smooth-limb model at grazing sites. The comparison does not determine how much error comes from each. Eclipse contact accuracy remains open. [2023 observations](https://iota-es.de/JOA/JOA2023_4.pdf) [2024 observations](https://iota-es.de/JOA/JOA2024_4.pdf)

## Physics solver settings and speed caps (own solver)

Breakable objects (`@margoengine/physics/breakable`, BREAK-01, 2026-11-27):
- Enforced: 2 to 256 cells; sizes, strengths, densities, impulses and radii positive and finite; restitution 0 to 1; a geometry whose points span a volume. Bad input throws `MargoError` (`unsupported`) with the `#physics-breakable` help link.
- By method, the shape: a mesh breaks as its convex hull, so a concave mesh fills in; split it with `convexDecomposition` first. Cut faces are flat (Voronoi planes), with planar UVs.
- By method, the cells: a cell whose inscribed ball about its centroid is under 1/1000 of its own diagonal is a sliver and is dropped, so its volume (and mass) is lost. Only a site outside the body or two sites almost on top of each other make one; sites inside a box never do (`tests/breakable.test.js`, every pattern and seed at 1e-9 of the volume). Sites of the built-in patterns come from the body's bounds, so a non-box shape loses the cells of sites that fall outside it (fewer, larger pieces) and a little volume at those slivers (under 1 % in the octahedron test).
- By method, the damage: a bond holds an impulse budget (N s), not a stress or a fracture energy. A contact's damage is the rise of the pair's normal impulse over its last step, so a carried load wears nothing, but a body placed already touching another takes its first step's weight impulse (m g dt) once. That step impulse depends on the time step. Damage falls off linearly to `impactRadius`; an area weight holds a bond to 0.35 to 2.5 times `bondStrength`. A fixed structure's pieces take 0.75 of a direct `applyImpact` impulse (0.35 of a contact's) shared out by distance, as the contact itself pushed only the fixed body.
- State: bond damage, runtime splits, debris timers and the contacts' last impulses live outside the world's snapshot: take `breakable.takeSnapshot()` with `physics.takeSnapshot()`. A snapshot holds for the pieces live when taken; a restore across a break is refused (`state`), as the world's own snapshot needs the same bodies.
- Size: the entry is 18,787 B gzip (the clipper, mass properties, bond graph, debris policy and debug view in one entry).

Elastic rods (`@margoengine/physics/rod`, 2026-11-26):
- Enforced: 2 to 4,096 links; radius, density and moduli positive and finite; damping 0 or more; `loads` a provider with `apply`. `segmentLoads`: roughness, drag, added mass and viscosity finite and 0 or more, period above 0 (Infinity a steady current), a Strouhal number above 0.
- By method, the links:
  - A rod is rigid capsule links. It bends between links, at joints EI / l apart. A link's capsule radius is cut to half its length, so keep links longer than the rod is thick.
  - Links of one rod do not touch each other unless `selfContacts` is set.
- By method, the ends:
  - A clamp to `'fixed'` at the start is the tree's root and solved with its springs; any other clamp turns as a joint spring in the joint passes, which holds a light link only up to about EI / l of a few links.
  - A pin's gap under a load F is F h^2 / (10^6 m), m the end link's mass, and its pull is handed to the other body after the tree's solve.
  - A line pulled taut by a kinematic body stretches without end, as a kinematic body cannot be held.
- By method, the water:
  - The surface is read at a link's two ends and taken straight across it.
  - Added mass is put on a link's mass all three ways, so along the link it is overstated by C_a rho V, which the chain mostly carries.
  - One wake oscillator per link and the same phase start for all, so the shedding is in step along a rod.
  - Drag, flow and pins act only on links of a multibody tree (kernel FLOW_X, DRAG_ACROSS, JOINT_PIN). The water's loads come from the `loads` provider (`segmentLoads` of `@margoengine/physics/loads`).
  - The drag across the drag crisis (Re 2e5 to 5e5) is a straight line in log Re, without the crisis's dip; below Re 1 it is held at the fit's Re 1 value. KC comes from the waves' `period`; a steady current is `period: Infinity`.
- State: the loads provider's wake oscillators live outside the world's snapshot: take `rod.takeState()` with `physics.takeSnapshot()`. In a `PhysicsWorld`, `RigidSolver` carries them (KB-PHYS-RODSEEK1).
- By method, the air (`segmentAirLoads`, 2026-11-27): the water's loads with no surface (one a light year up) and the standard atmosphere's density and viscosity; the air's buoyancy and added mass are kept.
- By method, direction (2026-11-27):
  - `rod.setTarget` pulls each link with a spring on its own mass, held over a step, so its frequency is held to 0.5 / (2 pi dt) (4.77 Hz at 60 steps a second) and its damping to what the step can take; the pull is a force, so a heavy load or a stiff rod keeps the rod off the shape by load over spring.
  - `swayFlow` is three seeded sines (weights 0.6, 0.3, 0.1; periods 1, 0.53, 0.29 of `period`), each travelling at its own heading within 30 degrees of `direction`: film direction, not a measured gust spectrum.
- Work counts (`packages/physics/tests/rod-film.test.js`, 2026-11-27, the same on every machine): a rod of n links is one island of n bodies; the broad phase looks at 2n - 3 pairs (none solved, the joints filter them) and the solver solves n joints a step, so a 4,096-link rod does four times a 1,024-link one's work, and 64 rods of 24 links 64 times one rod's. The tree solve is linear in the links. Wall-clock time is a speed-phase item.
- Open: a capsule-chain rod under tension over a bollard blows up (KB-PHYS-RODWRAP1); seabed chains wait on it.
- `WrappedRope` (2026-11-27): mass in nodes (lump the rope's own mass into them; a span between two nodes is straight, so
  sag comes from nodes between); one wrap at most between two nodes (put a light node between two pulleys); wraps on fixed
  cylinders, the rope across each axis in the plane through its centre; a node reaching its cylinder stops the rope with a
  `state` error; a fixed node holds whatever its side needs, and its reported tension is the least that holds (the load over
  the capstan ratio). Exact for the capstan Atwood machine; between two wraps an inextensible rope's middle tension is not
  fixed by statics, so it first slips at one wrap until the middle carries what the other needs. On moving bodies, use
  `WrappedRopeSolver`.
- `WrappedRopeSolver` (2026-11-27), the same rope coupled both ways to the rigid world through the physics framework:
  - nodes are free masses or points on bodies; wraps on fixed or moving, turning cylinders; the rope's pulls go to the
    bodies as `bodyForces`, held over the next rigid step (staggered: the rope sees the bodies a step behind, as every
    staggered coupling does);
  - one wrap at most between two nodes, as above: a span straight from one cylinder to the next, with no node between, is
    not built (it needs the tangent line between two circles and a contact arc at each end), so put a light node between;
  - a drum turns less than half a turn a step (each step's anchor is put back at the middle of the touching arc);
  - measured (`packages/physics/tests/coupling/wrapped-rope.test.js`): a winch drum turning at 25 rad/s on a deck heaving at
    0.5 m/s, a 2 kg and a 1 kg load slipping over it, within 3.4e-6 m/s and 2.1e-4 N of the closed form a = g (k m_B -
    m_A) / (m_A + k m_B) over 0.5 s and the tensions at the capstan ratio to 1.2e-7. What is left is the kernel's f32 drum
    pose (its centre about 1e-7 m off, its rotation about 1.5e-7 rad), taken out by the stretch correction, so it stays
    bounded. Between a free drum, a boat and a mass, linear and angular momentum are kept within 4e-7 of the start, the
    kernel's f32 velocities; the same state at 24, 30 and 60 frames a second, and a seek replays to the bit.
- Measured (`packages/physics/tests/rod.test.js`):
  - a cantilever in a current within 0.03 % of its springs and 0.06 % of the continuous beam at 32 links;
  - a line between pins within 0.007 % of its chain and 0.03 % of the catenary;
  - a taut cable's ring within 0.07 % of the beam-string frequency;
  - strumming that locks to the cable's frequency at reduced velocities 5 and 7 (within 0.3 % and 6 % of its frequency at the tension its bow along the flow gives it), swinging 0.57 and 0.60 diameters, and follows the shedding at 2 (0.014 diameters).
- A rod or cable its tension holds (tension times a link's length well above its bending spring): its tension's stiffness across the links is solved by backward Euler, so it is stable at any step, and its ringing is damped about 4 % of critical at 30 to 60 steps a second (0.7 % at 600); a rod its bending holds is unchanged (`packages/physics/tests/rod.test.js`, 2026-11-27). A pin that gives (a rod's pinned end) holds across at a thousand times its give, so it opens across a thousandth of what its half link stretches under the same load.
- `MooringLine` (2026-11-27): lumped masses on tension-only segments, explicit substeps the axial springs keep stable (a stiff
  line steps finely: 100 m of chain at EA 1e7 in 100 segments takes about 3 s of computer time for a minute; a near-massless
  line without damping can gain energy as its slack segments come taut, so keep its default damping); the seabed flat and
  horizontal, its friction Coulomb along and across the line (no static-to-kinetic step, no soil suction or bearing); the
  water's loads by Morison per segment with its wetted fraction (a node's buoyancy by its own depth); not yet coupled to
  rigid bodies or the framework (a fairlead on a ship is driven with `setEnd`). Measured (`packages/physics/tests/mooring.test.js`):
  - friction stopping distances within 0.08 % of v^2 / (2 mu g), along and across;
  - a clump's snap within 0.02 % of the closed form; a buoy's anchor pull within 0.001 %;
  - the elastic catenary with its grounded length within 0.3 % at 100 segments (held to 1 %);
  - the 33 m chain of Bergdahl et al. (2016), its top driven clockwise round circles of 0.075 to 0.2 m at 1.25 to 3.5 s: the
    measured top tension maxima (30 cases, read to +-5 %) within a mean of 2.7 % (bias +1.6 %), 23 within the reading
    error, the worst 7.4 % (at the two smallest radii and longest periods); held to 3.5 % and 8 %.
- Vortex-induced vibration against measurements (`packages/physics/tests/rod-viv.test.js`, 2026-11-27): the pipes of Fu et al. (2025, arXiv 2502.05748), measured values read from their Figs. 5, 7, 9 and 12. The wake's two amplitudes (`lift` 0.56, `drag` 0.53 at Re 5e4) were calibrated on the uniform 1.6 m/s case's cross-flow and in-line RMS (+2.5 % and -1.8 % after calibration; a change of 0.01 in either moves them about 1.5 % and 3 %); everything else is held out and held to the miss of the paper's own validated CFD on that case:
  - uniform 1.6 m/s: modes as measured (third across, fifth in line); the bow -8.3 % (CFD +9.8 %, held to it);
  - uniform 0.4 m/s: modes as measured (first and first, where the paper's CFD gives the second in line); across +2.4 % (CFD -23 %), in line +0.4 % (CFD -11 %), bow +8.4 % (held to 10 %);
  - linear shear to 0.6 m/s: modes as measured (first across, second in line); across +8.7 % (CFD +18 %), in line +52 % (CFD +93 %), bow -25 % (CFD +28 %);
  - linear shear to 1.0 m/s: second mode across as measured, bow -22 % (CFD +24 %); its RMS across -42 % and in line -18 % fall short (KB-PHYS-RODVIVSHEAR1);
  - not yet run against the paper's bidirectionally sheared cases;
  - the tensioners' springs are a soft axial stiffness (1e5 N and 2e4 N), so the bow changes the tension by a few per cent; the paper gives them none. The damping time gives the paper's damping ratio at the first mode (the rod's damping is stiffness-proportional, higher at higher modes).
- The wake's forces take the water's own speed across a segment, its motion turning only their direction; the fluctuating drag follows the cross-flow wake (q^2 less its mean) by default, so a symmetric swing drives only symmetric in-line modes. `inLineWake: 'own'` keeps Srinil and Zanganeh's separate in-line wake.
- `segmentLoads` `vortex.amplify` (default false) puts Vandiver's measured growth of the mean drag with the cross-flow swing, 1 + 1.043 (2 y_rms / D)^0.65, in place of the growth the drag on the relative flow already gives; on the towed pipe it bows the pipe 45 % past the measurement, where the relative flow's growth with the in-line motion is within 8.3 %.

The world's region allocator (`Arena`, 2026-11-26): a WebAssembly memory cannot shrink, so freed regions are reused by later ones that fit (lowest free block first) and the top comes down as the highest region goes, but the memory keeps its largest size. Its free blocks are a list searched in address order, a cost in the number of free blocks per call, fine for the few hundred regions a world holds. Regions are handed out on the main thread only, never during a threaded step. The rigid kernel lives in an arena's regions (its world's block, a 1 MiB stack and 720 KiB of batch-query records, about 1.8 MiB above the world's own size), one kernel per memory, and on a shared memory it needs the threaded build (`loadKernel({threads: true})`, about 247 KB deflated, loaded only on that call). Threads (`useThreads`, `stepAsync`) solve a step's islands only: the broad and narrow phases, the island build and the step's end run on the main thread, so a world of one big island gains nothing, and a thread is a worker with a 1 MiB stack region. `stepAsync` is asynchronous, so the engine plugin's `Physics.step` keeps stepping on one thread. The soft and 2D kernels still run in memories of their own until they move into world regions.

Substep levels per island in 3D (2026-11-25): an island steps at the world's substeps times 2^k, k chosen each step from its own state, and never finer than 7,680 substeps a second (the finest tick of `@margoengine/math/clock`): at a 1/60 s step that is 128 substeps, 2^5 times the default 4. A body in contact turning faster than 0.5054 rad per substep at that cap (about 3,880 rad/s) is stepped at the cap and may gain energy against friction; a structure that would need contacts stiffer than a quarter of the cap's rate to stand may tip. The cost of a level is that island's work times 2^k: the Physics-API replay scene, where a 1 to 10 cm body spun to 1,000 to 3,000 rad/s by the scene's torque impulses touches a 16-body cluster and keeps it at the finest level on about 35 percent of its steps, takes about 190 s per 1,000 steps on the Mac in Wasm against 3.2 s with fixed substeps; the kernel replay scenes take 0.4 s for 10,000 steps either way. The replay proof therefore runs that scene's 10,000 steps with fixed substeps and 500 with levels. Speed-phase item: a multirate solve, where a fast body steps at its own finer level inside its island while the rest of the island stays coarse, would take that cost back; until then the whole island steps at the level its fastest body in contact needs. `adaptiveSubsteps: false` turns the levels off.

The block solver is the 3D default (2026-11-25): each contact manifold's two to four normal rows are solved exactly together, and a manifold no assignment of its points settles to rounding goes to the sweeps (fewer than one in a hundred of a pile's manifolds). Friction is still solved a point at a time against the loads of the block. Accepted difference of `blockSolver: false`, which sweeps the points one at a time: a stop shared by several speculative points can be met with one point held and the body turning about it, an equally valid answer of the same inequalities that more passes settle on more firmly. A frictionless 0.4 m cube that a wall stops at 6 m/s is thrown 0.115 m up at 8 substeps and 2 passes (0.22 m at 4 passes, 0.0005 m at 1), where the block solve holds it at its rest height (`kernel/tests/voxel.rs`; KB-PHYS-SPEC1). Keep the default where bodies strike walls or stack; the sweeps stay for worlds that must replay hashes recorded with them (a snapshot keeps its solver setting) and for comparing solvers.

`setSolver` (contact stiffness and damping, maximum push speed, allowed penetration, joint shares and push speed, warm start share) checks every value: finite, at least 0, and shares at most 1; a refused call changes nothing. The contact stiffness is still held under an eighth to a quarter of the substep rate whatever is asked, because a stiffer soft constraint shakes a pile the passes cannot settle. A warm start share under 1 forgets part of each contact's carried impulse at every substep, so a cold start (0) rests a box but costs more passes for a stack; joint warm starts keep their own energy test and ignore the share. `maxLinearSpeed` and `maxAngularSpeed` cut a dynamic body's velocity to its cap twice a substep, before the poses move and after the relaxing passes, keeping its direction; a collision can still move a body faster than its cap by a position correction of up to `contactMaxPush`. Kinematic bodies are never cut. The prediction distance (the 0.04 m margin of the broad phase) is not yet settable.

`body.additionalPgsIterations` in 2D (Rapier's additional PGS iterations) is any whole number of 0 to 4,294,967,295; the cost is that many more passes, a pass over an island's contacts and joints each, a substep each. The extra passes visit the contacts one at a time (the four-lane blocks keep the world's passes, so an island that asks costs more per pass than one that does not), and the soft contact's spring rate stays what the world's pass count chose (an eighth of the substep rate for an unloaded chain pair at one pass), so more passes converge the same soft contact further and do not make it stiffer. The island runs the most any of its awake bodies asks for. Proof: `packages/physics2d/kernel/tests/passes.rs`.

`maxCcdSubsteps` in 2D (`physics.setSolver`; Rapier's `maxCcdSubsteps`) is a whole number from 0 to 65535, default 1; 0 turns continuous collision off for the world. With 1, a body with `ccd` that meets something is stopped where it touches, keeping its velocity, and the next step's contact answers it. With more, an impact before the last is answered at once, as the contact solver answers a contact: a normal impulse that stops the approach, friction along the contact within the pair's friction times that impulse (the pair's `sqrt(mu_a mu_b)`, or a hook's), then, when the approach was faster than `restitutionThreshold`, the impulse that leaves the pair at the larger of the shapes' restitutions (or a hook's) times the approach, shared with a body that moves by its mass and inertia, at the mean of the touch points. The body goes on for the rest of the step under gravity and its scale, its forces and torques and its damping, along the exact arc, from where the surfaces meet (the gap the sweep stopped short by is spent before the collision).
