The impact goes through the same rules as a solved contact: shapes whose solver groups do not meet, the back of a one-sided chain, and a `modifyContact` answer that makes the contact inactive or the closed side of a one-way platform are gone through (with any number of impacts, so a fast body no longer stops under a one-way platform), and a hook's friction, restitution and conveyor speed apply. An answered impact is reported as a touch that began and ended (`contactstart` and `contactend`) and its impulse over the step as a contact force, with the thresholds of a solved contact; these come after the step's other events. The last of the allowed impacts stops the body where it touches, as the first does with 1, and the next step's contact reports and answers it. Accepted difference from Rapier: its substeps do not carry a body on through the whole of what is left of the step (with 300 m/s between two walls and 2 impacts it stops 3 cm past the first wall with its velocity turned, and with 4 it has covered 3 of the 5 m), so a fast body ends the step in a different place; with 0 and 1 the two agree to 2 cm. Proof: `packages/physics2d/kernel/tests/ccd.rs`, `packages/physics2d/tests/ccd2d.test.js`. `minCcdDt` (seconds, default 0), `ccdTolerance` (world units, default 5 mm, at least 1e-7 m) and `ccdMaxAdvances` (0 to 4096, default 32) are the 3D world's names and meanings for the sweep's constants: an advance shorter than `minCcdDt`, running out of advances, and 0 advances all stop the body at the time reached, which is before any touch (with 0 advances, where the sweep began), so a floor on the time or on the count makes the sweep lose time and never tunnel; `ccdTolerance` is how close it stops to what it meets. The snapshot is version 12 and reads versions 5 to 11 with the defaults.

`body.additionalSolverIterations` in 2D (Rapier's `additional_solver_iterations`) is any whole number of 0 to 4,294,967,295 extra substeps for the body's island: it is solved with the world's substeps plus the most any awake body of the island asks for, each shorter, and the islands that do not ask keep the world's. Each substep count is one solve of the islands that take it, the other islands held fixed for it, so an island's result is what a world set to its count gives it, to the bit; a kinematic body, which is in no island, starts each solve where the step began and ends it where the world's own count leaves it (the last solve), so a platform's step is the same whoever rides it; a step with no body asking is one solve and is unchanged. The cost is the extra substeps of that island alone. Differences from Rapier: a contact between an island and a body that is fixed or kinematic is solved with the island's substeps, as Rapier's islands do; a kinematic body is moved by the world's count and not by each island's. Proof: `packages/physics2d/kernel/tests/passes.rs`, `packages/physics2d/tests/passes2d.test.js`. The snapshot is version 13.

`FilmClock` (`@margoengine/math/clock`): frame rates and sub-frame offsets are fractions of whole numbers below 2^31, a frame is a whole number up to 2^53 - 1, and a tick count past the safe integers (2^53 - 1) throws a `RangeError` instead of rounding; at 7,680 Hz that is about 37,000 years of film. `time` is a double for display and uniforms; tick counts and `alpha` are exact. Proof: `packages/math/test/clock.test.js`.

`VFXOptions.clock` (`@margoengine/vfx`): an effect given a `FilmClock` steps in ticks of 1/120 s and runs every tick it owes in the next drawn frame, one simulation pass each, so a seek or a hidden stretch of T seconds costs 120 T passes in one frame (no cap, so no time is dropped and no `settle()` is needed). A 60 fps frame runs two passes where it ran one. Births from `burst()` are born in the first tick of the next drawn frame, so a burst asked between two frames lands on the tick the next frame reaches first. `Flame`, `Smoke`, `FireFront`, `BlownSand`, clouds and gunfire keep their own frame-delta clocks for now. Proof: `packages/vfx/test/film-clock.test.js`, `packages/vfx/test/film-clock-check.mjs`.

## Physics world parameters and readings (own solver)

`maxCcdSubsteps` is 0 (CCD off for the world) or any number that runs the one pass a step takes: the sweep resolves a body's whole step in that pass, so 2 or more is the same as 1, where Rapier uses the substeps to carry on after a first impact. `lengthUnit` scales the contact reach, the allowed penetration, the push-out speeds and the sleep speed only; the kernel's other constants (the CCD touch distance of 1 mm, the hull skin) stay in metres, so a world in kilometres or smaller than centimetres needs its own check. `timing` is wall-clock milliseconds from `performance.now()`, with the step and seven phases; it is not part of a snapshot, so a restored world reads the last step it ran, and Rapier's finer solver timers are not split out. `forEachActiveBody` lists awake dynamic bodies and moving kinematic ones as the solver's awake list holds them, in its order, not the order of creation. A vehicle's `rollInfluence` (default 0.1) moves the point its sideways grip pushes at toward the centre of mass: a car with the default does not tip over in a bend, where a value of 1 (the physical one) rolls a light, grippy car. A body whose only collider is switched off keeps its mass in the own solver and falls; Rapier works the mass out again and leaves the massless body where it is.

## Physics joint breaking and PID controller (own solver)

A joint's break load is read at the last substep of a step, from the impulses its rows carry over that substep's length, so a limit is met by the load at the end of the step rather than the peak inside it, and a short spike that the soft rows spread over a few substeps reads lower than its peak. Linear rows count the three lines of frame A and angular rows the three turns about it, motors excluded. `PidController` returns an acceleration and applies it as an impulse of mass or world inertia times that acceleration times the step; it does not compensate gravity or contacts, and its angular error is twice the vector part of the short turn, which is the angle to 0.1 percent below 0.1 radian and a little under it beyond. `PdController` is the same law with no integral. A cap (`maxLinear`, `maxAngular`) scales the whole command vector down to its length, keeping its direction, and holds the integral while the command is at the cap (conditional integration); the integral is not bled back down, so a load larger than the cap leaves it where it was when the cap was reached. The angular gains default to the linear ones when they are set at construction; setting `kp` later changes only the linear gain.

## Physics debug lines (own solver)

`debugRender` draws what the kernel holds at the last step: a sphere as three rings of 24 segments, a capsule, cylinder and cone as rings and lines (their rounded borders are not drawn), a hull by its edges, a mesh by each distinct edge once, a half space as a 20 m grid on its plane through its origin, a voxel grid as its box, and a compound by its parts. Poses are the step's, not the interpolated ones, so a drawn body can lead its mesh by up to one step.

## Physics cone rotation motor (own solver)

A cone joint's rotation motor is three turning motor rows along the axes of the target frame, with their own carried impulses, and the joint's limits solve after them in the same pass. A force-model motor stiffer than the limit's own soft stiffness (the effective mass times (2 pi 120 Hz) squared, held under a quarter of the substep rate) pushes past a limit by that ratio, so a light limb with a very stiff force-model motor can leave its cone by a few degrees; the acceleration model scales both alike and keeps the limit. The cone's twist motor and its rotation motor share the gains of the twist axis.

## Physics multibody joints (own solver)

A multibody has no cap on links or joint speeds: each link keeps its working numbers (a 6 by 6 inertia, a 6 by 6 inverse and a few vectors, 115 doubles of the 128 its joint's scratch rows hold) in the scratch of the joint that holds it, so the memory grows with the world's joints, and the projection is one backward and one forward pass over the tree, O(links) with 6 by 6 matrices (a 200 link chain steps 120 times in about 0.4 s in Node). Its joints are `fixed`, `revolute`, `prismatic`, `spherical` or `generic` (locks only; cone, rope and spring joints are not in one). The pose pass puts a link back only once it is more than 1 mm or 1 mrad from where its joints place it (`DRIFT` in `multibody.rs`): a smaller correction every substep took 0.5 percent of a pendulum's energy a second, so a joint of a tree can stand open by up to a millimetre, and a hinge may stand past its limit by up to 1 mrad. A joint with two free turning axes keeps its rotation whole in the pose pass and drifts as a plain joint does. A broken joint in the tree leaves the whole tree to the plain joint solver until it is repaired or removed. The velocity projection is O(links) a substep. The pose pass and the coordinates and inverse kinematics calls in TypeScript look each link up by its row in a list, so they cost O(links squared) in the tree size, which a few hundred links does not feel. Inverse kinematics poses the tree where it ends and keeps no velocities; it keeps hinge and slider limits but not a ball joint's cone. Rapier's own multibody ignores a body's speed and pose when the joint is made, which the oracle test works around by starting both chains from a tilted root at rest.

A joint's armature acts only while the joint is in a multibody: a plain joint between two bodies has no joint coordinate to load, and `setArmature` on one is kept until it joins a tree. The rotor's speed is read from its links as each step begins, before the impulses given since the last step land, so a body's velocity set between steps carries its rotor with it while an impulse is shared with it; a rotor on an axis held at a limit stops with it. The joint rows solve in the bodies' own coordinates and the projection adds the rotor after them, so a damped or driven hinge with armature reaches the augmented mass's implicit step to about 0.1 percent of what a step takes from its speed, not exactly. `augmentedMassMatrix` leaves out `acceleration` motors, whose stiffness and damping scale with the link's own mass along the axis.

## Physics locks at the end pose: the Newton solve's size (own solver)

Each path of solving joints closes its locks at the pose a substep reaches with a dense Newton solve over its n lock rows (`newton_right` in `packages/physics/kernel/src/joints.rs`, KB2161): a slice of the world's NEWTON words a path, sized each step by `newton_words`, about 4 n^2 + 71 n words (two n by n matrices of doubles, the rows' entries and ten short lists), and Householder QR with column pivoting of order n^3 for each Gauss-Newton iterate, up to 24 an iterate stage and two stages a substep. A chain of 50 spherical joints has n = 150, about 101,000 words (0.4 MB) and 3.4 M multiply-adds an iterate; a path of 1,000 such joints would need 36 M words (144 MB) and 2.7e10 an iterate, so long locked paths are slow long before memory runs out. The world's memory grows to hold the longest step's paths together and is not given back; when it cannot grow, the step sets the failure word and the paths take no closing push. A path of 64 lock rows or more solves on the band of its matrix instead (`newton_banded`, 2026-11-28): a joint's rows meet only its neighbours', so the band's half width w is about two joints' rows (9 on a chain of hinges) and the elimination is O(n w^2); 50 hinges (250 rows) take 0.13 s for 30 steps against 3.19 s dense. Its memory is still the dense slice, as a band whose pivot fails (a row that may depend) goes back to the dense QR, which finds and drops it; a ring's closing joint makes the band the whole matrix and takes the dense solve. A tree (paths meeting at branch bodies with no loop, `group_trees`) is one solve over all its paths' lock rows: a ragdoll of 15 spherical and hinged joints is about 60 to 90 rows, dense QR of about 0.7 M multiply-adds an iterate and about 33,000 words; its band is wide where several paths meet, so it mostly takes the dense solve. Rings and grids are not projected (their passes keep their share of the gap), so they take no NEWTON work at all.

## Ragdoll balance on the kernel: motors alone hold a standing pose (accepted difference)

On Rapier a powered ragdoll with no balance controller sank to 0.74 of its standing height in three seconds, its ankles rolling over (foot cone 0.66 rad), and `balance.test.js` asserted that. On the kernel the same motors hold the pose (hips at 98.4 percent of their height, still after ten seconds, feet deflected 0.24 rad). A straight standing pose needs about no ankle torque, and the motors are the same spring on both solvers: a rod on a spherical or a cone joint under a force-model motor sags by the closed form m g L / (2 k) (0.049 rad at k = 200 against the kernel's 0.049, spherical and cone alike, and Rapier's 0.056, within 15 percent, with a `maxForce` cap acting the same on both; `packages/physics/tests/next-cone-motor-oracle.test.js`). So the old expectation encoded Rapier's softer joints and contacts, and the test now asks that the motors hold the pose. Push recovery is not part of this difference: it is a ragdoll controller fault (KB-PHYS-SWITCH-BAL1).

## Ragdoll ankles on the kernel hold their limits under ground load (accepted difference)

The ragdoll on Rapier held its cone limits with its own projection, once a step, after the solver: under a planted foot the ground pushed the foot back every step, so the projection did not hold the ankle. Pushed left at 1.5 m/s, Knight's stance foot turned to a twist of -2.76 rad against a +-0.2 limit and a swing of 1.36 rad against 0.6 within 12 frames, and the body pivoted over a flat foot (measured with `packages/ragdoll/scripts/balance-ab.mjs --trace`). On the kernel the cone joint holds the ankle inside the solver, with the contacts (0.60 and -0.21 in the same run), so the foot rolls onto its edge instead. The same A/B with the earlier ball joint and projection on the kernel recovers all four pushes as Rapier did, so the two solvers agree and the difference is the limit that now holds. With limits that hold, the balance controller as it was recovered 1.2 m/s pushes in 116 of 120 cases of the solver sweep and 1.5 m/s in none (KB-PHYS-SWITCH-BAL1). Three controller faults the free ankles had hidden were fixed: the swing foot's target ignored the body's heading and the joint limits, a planted foot that a push lifted set its own target in the air, and every step took the full `stepTime` while the capture point ran away from it. With step timing adapted to the capture point (`stepDuration` in `balance.ts`) the controller recovers the tests' 1.5 m/s push in all 120 cases of the sweep (iterations 2 to 6, substeps 4, 8 and 16, warm start on and off, four directions), with the ankles inside their limits. Measured before release on Knight only; other figures pass the settle and push tests of `balance.test.js`.

### ASCII post effect (`@margoengine/post/ascii`, 2026-11-24)

An LDR PostStack stage on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer. Enforced: `characters` 2..250 and `edgeCharacters` 4, printable ASCII (32..126) unless `font` is set; `cellSize` whole pixels 4..64 on each side (default 12 x 16); `fontSize` above 0 up to 256; colours `'scene'`, `#rgb` or `#rrggbb`; `intensity` and `edgeThreshold` 0..1. By design: one character per cell chosen by mean display-encoded Rec. 709 luminance, plus four edge directions from the cell's structure tensor (coherence at least 0.5, fixed); no glyph shape matching, no proportional fonts, one code point per character; a CSS font needs a 2D OffscreenCanvas and must be loaded before it is first drawn; colour is the cell's mean in 8 bits; `text()` reads the last drawn frame (with several views, the one grid of the whole drawing buffer as last drawn) and carries no colour. The character grid is ceil(width / cell width) by ceil(height / cell height); cells cut by the right or bottom edge average the pixels they have. GPU cost not measured: each pixel is read twice a frame, and with `edges` the character pass reads five texels per pixel.

Entry size: 0 to 8,976 B min+gzip (ceiling 9,246 B); core plus stage unchanged at 24,797 B.

## Culling occlusion queries (`@margoengine/culling/occlusion`)

`OcclusionQueries` queries at most `capacity` objects a frame, 1 to 65,536 (default 1,024; WebGPU caps a query set at 4,096 queries, so each 4,096 take their own query set and render pass). GPU memory: 8 bytes a query for the resolve buffer and for each of three readback buffers (plus 8 bytes each), 24 bytes an object of box data, a 432-byte cube and a 64-byte camera uniform: about 56 bytes an object, 57 KiB at the default. Results land one to three frames after their query (three readbacks in flight; a fourth frame waits and its objects keep their last result), so an object uncovered this frame reads occluded for up to three frames unless `retries` and `strategy` force it. `samples` is a flag, not a pixel count: WebGPU promises only zero or nonzero and D3D12 and the WebGL2 compatibility layer (`ANY_SAMPLES_PASSED`) report 1, so Babylon's accurate/conservative choice has no counterpart (every result is an exact per-sample test; WebGPU offers no conservative query). Boxes are axis-aligned world boxes grown by 0.1% of their largest side; a mesh uses its geometry's bind-pose box, so skinned or morphed vertices outside it can read occluded while showing. One view is queried per frame (`view`, default the canvas's first view). Depth written by passes after `order` (default 1) does not occlude. Core's WebGL2 preview refuses the entry (`unsupported`). Core and stage unchanged.

### Zoom and spin blur (`Blur` kinds in `@margoengine/post/blur`, 2026-11-24)

Enforced: `strength` and `decay` 0..1; `samples` a whole number 2..128 (default 32); `center` [x, y] in -10..10;
`innerRadius` and `falloff` 0..10 view heights; `rays` 0..8; `threshold` 0..64. By method: one pass of `samples`
bilinear taps per pixel, not jittered, so a streak longer than a few pixels per sample shows steps; taps past the view
edge read its nearest pixel; `rays` has no occlusion pass, so any pixel above `threshold` casts a ray (Mitchell, GPU
Gems 3, 2007, chapter 13). `radius` applies to `gaussian` and `box` only. Checked on a real GPU
(`packages/post/test/radial-blur-browser.mjs`); GPU cost not measured.


## Asset containers (scene/container)

A core mesh belongs to its scene for life and core has no detach (removing a mesh disposes it), so `removeAllFromScene` hides each member root: hidden trees are not drawn or picked and cast no shadows, but the meshes stay in `scene.meshes`, `traverse` still visits them, their geometry and model GPU data stay allocated, and other code that reads them (physics bodies, an `Animation`, a plugin walking the scene) keeps running. The container remembers each root's `visible` and puts it back; a write to it while the container is out is overwritten. Core can only dispose a removed plugin, so a container holds plugin factories: each add runs them again and a plugin starts fresh, with no state carried over. A plugin already attached, or one the container did not make, stays where it is, `moveAllFromScene` moves root meshes and models only, and the camera and scene lighting are not members. `moveAllFromScene` cannot tell a mesh that some plugin made for itself from yours; leave it with `keep`.

A member is a root mesh, a loaded model (a plugin with `root`, `nodes` and `dispose`) or a factory, and is in one container at a time. The container owns each member tree: `dispose` takes meshes hung under a member too, except another container's members and other models. `instantiate` copies meshes and models, not plugin factories. A mesh tree is copied with `cloneSubtree` (same limits: core meshes only, so a model hung inside a tree copies as empty nodes); a model with `cloneModel`, by default that of `@margoengine/animation`, which takes gltf/pbr models, starts each copy from the source pose and rebuilds materials from the file, so meshes you hung on its nodes and runtime material edits are not copied. `cloneMaterials` copies the core material values of mesh trees only; textures a package keyed to a material object stay with the source. Copies of one geometry draw as instances. The default loader is `loadGLTF` of `@margoengine/gltf/pbr`; both packages are optional peers, loaded on first use. New entry 0 to 3,719 B gzip, ceiling 3,975 B; core and stage source unchanged. Capability list read from public documentation, no source read: Babylon.js documentation, "Asset Containers", 2026, https://doc.babylonjs.com/features/featuresDeepDive/importers/assetContainers.

`add`, `addAllToScene`, `instantiate` and `loadContainer` are all or nothing. Removal and disposal cannot be undone: when a plugin's `dispose` throws, the rest still goes and the first error is thrown. Adding and removing attach and remove plugins, which core refuses during a frame, so call them outside plugin and frame callbacks.
## Geospatial camera and geo maths (2026-11-25)

- `@margoengine/math/geo` geodesics follow Karney (2013) and converge for every pair, antipodal included; a round trip of 6000
  random pairs (a third near-antipodal) misses by under 1e-6 m. The Fourier series of the paper are replaced by 16-point
  Gauss-Legendre quadrature of the same integrands per quarter turn (exact to double precision), so a call costs about
  50 to 1000 kernel evaluations: do not call it per vertex of a large mesh.
- `GeospatialControls` collision keeps the eye and the four near-plane corners `clearance` above `heightAt` (up to 6 lift
  iterations) and sweeps the arm from the orbit centre to each of them against the scene and `raycast` (front faces
  only), with a down ray of twice `clearance` per point for roofs and tiles. It tests the pose of each update, not the
  path between updates, so a fast move can cross a thin ridge the arm does not span; and when the orbit centre itself
  is inside a mesh (a centre under a roof), nothing pulls an eye inside that same mesh out. About 10 scene rays per
  update. `underground: true` turns collision off. `@margoengine/tiles` streams terrain without a height query, so pass
  your own function (grid, raycast). No physics is involved.
- Picking (zoom-to-cursor, anchored pan, the turn pivot) takes the nearest of the engine scene (bvh Raycaster), your
  `raycast` and a march over `heightAt`; only a miss of all of them falls back to the ellipsoid at the centre height.
  The `heightAt` march takes at most 512 steps of half the height above the ground, so a slope steeper than about 63
  degrees across one step can be crossed unseen, and a grazing ray past 512 steps misses; pass an exact `raycast`
  (terrain/query) for cliffs. Scene picks are float32 in core: about 0.5 m at Earth-centred coordinates unless the
  scene is in a local `frame` or under a floating `origin`, where they are as exact as near the world origin. Zoom keeps the cursor point to a tenth of a pixel (the view re-levels at its new centre).
- Flights follow van Wijk and Nuij's path in the plane of the geodesic: the pan u runs along the ground geodesic and the
  path width becomes the range (range = w / (2 tan(fov / 2))), so the climb ignores the globe's curvature (a hop of
  thousands of km climbs a little less than the paper's flat-plane optimum would over a sphere). Height, heading and
  pitch ease linearly with the eased progress, not along the path. The automatic duration is the path length over
  `speed` within [1 s, `maxDuration`]; a press or the wheel cancels a flight unless `cancelOnInput` is false, keys do not.
  `fitBounds` frames a sphere around nine points of the box, so a thin long box is framed looser than its outline.
- Navigation modes: first person (`fly`, `walk`) looks to within 0.01 rad of straight up or down. `walk` follows the
  higher of `heightAt` and the first scene or `raycast` surface below the eye, so it climbs steps up to `eyeHeight`
  and walks through a wall taller than that (no sideways collision beyond the near-plane collision of the view).
  In walk the collision clearance is at most half `eyeHeight`, so the default 2 m does not lift a walker. The walk height snaps to the ground each frame, without smoothing. A mode switch that must move the camera eases
  the orbit view (centre, height, heading, pitch, log range) over `duration`, so the eye path is a swing, not a straight
  line. Keys move only in fly and walk.
- `followPath` interpolates the orbit centres in ECEF, so between two views far apart (hundreds of km) the centre dips
  below the surface along the chord (the range and the collision floor still hold the eye up); add views for long
  legs. Progress along the path follows the knots (square roots of each leg's length in screen widths), not true arc
  length, so speed varies a little between legs. One path at a time; it is a flight and cancels like one.
- Glide: the fling velocity is a blend of the last drag steps (event `timeStamp`), so a single jittery event can still
  tilt it; a pause over 80 ms before release, a `pointercancel`, first person and reduced motion give no glide. Pan
  glide follows the geodesic from the centre at the release bearing. Wheel zoom has no glide (each notch is exact).
  Keys pan by the height above the surface below the eye, at least 2 m. The dcc preset drags zoom 2 x per 200 px.
- Touch: the first two fingers make the gesture and a third is ignored; after a gesture the remaining finger does not
  pan until it is lifted and pressed again. The gamepad is the first connected pad with four axes in the standard
  mapping (axes 0 to 3, triggers on buttons 6 and 7, boost on 10); it is read only when `gamepad` is true, and other
  pads are left to the page.
- `frame` is any invertible affine ECEF-to-world matrix (rigid in practice: a scale changes metres per world unit, which
  `clearance`, speeds and ranges do not follow). `ground` reads world Y at world (x, z) with Y up, so it fits a frame whose
  Y is the local vertical (a tileset's ENU frame, a site frame); far from the frame origin (tens of km) the frame's
  flat ground and the curved Earth part by d^2 / 2R (8 m at 10 km), which is the world's own flat-earth error.
  `tilesHeightQuery` hits only the tiles drawn now: where a tile is not loaded yet it answers undefined and the
  camera falls back to the ellipsoid floor; each call is one bvh ray over the drawn tile models.
- Planet scale: near is 1% of the eye's height above the `heightAt` ground (at least 5 mm; the ellipsoid without
  `heightAt`, so a camera low over a scene mesh with no `heightAt` gets a near plane from its height above the
  ellipsoid), far is the eye's horizon plus the horizon of 9,000 m ground. Core's reversed float32 depth carries that
  ratio (up to about 10^7). With `origin`, controls math stays float64 and only the camera written to core is local;
  `raycast` and scene queries then work in local coordinates. Without `frame` or `origin` the camera sits at
  Earth-centred coordinates and core's float32 view matrix collapses near the ground (docs/large-coordinates.md).
- Follow camera (`ThirdPersonControls`, 2026-11-25): velocities and accelerations of meshes, models and position
  functions are measured from their motion (smoothed over 0.1 s), so a teleport reads as a burst of speed for a few
  frames: call `snap()` after one. A flock is framed by its bounding sphere about the centroid (1.15 x margin), not
  its projected outline. Chase, side and lock turn only while the ground speed is above 0.5 m/s; below that the arm
  holds. Bank reads the first subject's roll from its rotation (FollowTarget only; meshes stay level). Ground
  clearance needs a world y-up `ground` query; the arm sweep against meshes is unchanged. A flyby station is placed
  without a sweep, so it can sit inside a mesh beside the path. Contract: docs/physics-framework.md, section 4.
- Sea level: `geoid` defaults to `'egm96'`, the EGM96 15-minute grid of `@margoengine/controls/geoid`, fetched (2,077,922
  bytes) the first time `heights` is read; `heights.seaLevel` is null until it is in, and stays null with a
  `geoid-error` event when the packed file is not installed (it is made by `scripts/geoid/pack-egm96.mjs` from NGA's
  WW15MGH.GRD, which the repository does not download for you). The lookup is bilinear between 15' nodes, within about
  0.1 m of NGA's own spline interpolation; heights are stored to 1 cm. EGM96 is a degree-360 model (about 55 km
  resolution): it misses short geoid features that EGM2008 resolves, by up to a metre or two in mountains. `orientation` is in the eye's ENU frame, so an
  orbit camera that is level at its centre shows a roll of about range / Earth radius (5e-4 rad at 3 km). The `compass`
  event follows the view heading. The hash keeps 7 decimal places of degrees (about 1 cm) and 0.01 m.
  `parseHash` treats a hash as untrusted: a field that is not finite or is out of range (latitude +-90, longitude and
  heading +-360, pitch +-90 degrees, height -1000 km to 4 equatorial radii, range above 0 up to 10 equatorial radii)
  gives null; range and pitch are then clamped to the controls' limits. Every view (setView, flyTo, restoreView) rejects
  a non-finite field, a latitude past +-PI/2 or a height outside that range with a `controls-arguments` RangeError.

### Overlay effects (`@margoengine/post/overlays`, 2026-11-25)

LDR PostStack stages on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer. Enforced: `opacity` 0..1, one of 14 blend modes, `maskRange` two
different numbers; Ramp 2..8 stops in rising order, `bias` and `gain` inside (0, 1); Grid `cellSize` 2..4096 and
`lineWidth` above 0 up to 4096; DepthView `near`/`far` at least 0 and different; TextureOverlay `scale` not 0. Blends
work on display values of the LDR stage, so HDR values are not blended. Gradients can band on wide 8-bit ramps (no
dither). TextureOverlay reads mip level 0 with bilinear filtering, so an image drawn far smaller than its size aliases;
its texture must be 2D and filterable, with straight alpha. An ImageBitmap is uploaded when `source` changes and must stay
open (a device restore uploads it again). One of each effect per stack. Entry
10,454 B gzip; core plus stage unchanged.

Material sort modes (`setMaterialSortModes`, `@margoengine/materials`, 2026-11-25): one setting per engine for opaque and for transparent material meshes, not one per layer mask; distance is measured to the mesh's first primitive origin, not its bounds; raw-shader, gltf/pbr model and sprite draws keep their own order. Accepted difference from PlayCanvas layers, which sort per layer. No core change; the materials root entry grows by the function's few bytes.
Texture download caps (`loadTexture`, `@margoengine/materials`, 2026-11-25): defaults stay 64 MiB and 16,777,216 decoded pixels; `maxBytes` and `maxPixels` raise or lower them per call (`maxBytes` on `loadKTX2Texture` too). `loadCubeTexture` takes both: `maxPixels` caps every face, `maxBytes` is one budget for all six faces (downloaded one after another; without it each face keeps 64 MiB and they download side by side). A device with a smaller `maxTextureDimension2D` still rejects the upload. `restoreMaterialLibrary` takes the caps only from its own `limits` option; a material file's texture options cannot set `maxBytes` or `maxPixels`.

## Sky depth and fir spray geometry

Automatic sky depth requires an active sampleable scene capture. An explicit callback selects another pass. Clouds
use the empty-sky depth test when no source is available. Fog needs a surface depth. Masked foliage participates
through its main-pass depth writes, including during a camera turn.

The optional `@margoengine/procedural/fir-sprays` entry accepts a height from 0.1 to 250 m, a crown base up to 95%
of the height, a radius from 0.01 to 100 m, and one to 64 normalized atlas regions. It returns three CPU geometry
levels with consistent main branch directions. Texture pixels and tree placement are supplied by the caller.
The optional entry measures 1,468 B gzip. Core and stage remain at 24,797 B gzip.

## Fixed terrain clipmap anchors

Terrain rings keep a world XZ anchor by default. Their outer extent is set by `cellSize`, `resolution`, and the ring
count, up to 12 levels. Choose an anchor and extent that cover the visible ground on a bounded camera route.
`BiomeView` shares one anchor for the world and horizon. Streaming terrain defaults to a moving selection on the world
lattice. Height data updates still change the surface by design.

## Alpine treeline placement

The optional Biomes treeline graph supports nominal elevations from -500 to 9,000 m, vertical transitions from 12
to 400 m, and world-space shelter patches from 20 to 2,000 m. Its density multipliers apply within the selected
species and biome envelopes. The artist supplies the local elevation and the cohort meshes.
The optional entry measures 4,407 B gzip with graph construction and validation. Core and stage remain at 24,797 B.

## Distant vegetation surface height

`BiomeView` keeps its distant forest and supplies a world-height raster of the actual terrain triangles. Its dimensions
match the source UVs and cap at 2,049 texels per side. The R32F target costs at most about 16 MiB. The half-float
compatibility tier uses RGBA16F at most about 32 MiB, with the precision of that format. LDR hardware uses the original
height field. Texels outside the drawn mesh retain the source height. The canopy density graph uses the world region grid.

Measured gzip before and after the grounding fix is 16,671 to 17,402 B for `@margoengine/terrain`, 13,366 to
14,072 B for `@margoengine/terrain/stream`, 3,089 to 3,539 B for `@margoengine/biomes/cover`, and 3,849 to 4,331 B
for `@margoengine/biomes/far`. Terrain's optional height capture reuses the active rings and their GPU buffers.
Biomes shares the placement graph evaluator between the near and far forests. Core and stage remain at 24,797 B.

The Biomes worker measures 40,935 B gzip and 108,708 B raw, up from the last recorded 40,763 and 108,185 B.
The extra bytes keep regional curvature and tile curvature in the same integer units and let the canopy task load
the existing graph part on first use. Keeping those calls in another part would still require the same sampler and
worker dispatch. The graph evaluator stays in its existing optional worker file.

On 2026-11-25 the worker measures 41,108 B gzip and 109,131 B raw, up from 40,935 and 108,708 B, and its test ceilings
are 41,200 and 109,300 B. The whole difference is each paint layer's own blend width (`PaintLayer.ecotone`,
`ec34c7f3be`): without it a 2 m painted hedge is averaged across the world's 24 m ecotone and almost vanishes. The
classification's paint feather runs on every tile a worker makes, so a separate worker file would be loaded by every
painted world.

## Terrain relief lighting (2026-11-23)

The optional relief-lighting entry adds 8 bytes per height sample for a filterable RGBA16F bake, about 8 MiB
for a 1,024×1,024 map. The heightmap is borrowed. One 48-byte uniform buffer is released after the submitted
bake finishes. Each bake takes up to 32 sky azimuths plus the directional sun and 256 samples per ray, bounded
by the configured radius and the heightmap edge. The lit draw adds one bilinear lookup. The bake captures a
single sun direction and a static heightmap. Changing either needs `rebake()`. A heightfield cannot represent
overhangs, and distant features between samples may be missed. No light is bounced from one slope to another (the
terrain-reflected term of Dozier and Frew 1990, "Rapid calculation of terrain parameters for radiation modeling from
digital elevation data", IEEE TGRS 28(5), https://doi.org/10.1109/36.58986), so a gully loses sky light and gains
nothing from the walls around it. `BiomeView`'s `relief` shades the world's terrain, not its horizon ring
(KB-BIOMES-HORIZONRELIEF1).

## Open-ocean horizon depth (2026-11-23)

Water with `horizon: true` keeps the scene far plane for its displaced grid. Its flat extension reaches 10,000 km
in each world-horizontal axis from the snapped grid center and covers only rays beyond the original far plane.
Depth there is reversed-Z zero, the same as the sky. It supports the existing Water colour and reflection passes.
It adds four vertices and six indices to the same draw and uses no new buffer, texture, pass or package option.
The horizon remains a flat ocean approximation. See [GPU evidence](architecture/operational-playbook.md#section-5-evidence-open-ocean-horizon-depth-2026-11-23).
Blob and planar shadows (`@margoengine/materials/fake-shadows`, 2026-11-25): the planar shadow projects on the CPU in `update` (cost grows with the caster's vertex count, so characters and props, not levels); it flattens onto one plane, does not follow terrain, and overlapping parts of one caster darken twice (translucent blend, no stencil); with a point light, keep the caster between the light and the plane. The blob is a vertex-alpha disc, not a blurred render of the caster's silhouette. Drawn pixels are checked on a real GPU, WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer (`node packages/materials/test/features-browser.mjs fakeShadows`, 2026-11-25): along a blob spoke every pixel is within 3 of 255 of 1 - opacity x the rings' alpha (measured within 0.5), and the planar shadow of a square under a directional and a point light covers exactly the footprint the light projects, at 1 - opacity. No core change.


## Grade tonal ranges (`@margoengine/tonemap/grade` `ranges`, 2026-11-25)

Enforced per range (global, shadows, midtones, highlights): hue 0..360, density 0..1, saturation 0..4, exposure -8..8
stops. Applied to display-linear 0..1 after the primaries and before the wheels, clamped after the gain and after the
saturation; the three tonal ranges mix by the wheels' luminance masks, which are not adjustable. The tint keeps the
luminance of a grey before clipping, not of a saturated colour, and a negative density is not accepted (turn the hue by
180). No settings-table rows. Compiled only while a range changes something. GPU frames are within 1.02 levels of a CPU
oracle on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer (`tests/grade-browser.mjs`). Measured min+gzip: grade 1,877 to 2,426 B, hue 2,596
to 3,158 B, export-cube 1,360 to 1,431 B, 3dl 2,367 to 2,434 B; core and stage source unchanged. Controls as named in
the Babylon.js `ColorCurves` API documentation (no source read), 2026,
https://doc.babylonjs.com/typedoc/classes/BABYLON.ColorCurves; the maths is Margo's own (HSV hexcone, A. R. Smith,
"Color Gamut Transform Pairs", SIGGRAPH 1978, https://doi.org/10.1145/800248.807361).
Scene helpers (`@margoengine/scene/helpers`, 2026-11-25): `worldBounds`, `center` and `resize` read every vertex of every mesh under the root on each call (call them when the model loads, not every frame); a mesh with no geometry is skipped, and `center` moves `root.position`, which is in the parent's space (equal to world space under an unrotated, unscaled parent). `resize` scales uniformly and multiplies `root.scale`. `float` writes `position.y` and the three rotation angles from the values the mesh had when it was created, so do not animate those yourself meanwhile. `InteractionPrompt` is timing only: you draw the hint. Accepted difference from drei: functions you call, not React components that re-render.

## Recorded frames as a texture (2026-11-25, GAP-FILM-VIDEOTEX)

`@margoengine/video/frames` `FrameVideo` takes straight-alpha sRGB RGBA8 frames from the caller, 1 to 16384 pixels a
side (the GPU's `maxTextureDimension2D` also limits it), and puts the frame of a film time in a materials `Texture`.
One frame is held on the CPU and one texture per device (mip chain included). Each new frame uploads the whole picture
and regenerates the chain; upload cost is not measured. It decodes no video: ffmpeg or another decoder gives the pixels.
Materials and glTF PBR meshes only. Measured: `packages/video/test/frames-gpu.mjs` (Node, WebGPU) reads four frames of
a 64 x 48 clip and a four-frame `renderFrames` sequence back within 1 level of the source, a seek back gives the same
bytes, and a quarter-size draw of a black and white checker reads 188 (the linear-light average);
`frames-check.mjs` draws the frames on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer within 2 levels, as a map and as a glowing screen.
UV transform centre (`uvTransform.center`, `@margoengine/materials`, 2026-11-25): applies to `new Material({ uvTransform })` and `setUVTransform`; it folds into the offset, so `transformUVs`, the atlas packer and `setUVTransformAt` on instances still take a plain `KHR_texture_transform` without `center`. Metaballs (`Metaballs`, `@margoengine/procedural`, 2026-11-25): each `geometry()` call re-polygonizes the whole grid on the CPU (resolution up to 128 per axis, the marching-cubes limit), so a 40-cube grid per frame is fine and a 128-cube grid is not; the pull is the finite-support cubic of Wyvill et al., not three.js's 1/d^2, so a ball's surface radius is under its `radius`.

### Thermal conduction (`@margoengine/physics/thermal`, FIRE-06)

The heat grid is Cartesian and cell-centred, with isotropic conductivity and piecewise constant sensible heat capacity. Phase change is isothermal and of fixed volume. Exterior faces support insulation, fixed temperature, convection using half-cell and film resistances in series, diffuse-grey radiation to fixed-temperature surroundings, and prescribed heat flux.

The solver and scratch regions occupy 144 bytes per cell, including the copy region for borrowed heat sources, and a 40-byte geometry record in world memory. Backward Euler adds 8 bytes of scratch per cell. A grid with radiating faces adds another 8 bytes per cell and 40 bytes per radiating face. The field registry adds its mirrors and any accumulated sources. The solver supports plain and shared Wasm memory with SIMD. Each native participant uses a 64 KiB stack plus alignment in world memory. Explicit grids also use a 56-byte job record and 32 bytes of work counters per participant, plus worker control words for shared execution. The decode and interior stencil are split across participant ranges. Radiation and accepted-state publication run in caller order. The solver chooses the world rate from the finite-volume diffusion bound and subdivides a tick when needed. The numerical limits follow the world's Wasm address space and the kernel's u32 subdivision count. Forward Euler uses a step diffusion number at most 1/2. Backward Euler subdivides above 2 to bound the stationary iteration's convergence rate. Very stiff large grids still need a scalable sparse solve. The optional entry measures 9,686 B gzip. Each of its two lazy Wasm builds measures 16,560 B raw and 6,945 B gzip. A browser without shared memory support loads the plain build.

Thermoelasticity solves quasistatic small-strain equilibrium in a bonded solid on the same Cartesian grid. Each
cell is decomposed into six tetrahedra, with a common per-cell temperature and isotropic elastic properties. The
solid takes prescribed nodal displacements and has zero traction on free surfaces. Coupling is one-way from the
heat grid. A supplied liquid-fraction field rejects any positive melt fraction. Plastic flow, fracture and stresses
within a fluid are outside this elastic model.

Before alignment and the registry's mirrors, the elastic solver uses 144 bytes per cell, or 152 when a melt field is registered, and 65 bytes per nodal degree
of freedom, and a 72-byte geometry record. The grid count is limited by the Wasm address space. A solve fails before
publishing new mechanical results when the residual remains above the requested tolerance after its iteration budget.

Heat haze accepts a temperature volume with the device's 3D texture dimension limit and one r32float texel per
cell. The field fades to ambient at its exterior sample centres. The optional path uses a single reference
wavelength, fixed local pressure, small-angle deflection along the camera ray, and the frame's existing colour
and opaque depth. The effect samples the displaced colour inside the frame. Off-screen background
and light paths that require large-angle or multiple refraction are outside this screen-space model. The heat-haze entry grows from 11,008 B to 13,299 B gzip for volume upload, ray integration and lifetime management.

The shared sparse solver for stiff heat grids, temperature-dependent material properties, mushy melting, melt convection and the original kiln and turbofan scene integrations remain open.

#### FIRE-06 gallium melting across a heated vertical plate

The 1986 gallium test measured the front after 3, 10 and 17 min at three heights in an 88.9 mm wide cavity. Conductivity and sensible and latent heat come from separate material references. Boundary and initial temperatures come from the experiment's apparatus. The production model predicts a height-invariant 30.67 mm front after 17 min. The measured bottom, middle and top sample distances are 23.7, 59.7 and 70.3 mm. Doubling the grid in the simulation plane shifts the front by at most 0.0112 mm across all times. Varying the reported initial undercooling from 1 to 2 K gives 30.35–30.99 mm at 17 min. One of nine sparse measured samples overlaps the grid and undercooling range plus the estimated 0.7 mm plot-reading allowance. The experiment shows buoyancy-driven flow that the thermal entry does not solve. The figure allowance represents extraction precision and the source gives no instrument uncertainty for these samples. [Gau and Viskanta (1986), Fig. 2(a)](https://doi.org/10.1115/1.3246884). [Meyer (2016), Figs. 5.7–5.8](https://publikationen.bibliothek.kit.edu/1000058183/3880102). [Diagnostic](../packages/physics/scripts/fire06-gallium-measured.mjs).


## Collective animal motion

`@margoengine/physics/schooling` uses a deterministic grid over local coordinates, with f64 distance and
field rows. A rank limit applies only to neighbours within the outer radius and the visible sector. The
model assumes a predator holds velocity over the prediction horizon. Dense groups or very large sensing
radii increase the number of candidates. The kernel uses world memory and a private per-instance arena region
for its stack, static data, and grid work. Its capacity grows with the number of configured members.
Membership and port layout stay fixed for a solver's lifetime. Use a fresh world setup for a different row layout.

The point-mass model represents inertial mass, thrust and quadratic drag. Its local curvature bound concerns
propulsive acceleration relative to the medium. A spatially varying current can also bend the trajectory.
Body bending, contact, wing lift, flap power and tail propulsion belong to the body solver. The intent
fixture verifies the field hand-off and a bank derived from lateral acceleration. The original film shots
still need playback checks.

The optional entry is 4,998 B gzip. The plain SIMD kernel is 4,464 B gzip (8,622 B raw). The shared variant is 4,523 B gzip (8,710 B raw).
That budget covers the field adapter and the point-mass mode in one import. Core and stage gain zero bytes.

## Rooted plant mechanics (BIO-01)

The optional vegetation kernel integrates two small-angle transverse modes about an upright root. The crown is a
mass and drag distribution along the stem. The model uses fixed geometry and has no branch hierarchy, axial motion,
finite-angle reconfiguration, growth or reciprocal flow. Fluid effects are integrated at three stations on the stem
and three on the crown. Plant roots and station coordinates translate into the sampled air or water field's signed
origin using the configured cell size. Negative density and unrepresentable finite differences are refused. The
sampled medium controls default added mass and buoyancy. Wind and water require separate plant solvers. Stem
rupture is checked at nine cross-sections and uprooting uses an authored limit.

The caller samples fluid and distributes independent plants across one to sixteen native partitions. Shared browser
execution needs an isolated world Worker. Each native phase writes candidates and reports actual work. The caller
commits accepted modal rows after all workers succeed. The dry uniform solution and signed-origin replay are checked.
Frame-zero rigid snapshots replay through the first impact and release.

Observed stripped and intact tree angular frequencies are 11.4 ± 0.5 and 3.78 ± 0.09 rad/s. The nominal modeled
frequencies are 11.93 and 7.10 rad/s. Separate geometry and stiffness sensitivity cases bring the stripped case
inside the observed spread. The intact case remains outside the tested range. Two measured wet blade excursions
of 5.0 and 175.0 mm compare to predicted 9.51 and 195.73 mm. Both stay outside the ±2 mm resolution estimate
across the input sensitivities. The equivalent section retains independently measured stiffness and loading
geometry. These cases exercise the small-angle model beyond its intended deflection range.

The optional Physics entry is 12,687 B min+gzip within a 13,068 B ceiling. Each slot-3 Wasm image is 7,951 B raw
and 2,974 B gzip. The Scatter test uses the existing optional adapter. Core and Stage gain no bytes.

`@margoengine/scatter/plant-motion` copies four modal displacements per plant to a 32-byte GPU record and maps
instances to one root per selected X/Z cell. Bin indices and displacement use float32 for rendering. The input
root and mesh pivot need to share a cell, and the rendered reach must fit Scatter's culling radius. A zero-strength
Scatter wind enables its existing doubled reach while the solver poses mapped roots. The normal transform
uses the derivative of the same displacement as the colour, depth and shadow geometry.

The rigid adapter uses a fixed standing trunk proxy, so the rigid impact sees a fixed obstacle until release. It
passes normal impulse to the bending modes at the stored contact heights. A released stem uses one authored rigid
geometry with the pose and velocity of its detached chord. Release needs a preallocated dynamic fragment at the
matching section height. Scatter can hide the entire failed instance when a separate body draws the fragment.

### Catchment runoff (HYDRO-02, 2026-11-25)

`@margoengine/physics/runoff` uses fixed directed drainage links and one active soil-water layer per cell.
The surface rating assumes a wide Manning section. Use the shallow-water solver for backwater, reversed flow
and two-dimensional inundation at an outlet. The next soil step takes up routed water left upstream or downstream
by the current routing step. Climate-only BiomeView flows use a quantized local climate representative of the
contributing area. Event hydrographs use the live field. Calibrated flood return periods must come from separate
hydraulic runs or from measurements.

Green-Ampt uses one wetting front per cell. Interstorm drying attenuates remembered wetting-front
depth in proportion to remaining soil storage. Layered soil profiles and physically resolved
redistribution remain open. The topographic index reduces local available soil storage and a linear
reservoir supplies deep drainage. The receiving shallow-water solver takes the outlet hydrograph.
Backwater feedback to upslope storage remains open. A nonfinite candidate does not publish.

The optional worker path partitions the native rain, snowmelt and soil stage. The topographic
means, per-cell budget fold and downstream graph retain serial order. Thread scratch uses five
f64 words per cell and a dedicated stack per helper. A single-threaded world can advance in a
browser window. Shared threads use Node or a cross-origin-isolated browser worker. Work counts
describe the executed grid visits. Wall-clock throughput is unmeasured.

The optional runoff entry is 7,105 B min+gzip under a 7,192 B ceiling. Lazy SIMD Wasm images are
23,699 B plain and 23,787 B shared raw, or 6,427 and 6,489 B gzip. Water's inland surface is
1,716 B gzip under its 1,962 B ceiling. Core and Stage gain zero bytes.

### Aquatic locomotion (`@margoengine/physics/life`, LIFE-03)

The linearly implicit swimmer treats mass and inertia as an ellipsoid with semi-empirical resistance and
potential-flow strip added mass. It represents slender-body tail propulsion, pectoral steering and sculling,
free-surface crossing and stationary control in an ambient flow. Local sea elevation and slope determine wet
volume and its centroid. Added inertia scales with wetted fraction. The solver samples one material acceleration
at the submerged centroid. Wave breaking, slamming, a resolved vortex wake and muscle bodies remain open.

The default feedback ceiling follows the fast envelope from Sánchez-Rodríguez, Raufaste and Argentina (2023)
with fitted parameters 22 Hz, 0.4 m and curvature 4. It is a population envelope. Set an explicit
`maximumFrequency` when species, swim mode or measurement calls for another limit. Open-loop control uses the
authored frequency. Form drag still defaults to a coefficient of 0.1 times frontal area. Induced fin drag and
large-amplitude propulsion remain open. The analytic cap check does not validate reached speed.

Native SIMD pairs X/Y components of the diagonal linear and angular updates. Workers split the body rows,
including passive-reaction rows when enabled. The caller samples water, sets control, checks native receipts and
commits the fields. Multiple partitions need shared world memory, with an isolated world Worker in a browser.
The default uses one partition. Position and wake fields carry the solver's signed origin. Work receipts report
the last accepted tick and are outside snapshots. The passive-water receiver was exercised with a shared origin.

The three independent juvenile rainbow trout trials reach 0.253, 0.421 and 0.541 m/s against 0.22, 0.48 and
0.74 m/s observed. The predicted Strouhal numbers are 0.324, 0.316 and 0.310. Mass, height, width and tail span
could not be recovered for each specimen. The highest observed speed remains outside the geometry sensitivity
range. Removing form drag alone still underpredicts it by 12.8%. The full measured-range check remains open.

The optional Physics entry measures 10,214 B gzip within a 10,482 B ceiling. The plain and shared Wasm
files are 7,666 and 7,757 B raw, and 4,277 and 4,340 B gzip. Core and Stage gain no bytes.

## Falling plates, winged seeds and hail (AERO-05)

The plate model uses the 2005 Andersen, Pesavento and Wang quasi-steady coefficients for the intermediate-Re
measurements (about 100–1,000). It represents an elliptical cross section, a fixed rotation axis and a separate
spanwise drag term. The autorotating wing model resolves three translation axes and spin about a fixed axis.
The authored wing strips have rigid pitch and coning is zero. Airflow is sampled once per body per world tick at
the predicted midpoint. The fluid is prescribed and neither model reconstructs the shed wake.

Sphere contact is one-way against fixed, nonsensor geometry. The swept chord approximates the curved path over
one world tick, and contact applies normal restitution without a tangential friction law. Plates and seeds are
airborne models. Shape casts and Hail drawing use float32 in their respective coordinate frames. The physics
solver has f64 state and uses local dyadic RK4 substeps with a relative/absolute defect target of 1e-8.
The kernel requires Wasm SIMD. Its plain and shared variants occupy static window slot 7, with per-instance stacks.

The optional Hail source reads one 32-byte vertex-storage record per visible stone on WebGPU. The batch is
created at setup. Supply a world-scale placement and advance the world before rendering. Camera-wrapped
emission, chip splashes and collision-driven emission are independent effects. The world-stepped draw uses
the supplied diameter, positions and velocities.

Two independent Norway maple drop studies test the sycamore-based fixed-axis model. The solver predicts
0.776 and 0.723 m/s against observed means and sample spreads of 1.00 ± 0.10 and 1.10 ± 0.24 m/s.
The predicted spin rates are 21.11 and 14.97 Hz against 16 ± 5 and 12.96 ± 4.39 Hz. Refining the
blade strips and solver step does not resolve either speed gap. Varying the measured wing loading
over its published spread leaves both speeds low. The model does not resolve the observed 12 ± 5°
cone in the first study. [Ortega-Jimenez et al. (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsif.2018.0456).
[Nave et al. (2021)](https://doi.org/10.3390/biomimetics6020023).

The optional falling entry measures 8,693 B min+gzip with an 8,954 B ceiling. Each unchanged lazy Wasm
build measures 10,501 B raw and 4,498 B gzip. Accepted pose preparation adds one 104 B scratch row per body.
Draw preparation adds one 32 B scratch row per sphere. The Hail overlay measures 5,443 B and its optional
world adapter 1,056 B min+gzip. Core and stage receive zero bytes.

### Moist convection and resolved cloud extinction (ATMO-03)

The MAC pressure correction solves a closed homogeneous-Neumann grid. Relative L2 residual is bounded at
1e-10 over at most 400 PCG iterations. The implementation also recomputes divergence of the corrected faces
with a binary64 roundoff bound. If the solve fails or the temperature, moisture or exported rain is unrepresentable,
the candidate state and atmospheric clock are discarded. One world tick or one rain sedimentation interval accepts
at most 4096 explicit substeps. The grid cap bounds the accepted and candidate transport state plus the pressure
workspace. Re-record snapshots created before the accepted mean wind and projection diagnostics were stored.

The scalar constructor and optional native projection share the same Boussinesq cloud model. Only the Neumann
stencil is partitioned. The advection, warm-rain closure, sedimentation and ordered PCG reductions run on the caller.
The optional Physics entry measures 11,523 B gzip within 11,799 B. Environment density-volume
measures 5,140 B gzip within 5,396 B. The plain and shared Wasm files load separately at 1,814 B raw and
943 B gzip each. Neither Physics nor Environment adds bytes to Core or Stage.

`CloudDensityVolume` converts the accepted liquid-water mixing ratio into extinction using constant dry-air density
and droplet effective radius within the supplied box. It uses cell-centred interpolation and the Environment volume
march. The fixed-frame fixture uses a live boundary-layer wind. The separate procedural Sky route, original film
installation, ice microphysics, terrain lift, conserved scalar transport, anelastic motion and independent measurement
remain open. The idealised Bryan–Fritsch benchmark and observed RICO or ARM cloud fields require complete input
soundings and forcing that this tier does not yet accept.

### Surface-layer wind and native registry grid (ATMO-01)

The resolved surface layer uses an authored roughness and an independent stability length. Reported
altitude and temperature follow dry standard air. The mean profile is for the atmospheric surface
layer. Above the finite gust box, only that mean and the standard atmosphere are supplied.
The taper prevents vertical periodic repetition and enforces zero disturbance at the roughness
height. Its post-processed velocities are not a projected divergence-free field. Greater horizontal
extent needs a correspondingly longer box or separately authored regions.

The optional Physics grid stores five f64 values per sample in X/Y/Z index order, one accepted state
and one candidate. A frozen Mann field stores three f64 planes. Continuous Wind queries use a private
one-row native pass at arbitrary finite signed time. They do not step the registry grid. The browser
thread path joins on the world Worker under cross-origin isolation. State and probe rows use local
coordinates and exact origin cell metadata. Boundaries, positions, parameter values and non-finite
results are checked before the field is accepted.

At 49 MOSAiC times the higher sensors provide 98 held-out wind readings. With an external roughness
and only the lower wind and stability as inputs, top-sensor RMS is 0.382 m/s for stable, 0.500 m/s for
unstable and 0.615 m/s for near neutral profiles. With independent lower-level friction velocity
the values are 0.262, 0.382 and 0.405 m/s. Per-record uncertainty in the supplied flux and stability
remains unavailable. The use of a flat surface layer leaves terrain effects and flow feedback open.
[Measured MOSAiC archive](https://doi.org/10.18739/A2PV6B83F)

The optional Physics entry is 5,604 B gzip within a 5,769 B ceiling. The Weather entry is 3,408 B gzip
within a 3,664 B ceiling. Each Wasm variant is 11,852 B raw and 4,483 B gzip. Neither entry adds bytes
to Physics World, Core or Stage.

### Sediment transport and bed change (HYDRO-03, 2026-11-25)

`@margoengine/physics/sediment` works on one co-located rectangular TerrainBed and shallow-water grid. It uses a
representative bed diameter and a representative suspended diameter for dilute transport. The bank model uses
bank-parallel velocity relative to the depth-weighted, connected wet band perpendicular to each wet/dry face.
The signed mean establishes the downstream direction. A single wet cell across the channel or a band with no
net tangent discharge gives no resolved bank perturbation. Rotated banks follow their Cartesian faces. Optional
root pressure reduces exchange. Mixed grains, secondary circulation and natural meander rates remain open.
The vertex reserve covers the mobile layer the caller declares. Set it to the bedrock clearance when TerrainBed
has a floor. Fluid momentum and bed evolution exchange one field update per world tick. An open boundary exports
sediment. External inflow at that edge carries clear water. Flood and ShallowWaterSurface tint require their
source's own rectangle and cell order. ShallowWaterSurface uploads the accepted concentration once per draw
through Water's existing tint effect. The renderer expects a finite float32 concentration in kg/m³ and uses
its existing optical concentration range. The floor and the live bed control available physical geometry.

Native shared workers split cell preparations and proposed face fluxes. Sediment movement through shared
vertices, donor accounting and budgets retain their canonical order. Scratch changes are accepted only after
native arithmetic, mass inventory and float32 publication checks. Counts report actual cell and face visits
from the previous accepted tick and are independent of snapshots. Threaded browser worlds require shared
memory and execution outside the Window thread.

Eleven independently measured sediment capacities at two slopes were 3.48 to 4.40 times the native prediction
with the independently prescribed rectangular-channel flow and grain properties. The source provides no
per-capacity measurement uncertainty. The comparison does not simulate the experiment's sediment feed or
subsequent aggradation. [Eslami and Radice (2025)](https://doi.org/10.5194/esurf-13-437-2025) ·
[Measured capacities](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.14883164)

The optional sediment entry is 7,963 B gzip under an 8,101 B ceiling.
The plain and shared SIMD Wasm are 19,505/19,596 B raw and 7,606/7,667 B gzip.
Water's optional shallow-surface mirror is 3,003 B gzip under a 3,259 B ceiling.
Core and Stage gain zero bytes.

### Pedestrian contact and crowd motion (LIFE-05)

`@margoengine/physics/pedestrians` models horizontal translation, finite shoulder turn rate, and
a specified ground height. Its uniformly oriented ellipses give an analytic projected footprint.
An approximate support along the line of centres is used for ellipse pairs. It computes the normal
and sliding impulse once per broadphase pair in canonical order. The density response is locally
compressible. The open approach uses the measured time-to-collision power law with a finite reaction
offset. The solver raises the dyadic rate so ideally dt·√(2k/m)≤1/2 for the lightest body and travel
per tick stays inside half the shortest footprint radius. Multi-floor surfaces use separate groups or
walkable route guidance with a height sampler. Injury, fall and ragdoll transitions use external
consumers of the force/pose ports. Doorway and terrain fixtures use simulated actors and route geometry.
The optional JavaScript entry is 7,275 B gzip against a 7,531 B ceiling. The plain Wasm is 12,620 B raw
and 6,086 B gzip. The shared Wasm is 12,708 B raw and 6,146 B gzip. Both use the existing static slot for
Rust's sort metadata and have a separate stack per native participant. Core and stage receive zero bytes.

The candidate movement, route cursor and projected ground publication are staged together. The two optional
worker phases partition drive and wall/integration rows. Pair order, spatial sort and encounter and density
accumulation retain their original serial order. The opted-in workers use the same arithmetic and states
as the caller.

The execution descriptor is 56 B plus 40 B per participant for work. The existing Wasm static slot has
884 B of Rust metadata in plain memory and 888 B in shared memory. Each participant uses its own
65,544 B stack plus the pool control block. Re-instantiation in the existing slot preserves the same bytes.

#### LIFE-05 measured single-file walking

Seyfried et al. report station-mean speeds of 1.24, 0.90 and 0.56 m/s with 1, 15 and 20 participants in their
17.3 m loop. Using the original 1.34 m/s free-speed default, the production crowd gives about 1.318 m/s
in all three cases. At 15 and 20 walkers the absolute misses are 0.418 and 0.758 m/s. Corresponding count-based
station means are 0.821 and 1.095 people/m, compared with 0.77 and 1.07 people/m from the manual fractional
estimator. The experiment used a 2 m station. An unreported bend profile is reconstructed from the recorded
lengths and widths. Doubling wall resolution changes the estimate by under 0.00004 m/s. A second
bend profile changes the 20-person result by about 0.016 m/s. The model lacks a validated steady headway-speed
relationship for following at equal velocity. No reported speed sets any input or parameter. [Seyfried et al. 2005](https://doi.org/10.1088/1742-5468/2005/10/P10002)

### Landscape evolution (HYDRO-04)

`LandscapeEvolution` uses one rectangular TerrainBed, a linear stream-power slope exponent and a fixed downhill
graph within each step. Closed depressions trap incoming sediment. Route floodwater, lake overtopping and rapid
flows with the shallow-water solver. Specified open edges supply fixed elevations and accept fluvial export. Hillslope and thermal exchange stop at these edges. The analytic open-parabola comparison records the resulting missing diffusive outflow.

The solver can estimate equilibrium Manning depth or consume a time-averaged shear field. Its independently
transported size classes share one bed porosity. The model tracks changing loose material and parent fractions,
with no hiding or exposure correction between grain classes. Thermal erosional transfer uses a parameterised
repose slope and coefficient. Weathering rates and rooted cohesion vary by terrain and must be supplied for
site predictions. The loose sediment field excludes material brought by external bed writers unless it is
initially supplied.

Bed changes are accrued in f64 and become TerrainBed elevations on the following tick. The geometry used to
choose downhill directions comes from the shared f32 bed field. A native candidate that exceeds the finite volume or rate range, or would publish a height outside TerrainBed's float32 range, is rejected before its state and contribution are accepted.
The biomes snapshot rounds the current terrain
to millimetres and keeps the relief's authored river lines. Use fixed boundary elevations if a snapshot must join
unchanged terrain outside the simulated rectangle.

The optional Physics and Biomes landscape entries measure 4,347 B and 614 B min+gzip respectively. The
plain and shared SIMD files are 12,166 B and 12,254 B before HTTP compression.

Shared workers partition the native per-vertex rainfall, uplift and drainage preparation. Uplift
sums keep their cell order. The graph's downstream order and its incision, transport and hill
exchange retain their serial ordering. Worker scratch needs one job, a receipt and a stack
per helper. The receipts describe work and stay outside snapshots. Throughput is unmeasured.

The optional physics entry is 7,653 B gzip under a 7,764 B ceiling. The Biomes adapter is 739 B gzip under 870 B. Optional plain/shared Wasm is
42,179/42,267 B raw and 11,467/11,530 B gzip. Core and Stage gain zero bytes.

### Utility passes (`@margoengine/post`: `kawase-blur`, `lut1d`, `color-average`, `depth-downsample`, 2026-11-25)

WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer. KawaseBlur: an HDR PostStack stage; `levels` 1..8, `offsets` 1..32 values of 0..64,
`scale` 0..8, `resolutionScale` 0.0625..1; not an exact Gaussian (the presets match its sigma within 15% up to
`very-large`), small bright points can flicker at a low working size, its `texture` is the reduced image of the last view
drawn. LUT1D: 2..65536 entries, linear interpolation, input clamped to the domain, display values only (use
`Tonemap.setLUT` for 3D and HDR-side grading); a texture source must have a linear format. ColorAverage: display values;
the overlay blend modes. DepthDownsample: single-sample reversed-Z source, output from 1/16 of the source size up to it;
`'representative'` is the median of at most 4 x 4 texels of the footprint; reading the stack's resolved depth needs an
order after 30. GPU cost of none of them measured.

### Render graph (`@margoengine/post/render-graph`, 2026-11-26)

WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer. Description `version` 1 only. At most one `scene` task; a graph with one must write
`'screen'`. One writer per texture; `'screen'` is an output only, never HDR or depth. Post effect tasks
(`effectTask`) draw at the canvas size, so their textures must be canvas-sized, and one effect class runs once per
graph (effects are plugins with fixed names). History textures swap once a frame, so with several views in a frame
all views share one history. A `clear` of the screen in a later view of a multi-view frame loads instead. Transient
textures share a GPU texture only with the same format and size. Not alongside a PostStack. Task order is
topological with description order breaking ties; tasks whose outputs nobody reads still run. GPU cost not measured.

### Trail texture (`@margoengine/post/trail`, 2026-11-26)

WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer. `size` 1 to the device's maxTextureDimension2D per side, fixed at construction;
`rgba16float`, one value in all four channels. At most 4,096 stamps a frame (`TRAIL_MAX_STAMPS`); later ones that frame
are dropped. `interpolate` caps the joining stamps at 256 per `move`, so a move longer than 128 radii is joined with
wider spacing. Speed is the frame's whole path length over its delta, the same weight for every move of the frame.
Texels below 1/1024 are set to 0 so the trail reaches black. Brushes are round in texels and drawn whole across the
texture edge (no wrapping). GPU cost not measured.

### Mesh blending (`@margoengine/post/mesh-blend`, 2026-11-26)

WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer; an HDR PostStack effect. Core meshes (a tag on a parent covers its child meshes),
gltf/pbr models, materials meshes and terrain can be tagged; other plugin-drawn surfaces (imposters, particles, water)
take part only as the untagged side of a seam. Keys are entity id + 1 in two float16-exact halves; a tagged model
takes a key counted down from 4,194,303, one per tag (65,536 before they repeat), so entity ids must stay below
4,128,767 for the two ranges to stay apart. Radii up to 65,504 world units. The tag pass redraws every core mesh, and
each tagged model and terrain through its capture hook with its own material (alpha masks, skinning and morphs as
drawn), once per view at 1x into an `rgba16float` target with its own `depth32float`; changing a model's radius
compiles its capture shader again. The radius table is 256 texels wide, one `r32float` per entity slot, rewritten each
frame. One seam per pixel: the nearest of at
most 4 candidates on the search spiral that passes the depth test; where three surfaces meet the nearest wins. The
search reaches `maxPixels` (128 at most), so a radius wider on screen is cut. A tag pass surface counts where its
depth matches the resolved scene depth within 0.2% and one pixel's depth span; a pixel whose centre holds no
matching surface borrows a neighbour's tag whose depth matches within 0.2% and that neighbour's own span, so a seam can
shift by a pixel. At mesh
corners the spiral sampling leaves a faint speckle at the edge of the radius. GPU cost not measured.

### Spatial upscaler (`@margoengine/post/upscale`, 2026-11-26)

Optional post/upscale is 5,110 B min+gzip (5,068 B as a new entry, previously 0 B; 2026-11-27 it holds the shared depth give-back of KB-XR-AREFFECTS1); core + stage unchanged. WebGPU and the WebGL2
layer. `scale` 0.25 to 1 per axis (default 0.67), `sharpen` 0 to 1 (default 0.8). One frame only: no history, so it
cannot add detail the render size lacks, and it does not anti-alias; feed it MSAA or TAA output. One full-canvas view
is upscaled; a frame of several views, a partial rectangle or a view into a target is drawn at full size. Runs instead
of TAAUpscale. Passes from order -75 to 45 run at render size; plugins after 45 draw over the full frame without the
scene's depth. Values above 1 are upscaled (clamped to the four nearest render pixels' range) but not sharpened.
A linear frame (float or -srgb format)
is encoded to sRGB for the filters and decoded after. Costs a render-size colour and depth target (plus 4x MSAA
attachments when the frame is multisampled) and one output-size colour texture. The shaders match the CPU twin
(packages/post/test/upscale-math.js) within 2 of 255 codes on WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer (8-bit rounding of the
intermediate). GPU cost not measured (build phase).

### Image filter graph (`@margoengine/post/filter-graph`, 2026-11-26)

WebGPU and the WebGL2 layer. At most 256 blocks a graph, aggregates 8 deep, 8 images and 32 params a block; `scale`
above 0 up to 4; `size` 1 to 16384 and every pass within the device's maxTextureDimension2D; a pass reads at most
`maxSampledTexturesPerShaderStage` textures; one fused `'texel'` read along any chain of a pass (a second starts a
new pass, which keeps shader size linear); a `'texel'` input is meant for one read a pixel, since a fused producer
runs again at each call. Images are uploaded as `rgba8unorm`, straight alpha, display (sRGB) values; intermediates are `rgba16float`. Merged and unmerged output differ by at most 1 of 255 per channel in 8-bit
output. By design: a block read with filtering (`'sample'`) is not substituted into its reader, so it costs a pass,
because evaluating it at the reader's coordinates would not equal filtering its texture; a block with two readers is
drawn once into a texture rather than computed twice; blocks are written in WGSL; there is no visual editor. A graph's
wiring, scales and constants are fixed when the runtime is made (values and `enabled` are live). `read` takes `rgba8unorm` or `bgra8unorm` output. After a device loss, borrowed
textures and closed `VideoFrame`s are gone: set them again. Video and camera input need a page
(`HTMLVideoElement`); in a worker pass `VideoFrame`s to `setImage`. GPU cost not measured.

## Contact and modal sound (SOUND-04)

Modal material presets contain authored resonances for a wood object, metal object, glass object and bell.
Use measured modes and gains for a specific object. Each rigid radiator uses one bank with effective
point-independent gain. The mono output is dry normalized PCM with linear superposition. Use a listener
for spatial transfer and a mixer for headroom. The snapshot includes the retained sample history.

Rigid contacts use the total normal impulse for a step, the last manifold's point weights, and relative
motion at those points. Impacts use the pre-step approach speed. A contact that forms and disappears
between published rigid steps may lack point data. With the current rigid interface, transients are
placed at the first sample of the observed range. Source timing is bounded by one rigid step on a matched
clock. The scrape and roll spectra use effective roughness profiles. Acoustic microcontact feedback, exact
geometry-dependent roughness, and elastic radiation into the room require additional field models.
The optional joint route computes equivalent scalar fracture excitation from supplied energy and mass.
A brittle-fracture producer can publish per-track excitation in the same field layout.

Each native participant renders disjoint whole tracks and preserves authored mode order within a track.
One track is one work unit. The plain and shared Wasm builds use the same f64 SIMD complex recurrence.
World memory holds 96 bytes per mode, 544 bytes per track for the surface states, drive and track job,
two PCM block banks at 8 bytes per block-capacity sample and a history ring at 4 bytes per retained sample
per track. This excludes registry mirrors, the 72 bytes of clock and history metadata and kernel working
records. Native work uses a 16-byte batch record, 32 bytes of counters and a 64 KiB stack plus alignment
per participant, and control words in shared mode. A port must match the sound solver's signed cell.
A rejected batch leaves the last accepted state, PCM and clock intact.

The optional entry measures 11,973 bytes gzip. Its plain and shared Wasm files each measure 2,470 bytes
raw and 1,299 bytes gzip. Native assets load on demand.

### SOUND-04 simply supported aluminum plates

The published plate dimensions and separate 6061-T6 material inputs give ideal Kirchhoff–Love frequencies
for six modes on each of two plates. The diagnostic feeds these predictions into the audio-rate resonator
and reads them back from production PCM. Doubling the sample rate from 24 to 48 kHz moves the inferred
frequencies at most 0.000031 Hz. The two calculated fundamentals are 89.05 and 135.21 Hz. The measured
speaker readings are 92.4 and 141.4 Hz, and the hammer readings are 90.4 and 139.8 Hz. Across 24 measurements,
maximum discrepancies are 14.19 Hz in absolute terms and 6.31% in relative terms, at distinct modes. Only five
readings overlap the bands for published rounding and PCM readout. The paper gives no total measurement
uncertainty and its two methods disagree by up to 20.5 Hz. None of those measurements sets the predictions.
The solver accepts frequencies as inputs. This comparison bounds the supplied thin-plate model plus runtime
frequency readout. Geometry-dependent modes, pressure transfer, gains and decay still require separate evidence.
[Dumond et al. (2019), Tables 3–5](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mex.2019.09.023).
[Leissa (1969)](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19700009156).
[Diagnostic](../packages/physics/scripts/sound04-modes-measured.mjs).

### Radiation fog and cold-air pooling (ATMO-08)

The shallow layer resolves one vertical bulk temperature, velocity and droplet population per ground column.
Ambient pressure, the background wind and external surface fluxes are held per coupling step. The longwave
model adds grey liquid-water opacity to a prescribed dry background. Its fixed grey option remains available.
Temperature stratification, droplet spectra, aerosol activation, mixed phases and spectral radiation remain open.
